title: encyclopedia article|a species of freshwater turtle and its conservation status
text:
The Yangtze giant softshell turtle (Rafetus swinhoei) is a critically endangered species of freshwater turtle in the family Trionychidae, distinguished by its large, flattened, leathery shell and broad, pig-like snout. Adults may reach shell lengths of over 100 centimeters and weights exceeding 100 kilograms, making it one of the largest freshwater turtles in the world. Its carapace is typically deep olive or gray-green with faint mottling, while the underside is pale; the shell lacks the hard scutes found in most turtles and instead has a flexible, rubbery texture adapted for life in slow-moving rivers, marshes, and large lakes.

Historically, the species inhabited the Yangtze River basin and associated waterways in eastern and southern China, including Lake Tai and the Red River delta of northern Vietnam. It was once recorded across Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Anhui, and Yunnan provinces, as well as in parts of Laos. As a benthic ambush predator, it feeds on fish, crustaceans, mollusks, frogs, and aquatic vegetation, spending much of its time partially buried in soft sediment. Females nest on sandy riverbanks, laying clutches of dozens of round eggs during the warmer months. Juveniles occupy shallow, vegetated wetlands before moving into deeper river channels.

Taxonomically, Rafetus swinhoei was first formally described in 1873 by the British zoologist John Edward Gray, based on specimens collected near Shanghai. For decades it was confused with related softshell species, and several regional populations were only recognized as belonging to R. swinhoei through later morphological and genetic studies. It belongs to a small genus whose other living member, the Euphrates softshell turtle, occurs thousands of kilometers away in West Asia, a disjunct distribution that reflects ancient climatic and drainage changes.

The conservation status of the Yangtze giant softshell turtle is among the most precarious of any reptile. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists the species as Critically Endangered, and many specialists regard it as functionally extinct in the wild. Surveys during the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries found that populations had collapsed because of exploitation for food and traditional medicine, widespread wetland destruction, dam construction, sand mining, river channelization, water pollution, and the loss of undisturbed nesting beaches. Its large size, predictable basking and nesting habits, and high market value made it especially vulnerable to overharvesting. Even after legal protection, accidental capture and degraded habitats continued to suppress recovery.

By the 2000s, only a handful of individuals were known. A famous male lived for many years at Suzhou Zoo in China alongside a female transferred from Changsha Zoo in a coordinated captive-breeding attempt. Although the pair mated and eggs were produced, none hatched successfully, and the female died following an artificial insemination procedure in 2019. The Suzhou male, long considered the last confirmed Chinese individual, died in 2023. In Vietnam, animals of profound cultural significance are associated with Hoan Kiem Lake in Hanoi, where a large individual known locally as Cu Rua died in 2016. Since then, conservationists have focused on confirming reports from remote reservoirs and river sections, and one surviving turtle in Dong Mo Lake near Hanoi has been intensively monitored.

Recovery efforts combine environmental DNA sampling, local interviews, fishery bycatch reduction, nesting-site protection, and attempts to locate a reproductively viable population. Captive technology, including semen collection, ultrasound monitoring, and carefully managed artificial incubation, may help if additional males and females can be brought together. However, with the number of confirmed individuals effectively at one or fewer, the species serves as a stark indicator of the decline of Asian freshwater turtle diversity and the urgency of protecting large-river ecosystems before extinction becomes irreversible.

Dear Valued Shareholders,

On behalf of the board of directors and leadership team of GreenHarvest Regional Grocers, I am writing to share a comprehensive review of fiscal 2024, a landmark year defined by deliberate, community-centered expansion that has strengthened our position as the leading neighborhood grocery provider across the Upper Midwest. When we laid out our three-year strategic plan in 2022, we committed to growing our footprint without compromising the core values that set us apart: locally sourced inventory, fair wages for team members, and accessible, affordable fresh food for the communities we serve. This year, we delivered on that promise, generating record top-line growth while laying a durable foundation for long-term value creation.

Fiscal 2024 total revenue reached $892 million, a 17% increase from the prior year, driven by 12 new store openings across Minnesota, Wisconsin, and northern Iowa, and a 6% lift in same-store sales from existing locations. Unlike many national chains that prioritize high-traffic suburban corridors, our expansion targeted underserved rural and mid-sized urban neighborhoods identified as food deserts by regional public health agencies, where 38% of residents previously lacked access to a full-service grocery store within a 1-mile radius. Each new location created an average of 42 local jobs, with starting wages 22% above state minimums, and reserved 30% of shelf space for produce, dairy, and packaged goods from regional family farms and small food producers, a commitment that drove $78 million in revenue for local supply partners this year. We also expanded our zero-cost home delivery program for low-income seniors and households with disabilities, now serving 21,000 households across our footprint, a 45% increase from 2023.

Our expansion was supported by targeted capital investments that improved operational efficiency and customer experience. We completed a 120,000 square foot expansion of our regional distribution center in Rochester, Minnesota, cutting last-mile delivery time to stores by 18% and reducing food waste by 23% through upgraded cold storage infrastructure, directly supporting our goal to cut operational food waste in half by 2027. We also rolled out our updated GreenHarvest Rewards program across all locations, which now has 1.2 million active members, allowing us to tailor promotions to local shopping preferences and pass additional savings to regular customers. Importantly, this growth did not come at the cost of financial stability: we maintained a strong balance sheet with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.42, well within our target range, and generated $68 million in operating cash flow to fund ongoing expansion and shareholder returns. This year, we increased our quarterly dividend by 8%, marking the 11th consecutive year of dividend growth for our investors.

We do not underestimate the headwinds facing the grocery sector, from persistent supply chain volatility to rising utility and labor costs, and we know that expansion brings new operational challenges as we integrate new team members and align new stores with our service standards. In the year ahead, we plan to open 9 additional locations, expand our private label product line to offer more low-cost, high-quality staple goods, and pilot an in-store health clinic partnership with regional healthcare providers to offer free blood pressure screenings and nutrition education to customers. None of this progress would have been possible without the dedication of our 7,200 team members, the trust of our customers, and your continued support as shareholders. We entered 2025 as a stronger, more connected company, and we remain committed to growing in a way that delivers value for investors, team members, and the communities we are proud to serve.

Sincerely,
Margaret Hale
Chief Executive Officer
GreenHarvest Regional Grocers

title: encyclopedia article|the life and career of a nineteenth-century railway engineer
text:
Sir John Hawkshaw (1811–1891)

John Hawkshaw was born on 9 April 1811 at Leeds, Yorkshire, the son of John Hawkshaw, a carrier with connections to the Aire and Calder Navigation, and his wife Sarah. Educated at Leeds Grammar School and then under the Rev. Charles Frazer at Hedon near Hull, he left school at fourteen and joined the staff of the road surveyor of the West Riding. In 1830 he became pupil and later assistant to Charles Fowler, engineer of the Calder and Hebble Navigation, where he gained experience of masonry, excavation and hydraulic works before moving in 1833 to supervise mining and railway surveys in Venezuela for the Bolivar Mining Association.

Tropical fever forced Hawkshaw's return in 1834, and the following year he was appointed resident engineer under Jesse Hartley on the Manchester, Bolton and Bury Canal Navigation and Railway. In 1839 he surveyed the line from Manchester to Leeds for the Manchester and Leeds Railway, and in 1845 he succeeded Thomas Gooch as its chief engineer. His 1846–50 reconstruction of the difficult summit section through the Pennines—including the 2,869 yd Summit Tunnel between Littleborough and Walsden, opened in 1841—demonstrated his command of heavy earthworks, tunnelling and gradient design. Hawkshaw argued early and forcefully against George Stephenson's preference for easy gradients and costly detours, maintaining that well-located steeper gradients served traffic more economically.

During the railway mania Hawkshaw built a substantial Westminster consulting practice, later Hawkshaw, Hayter and Hawshaw. He was engineer to parts of the Lancashire and Yorkshire, East Lancashire, London, Brighton and South Coast, Great Eastern, and Great Northern systems, and to the Charing Cross and Cannon Street lines in London. His bridges over the Thames at Charing Cross (1864) and Cannon Street (1866), with their paired wrought-iron bowstring girders carried on cast-iron cylinders, became familiar elements of the Victorian riverscape. He also designed the 850 ft Severn Tunnel, begun in 1873 and opened for goods in 1886 after prolonged inundations from the "Great Spring"; its completion was widely regarded as the outstanding feat of late-Victorian tunnelling.

Hawkshaw's practice extended well beyond Britain. He advised on railways in India, Mauritius, Germany, Russia, the Netherlands and Egypt, and in 1862 reported on the proposed Suez Canal at the request of the Khedive, contributing materially to confidence in the scheme. He served as president of the Institution of Civil Engineers in 1862–63, was elected FRS in 1855, knighted in 1873, and made a knight commander of the Order of St Michael and St George in 1879. In 1835 he married Ann Jackson (d. 1886), whose diary of their Venezuelan years was later printed for private circulation. Hawkshaw died at his London home, 33 Belgrave Road, on 2 June 1891, survived by a son and two daughters, and was buried at Bramott near Sevenoast. Remembered less for flamboyant public profile than for rigorous calculation and perseverance in adverse ground, he linked the heroic early railway age with the later era of large-scale imperial and metropolitan engineering.

Section 3: Core Demand Drivers and Unmet Consumer Gaps in the EU Electric Bicycle Market
Across the 27 EU member states, electric bicycle (e-bike) sales grew 11% year-on-year in 2023 to reach 5.5 million units, outpacing conventional bicycle sales for the second consecutive year, per data from the European Bicycle Manufacturers Association (EBMA). This structural shift is not a temporary post-pandemic blip: our survey of 4,200 consumers across Germany, France, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain, conducted Q1 2024, identifies three durable, policy-aligned drivers underpinning demand, alongside persistent unmet gaps that are shaping market entry and product development priorities for the 2024–2027 period.
The primary demand driver is the maturation of low-emission zone (LEZ) regulation across core urban markets. Sixty-eight percent of urban e-bike purchasers in our sample cited “avoidance of LEZ charges and car access restrictions” as a top-three purchase motivation, up from 49% in our 2021 survey. In cities including Amsterdam, Paris and Berlin, where LEZs now apply to two-wheeled vehicles with internal combustion engines and restrict private car access to central districts during peak hours, e-bikes have emerged as the lowest-cost modal alternative for trips of 3–15km: our analysis shows the total cost of ownership for a mid-range e-bike over three years is €1,270, compared to €3,820 for a small electric car and €1,890 for a monthly public transport pass across the five surveyed markets. The second driver is targeted subsidy design: 41% of purchasers in markets with means-tested e-bike subsidies (notably France’s *prime à la conversion* and Germany’s regional commuter e-bike grants) reported they would not have made a purchase without financial support, with subsidy take-up highest among households in the 2nd and 3rd income quintiles, a cohort that had previously been locked out of e-bike ownership by high upfront costs. Third, evolving commuter patterns have expanded use cases: 57% of employed e-bike owners reported using their vehicle for at least half of their work commutes, up from 38% in 2021, as hybrid work schedules reduce reliance on fixed-route public transport for multi-stop trips combining work, school drop-offs and errands.
Despite this strong demand trajectory, significant unmet consumer gaps are constraining market penetration outside of core early-adopter groups. The most cited barrier to purchase, noted by 62% of non-purchasers considering an e-bike, is concern over theft and lack of secure parking: 72% of respondents in large urban areas reported no access to locked, weather-protected e-bike parking at their place of work or residence, with official data showing 1.2 million bicycles (including e-bikes) are stolen annually across the EU, with a recovery rate of less than 10%. Second, range and charging anxiety persists for non-urban users: 48% of respondents in rural and suburban areas cited insufficient battery range for cross-town or inter-village trips as a key concern, even as average advertised battery ranges increased 22% between 2021 and 2024, a gap explained by widespread consumer distrust of manufacturer range claims, which are typically tested under ideal temperature and terrain conditions. Third, affordability remains a barrier for lower-income households: even with subsidies, the average mid-range commuter e-bike retails for €2,100, a sum that 58% of households in the lowest income quintile reported being unable to afford without access to low-interest credit, which is rarely offered for light electric vehicle purchases in most member states.
These dynamics point to a bifurcating market: premium, feature-heavy e-bikes targeted at high-income urban commuters are increasingly crowded, while significant unmet demand exists for durable, low-theft-risk, affordable models targeted at suburban, rural and lower-income consumer segments, aligned with upcoming EU-level funding for cycling infrastructure under the Urban Mobility Framework. title: BBC-style news article|a football club fined after fans invade the pitch
text:
The English Football League has imposed a £150,000 fine on Championship side Westbridge United and handed down a suspended three-match partial stadium closure order after hundreds of supporters invaded the pitch during the final minutes of the club’s decisive promotion play-off semi-final against Harrow Vale on 16 May. The governing body found the club failed to implement adequate crowd safety and stewardship protocols, despite repeated pre-match warnings about potential pitch encroachment.

The match, which Westbridge won 2-1 to secure a place in the play-off final at Wembley, was suspended for 27 minutes after spectators broke through segregation barriers and poured onto the playing surface. Television footage showed groups of fans surrounding players from both teams, tearing up corner flags and climbing on goal frames, while riot police and stewards formed human cordons around the tunnel to protect match officials and visiting staff. Two Harrow Vale players were treated for minor cuts and psychological distress after being jostled by encroaching supporters, and the club’s manager described the scenes as “a shameful breakdown of order that put lives at avoidable risk”.

In a 22-page written ruling published on Wednesday, the EFL’s independent disciplinary commission concluded that Westbridge United’s safety plan contained “significant and foreseeable gaps”. Stewards assigned to the perimeter of the home end were understaffed by nearly 40 per cent compared with the requirements laid out in the club’s own safety certificate, while several access gates were left unlocked in the final five minutes of the match to allow supporters to move freely between concourses and seating areas. The commission also noted that club announcements over the public address system were delayed until more than six minutes after the invasion began, and that initial warnings were described by witnesses as quiet and ambiguous.

Westbridge United has accepted the financial penalty but issued a statement expressing “disappointment” at the severity of the sanction, arguing that the actions of a minority of fans were “impossible to fully predict or contain”. The club has been ordered to pay a further £35,000 in costs and must deliver a fully revised safety management plan before its first home fixture of the 2025-26 season. The suspended stadium closure, which would involve shutting the 4,200-seat Riverside Stand, will be activated if any further serious pitch incursion or crowd disorder takes place before the end of the 2026-27 campaign.

Speaking outside the club’s ground, chief executive Daniel Foster said Westbridge accepted “ultimate responsibility” for safety inside the stadium and confirmed that three senior members of the matchday operations team had been suspended pending an internal review. “What should have been one of the proudest nights in our recent history was tarnished by the reckless behaviour of a small number of individuals,” he told reporters. “We unreservedly apologise to Harrow Vale, their players and supporters, and to every fan who attended the match expecting to be safe. This fine is a serious warning, and we will meet every requirement placed upon us.”

The Football Supporters’ Association said it recognised the governing body’s duty to enforce safety standards but urged clubs and authorities to distinguish between spontaneous celebration and deliberate violence. “Pitch invasions are never acceptable, but the response must be proportionate and focused on prevention rather than collective punishment,” a spokesperson said. “Clubs need properly trained stewards, clear communication and sustained engagement with supporter groups. Fines alone will not solve this problem.”

Harrow Vale has confirmed it is considering a separate claim for compensation relating to damage to equipment and the impact on its players. The EFL said the ruling sent “an unambiguous message” that clubs would be held strictly accountable for failures in crowd safety, and that stronger penalties would follow at any club allowing repeated disorder.

title: environmental impact statement|a proposed wind farm off the coast of New Jersey
text:
DRAFT ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT STATEMENT: ATLANTIC SHORES SOUTH WIND FARM
 Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, Northeast Regional Office | October 16, 2024
 Section 3.7: Marine Mammal and Sea Turtle Impacts (Excerpt)
This analysis evaluates impacts from the proposed 1,510 MW Atlantic Shores South Wind Farm, sited 10.3 nautical miles east of Atlantic City, New Jersey, across 113,200 acres of federal Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) lease area OCS-A 0499. The project, developed by Atlantic Shores Offshore Wind LLC (a joint venture of Shell New Energies US LLC and EDF Renewables North America), is scheduled to begin onshore construction at the former Oyster Creek Generating Station switchyard in Lacey Township in Q2 2026, with offshore pile driving commencing June 1, 2027, and full commercial operation targeted for December 2029.
Modeled pile driving noise for the project’s 79 14-megawatt Vestas V236 turbines (10-foot-diameter monopile foundations, driven 80 feet into the sandy OCS seabed) predicts a 160 dB re 1 µPa (rms) injury threshold isopleth extending 192 meters from each pile location during peak driving. This radius falls 68% below the 600-meter threshold projected in the 2022 Draft EIS, due to the developer’s committed use of dual Big Bubble Curtain (BBC) attenuation systems, which reduce broadband noise by 18–22 dB, per manufacturer testing. Mitigation requires a 500-meter exclusion zone monitored by three Protected Species Observers (PSOs) during all driving, with a mandatory 30-minute soft-start ramp-up to allow animals to vacate the area; work will be halted if any North Atlantic right whale (*Eubalaena glacialis*) is detected within 1,000 meters via passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) or visual survey.
Temporary behavioral disturbance (defined as >120 dB re 1 µPa rms exposure) is projected to affect 217 individual marine mammals across the 24-month construction window, per NOAA Fisheries 2023 Stock Assessment Reports. This includes 42 humpback whales (*Megaptera novaeangliae*), 17 fin whales (*Balaenoptera physalus*), and a maximum of 3 North Atlantic right whales, representing 0.07% of the species’ estimated 360 remaining individuals in the western North Atlantic stock. No mortality is projected, and disturbance will be limited to <1.2% of available habitat for all listed whale species within the New York Bight.
For sea turtles, pile driving is projected to cause temporary threshold shift (TTS) in 12 loggerhead turtles (*Caretta caretta*) and 2 Kemp’s ridley turtles (*Lepidochelys kempii*) over the construction period, with no permanent injury or mortality anticipated. The project will avoid all cable route alignment through the 2,300-acre Little Egg Harbor seagrass restoration site, completed by the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) in 2022, with horizontal directional drilling (HDD) used for all cable landfalls at Barnegat Light to avoid intertidal horseshoe crab spawning habitat.
Operations-related impacts are limited to a 0.8% increase in vessel strike risk for whales across the lease area, mitigated by a 10-knot speed limit for all project transits within 20 nautical miles of the coast, aligned with NJDEP’s 2023 Right Whale Vessel Speed Rule. Post-construction fish aggregation device (FAD) effects are projected to increase local striped bass (*Morone saxatilis*) biomass by an estimated 12–17% within the lease area by 2035, per monitoring data from the adjacent Block Island Wind Farm, the first operational offshore wind facility in the U.S.

title: encyclopedia article|a species of freshwater turtle and its conservation status
text:
Yellow-Spotted River Turtle (*Podocnemis unifilis*)  
The yellow-spotted river turtle is a medium-to-large freshwater pleurodire (side-necked turtle) in the family Podocnemididae, native to the Amazon and Orinoco river basins across Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, Peru, Venezuela, and possibly French Guiana. It inhabits slow-moving tributaries, oxbow lakes, seasonally flooded várzea forests, and blackwater rivers, relying on exposed sandy riverbanks and sandbars for communal nesting. Adults exhibit strong sexual dimorphism: females reach 40–50 cm in straight carapace length and may exceed 12 kg, while males are smaller, often 30–40 cm, with longer, thicker tails. Juveniles are distinguished by vivid yellow or orange spots on the dark head and scute margins; markings fade with age but often remain faintly visible in adults.  

The species is primarily herbivorous, feeding on fallen fruit, seeds, aquatic vegetation, flowers, and plant matter, although juveniles and opportunistic adults may consume invertebrates, small fish, or carrion. It plays a documented ecological role in seed dispersal for floodplain trees, particularly during high-water seasons when individuals move into inundated forest. Basking is common on logs and sandbanks, and nesting is synchronized with falling river levels, generally between late dry season and early wet season, depending on the basin. Females migrate to traditional nesting beaches, excavate 15–30 cm-deep nests, and deposit clutches commonly numbering 15–30 eggs. Incubation takes roughly 60–90 days, with nest temperature influencing developmental rate and aspects of hatchling phenotype. Eggs and hatchlings suffer high natural mortality from flooding, predators, and nest disturbance, while introduced and native mammals, birds, lizards, crocodilians, and fish prey on vulnerable life stages.  

 Conservation Status  
The International Union for Conservation of the Natural Red List currently classifies *Podocnemis unifilis* as Vulnerable, reflecting an extensive but fragmented range and evidence of substantial population declines over recent decades. The assessment notes that the species remains locally abundant in protected or remote watersheds, but many accessible populations have been depleted or extirpated. Its conservation outlook is shaped less by a single threat than by persistent, additive pressures operating across riverscape and terrestrial nesting habitats.  

Overharvesting is the most significant historical and ongoing threat. Adult females, eggs, and juveniles have long been taken for subsistence and local commercial trade across Amazonian communities. Because females aggregate predictably at nesting beaches, they are especially easy to capture during the reproductive season; collection of both turtles and nests can remove a disproportionate fraction of a local population’s annual reproductive output. Even low levels of sustained adult harvest can produce long-lived species declines, as *P. unifilis* requires several years to reach maturity and has relatively low recruitment under intensified egg predation. In some regions, enforcement of protected-area regulations has reduced large-scale commerce, but informal take continues where governance is weak and demand persists in urban markets and riverside settlements.  

Habitat alteration presents a second major threat. Large hydroelectric dams alter flow regimes, flood pulses, water temperature, and access to nesting beaches; reservoirs can inundast sandbanks, while regulated releases may disrupt the seasonal exposure required by nesting females. River channelization, dredging, mining, deforestation, agricultural expansion, and riparian degradation further reduce nesting and foraging habitat. Mercury contamination from artisanal gold mining and pollution from agricultural runoff may affect health and reproductive success, although population-level effects remain unevenly quantified. Bycatch in fishing gear, especially gillnets and seines, also contributes to mortality in intensively fished rivers. Climate change may add pressure through altered hydrology, increased nest flooding, sex-ratio effects linked to incubation temperatures, and shifts in the availability of suitable nesting beaches. International commercial trade is controlled under its listing on CITES Appendix II, and the species receives varying legal protection within range states, including closed seasons, egg-collection bans, and protected-area safeguards. Implementation, however, is inconsistent across remote jurisdictions.  

Conservation programmes have emphasized community-based nest protection, guarded beaches, translocation of eggs at risk from flooding or poaching, head-starting in selected projects, and harvest management involving Indigenous and riverine communities. Protected areas such as Manu National Park in Peru, Pacaya-Samiria National Reserve in Peru, and parts of the Central Amazon Conservation Complex in Brazil safeguard important populations, though reserves alone do not eliminate illegal take or downstream hydrological impacts. Sustainable-use initiatives, including certified harvest programmes in some Amazonian settings, attempt to balance livelihood needs with recovery, but their effectiveness depends on robust population monitoring and enforceable quotas. Captive breeding exists in zoological and research collections, but it is generally regarded as a supportive measure rather than a substitute for protecting free-flowing rivers and nesting beaches. Long-term conservation will require transboundary monitoring, stronger protection of key nesting sites, fisheries bycatch reduction, and participation by local people whose land and resource use largely determine the turtle’s future.

title: wire news story|a central bank holds interest rates steady amid slowing inflation
text:
The central bank announced Wednesday it would hold its benchmark interest rate steady at 5.25% to 5.5%, marking the fourth consecutive policy meeting where rates have stayed unchanged, as officials weigh clear progress on slowing inflation against lingering concerns that price pressures could reaccelerate if policy is eased too soon.

The decision, which matched broad consensus among economists and market participants, came alongside newly released data showing the central bank’s preferred inflation gauge, the core personal consumption expenditures price index, rose 2.4% in February on a year-over-year basis, down from 2.6% in January and the slowest pace since March 2021. Headline inflation, which includes volatile food and energy costs, fell to 2.5% last month, edging much closer to the central bank’s formal 2% annual target than most analysts projected at the start of the year.

In a prepared statement following the two-day policy meeting, central bank governor Elara Voss noted that “recent months have brought welcome evidence that inflation is moving sustainably down toward our goal, without the sharp rise in unemployment that many forecasters warned would be necessary to bring price growth under control.” The statement added, however, that policymakers “do not expect it will be appropriate to reduce the target range for the policy rate until we have gained greater confidence that inflation is on a persistent path to 2%.”

The national unemployment rate held at 3.8% in February, near 50-year lows, with monthly job gains averaging 225,000 over the past three months, a sign the labor market remains resilient even as higher borrowing costs have cooled rate-sensitive sectors including housing and commercial real estate. Residential mortgage rates, which hover near 7.1% for a 30-year fixed loan, have kept existing home sales depressed for 13 consecutive months, while business loan demand has stayed muted as firms hold off on large expansion plans waiting for borrowing costs to fall.

Market traders had priced in roughly three quarter-point rate cuts by the end of 2024 ahead of the announcement, expectations that shifted only marginally after the policy statement was released, with most analysts now projecting the first rate cut will come at the central bank’s June meeting. Voss pushed back against criticism from some lawmakers and industry groups that rates are being kept too high for too long, noting that core services inflation excluding housing, a metric officials have flagged as a key bellwether for persistent price pressures, still sits at 3.1%, well above pre-pandemic levels.

“Premature rate cuts would risk undoing the progress we have made over the past two years, forcing us to tighten policy again later and inflicting unnecessary pain on households and small businesses,” Voss told reporters during a post-meeting press conference. “At the same time, we are well aware that high interest rates create real burdens, from higher credit card rates to elevated auto loan costs, especially for low-income households. We will carefully parse incoming data on inflation, labor market conditions, and credit conditions as we weigh the appropriate path forward.”

The central bank also announced it would continue to slow the pace of balance sheet reduction starting in April, cutting the monthly cap on maturing Treasury securities it allows to roll off its balance sheet from $60 billion to $30 billion, a move aimed at preventing unnecessary strains in short-term funding markets as it maintains restrictive policy settings in the near term. Officials noted that growth in consumer spending softened slightly in the first quarter, dragged down by slower sales of durable goods, but that overall economic activity continued to expand at a moderate pace, with no imminent signs of a broad downturn.

title: travel guide|two days in Lisbon on a budget
text:
Two Days in Lisbon for Under €85: A Practical Guide

Lisbon doesn’t demand luxury. Its best pleasures come cheap: custard tarts from Belém, hilltop views after a steep climb, and grilled fish in neighbourhood tasca where the bill barely crosses €12. This two-day route, planned for a weekend in late September, costs roughly €80 excluding accommodation, using the Viva Viagem card and a good pair of shoes.

 Day One: Alfama, Baixa and Tagus Views

Start at Manteigaria in Chiado, Rua do Loreto 2. A warm pastel de nata costs €1.20; dust it with cinnamon and eat it at the counter. From there, walk through Praça de Comércio, the grand riverside square rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake, then head into the narrow lanes of Alfama.

Skip the expensive Fado Museum and instead climb to the Miradouro de Santa Luzia. The bougainvillea-covered terrace is free, with views over terracotta roofs and the cruise terminal. Continue uphill to the Castelo de São Jorge. Admission is €10 for adults; if the budget is tight, the surrounding medieval streets and nearby Miradouro da Graça offer nearly as much for nothing.

Lunch should be at Zé da Mouraria, Beco do Embaixador 58, a tiny tasca in Mouraria. The bacalhau à brás—shredded cod with potatoes, eggs and olives—costs around €11 and is easily shared as a substantial lunch. Arrive before 12.45pm or join the queue outside.

In the afternoon, take the tram? Walk. The famous Tram 28 is now €3.10 per ride and often packed with tourists. Following its route on foot through Graça, Estrela and Príncipe Real is slower but more rewarding. Stop at Miradouro da Senhora do Monte, the highest viewpoint in the historic centre, then descend toward Chiado.

For dinner, choose A Merendeira, Rua da Prata 52–54, near Baixa. A bowl of caldo verde and a plate of grilled chouriço with bread comes to about €8. Finish with a €1.60 imperial—draught beer—at an outdoor table in Praça da Figueira.

Day one total: about €22, including castle entry and €6.80 transit card.

 Day Two: Belém, LX Factory and Cais do Sodré

Begin early. Take the 15E tram from Praça da Figueira to Belém, around 25 minutes, using the same Viva Viagem balance. Go straight to Pastéis de Belém, Rua de Belém 84–92. Founded in 1837 beside the former sugar refinery, it sells tarts for €1.25 each. Buy two and eat them standing at the counter.

Belém’s major monuments can drain a budget quickly. The Jerónimos Monastery costs €12, but the church is free and its Manueline doorway alone justifies the visit. The Padrão dos Descobrimentos is €6 to enter, while the riverside angle is free. Better to spend money on the Belém Tower only if you care about queues; the exterior and Tagus-facing promenade are more atmospheric.

Lunch is at O Talho do Belém, Rua de Belém 54A, where a bifana—pork cutlet in a crisp roll—costs about €4.50. Add a bottle of water and sit by the gardens.

In the afternoon, walk or take one short tram ride to LX Factory in Alcântara. This 19th-century textile complex turned creative hub is free to enter. Browse Ler Devagar, the bookshop built around a printing press and bicycle suspended above the shelves, then cross the pedestrian Ponte 25 de Abril viewing walkway area for bridge photos without paying for the elevator experience.

Return to Cais do Sodré before sunset. Visit Time Out Market to look, but avoid eating most of a meal there; prices run €12–€18 per dish. Instead, walk five minutes to Cervejaria Ramiro, Avenida Almirante Reis 1, if willing to travel by metro. A half-dozen garlic prawns and bread cost about €14; reserve or arrive by 6.30pm. For a cheaper night, stay riverside at Sol e Pesca, Rua Nova do Carvalho 44, where tinned fish plates begin around €6.

End with a €2.50 ginjinha in a chocolate cup at O Ginjinha da Rua das Flores, then catch the metro back.

Day two total: about €28–€38, depending on sights and dinner.

Lisbon rewards walkers and early risers. Skip the tourist menu, follow the tiled streets, and spend money where it matters: pasteis, seafood, and one castle with a view.

text:
SECTION 3: MANDATORY BREACH DISCLOSURE TIMELINE AND NOTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS
 Personal Data Security and Breach Accountability Act of 2024
(a) APPLICABILITY AND DEFINITIONS. This section applies to any covered entity as defined in Section 2(4), including for-profit and non-profit entities handling personal data of 500 or more United States residents, federal contractors, and operators of critical infrastructure as designated by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). For purposes of this section, a “covered data breach” is defined as any unauthorized acquisition, access, or exfiltration of unencrypted personal data that compromises the security, confidentiality, or integrity of personal information, excluding inadvertent, good-faith access by an employee or agent that does not result in further disclosure or misuse of data. The 72-hour timeline mandated herein shall be calculated from the moment a covered entity’s senior information security officer, or equivalent designated leadership, confirms or has reasonable cause to believe a covered breach has occurred, excluding time necessary to preserve evidence or prevent further data loss, provided that such mitigation activities do not delay notification beyond the 72-hour window absent a written law enforcement exemption under subsection (d).
(b) NOTIFICATION CONTENT AND RECIPIENTS. No later than 72 hours after confirming a covered data breach, the covered entity shall submit a structured notification to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), the relevant state attorney general for each state in which 500 or more affected residents reside, and CISA for breaches impacting critical infrastructure systems. Such notification shall include: (1) a preliminary assessment of the scope of the breach, including the number of affected individuals to the extent known at the time of filing, and categories of personal data compromised (including social security numbers, financial account credentials, health information, biometric data, and account access credentials); (2) a timeline of the breach from initial suspected compromise to detection, including known threat actor tradecraft or exploited vulnerabilities where identified; (3) immediate mitigation steps taken to contain the breach and prevent further data exfiltration; (4) contact information for a designated entity representative available to respond to regulator and consumer inquiries; and (5) a preliminary plan for individual consumer notification, including free credit monitoring or identity protection services to be provided for no less than 24 months for breaches exposing financial or identity-related data. For breaches affecting fewer than 5,000 individuals, entities may submit a streamlined notification to the FTC, provided that state notification requirements are met consistent with subsection (c).
(c) INDIVIDUAL CONSUMER NOTIFICATION. Individual notification to affected consumers shall be completed no later than 7 days after submission of the regulator notification required under subsection (b), delivered via first-class mail, email (where consumers have opted in to electronic communications), and prominent website notice for breaches impacting more than 10,000 residents. Notifications shall be written in plain language, avoiding technical jargon, and shall clearly outline the specific data exposed for each individual where feasible, steps consumers can take to protect against identity theft, and contact details for entity support and FTC identity theft resources. Delays in individual notification are permitted only where law enforcement provides a written determination that notification would impede an active criminal investigation, in which case notification shall be delivered within 72 hours of that determination being lifted.
(d) ENFORCEMENT AND EXEMPTIONS. The FTC shall enforce this section pursuant to its authority under the Federal Trade Commission Act, with civil penalties of up to $10,000 per affected individual for willful failure to meet the 72-hour notification timeline, adjusted annually for inflation, and up to $1,000 per individual for negligent delays. Covered entities shall not be held liable for delays caused by exigent circumstances, including widespread cyberattacks that impair the entity’s own internal communications systems, provided that the entity notifies regulators within 72 hours of restoring operational capacity and documents all efforts to notify authorities as quickly as feasible. No exemption shall apply for breaches caused by third-party vendors: covered entities retain full responsibility for timely notification upon discovery of a breach originating in a vendor system processing personal data on the entity’s behalf.

title: BBC-style news article|a football club fined after fans invade the pitch
text:
The Football Association has fined a Premier League club 120,000 pounds after hundreds of supporters invaded the pitch following the final match of the season, in an incident that left two stewards injured and prompted fresh calls for stronger measures to prevent crowd disorder.

The independent regulatory commission found the club failed to ensure spectators conducted themselves in an orderly fashion and did not do enough to stop people entering the field of play. The punishment includes a suspended 40,000-pound fine, which would be activated if similar problems occur during the next two seasons.

Trouble broke out after the final whistle, when home supporters surged from several stands to celebrate what the club had described as one of the most important results in its recent history. Television pictures showed fans gathering in the centre circle, climbing on goalframes and confronting players and staff as they tried to leave the pitch.

Stewards and police eventually restored order, but the FA said two members of the matchday safety team required hospital treatment after being knocked over in the rush. A number of seats were also damaged and advertising hoardings torn down.

In its written reasons, the regulatory panel said the scenes were “dangerous, predictable and avoidable”. It noted that the club had urged supporters repeatedly not to enter the pitch, including messages on the scoreboard and in the match programme, but concluded that staffing and contingency plans were inadequate for a game with such high emotional stakes.

“Pitch invasions are not a harmless extension of celebration,” the panel said. “They expose players, officials, supporters and those whose job it is to keep people safe to serious risk. The fact that greater harm did not occur is a matter of fortune rather than effective planning.”

The club accepted the fine and issued an unreserved apology, while stressing that it had banned six people identified by CCTV and club footage. It said those supporters would remain excluded from the stadium pending a full review.

A spokesperson said the club understood the passion felt by fans but insisted there could be no excuse for entering the playing area. “The overwhelming majority of supporters behaved impeccably,” they said. “However, the actions of a significant minority put lives at risk and risked bringing severe damage to the reputation of the club.”

The fine is the latest in a series of disciplinary cases involving crowd conduct across English football. Managers and players have previously spoken of being jostled and abused during pitch incursions, while charities representing matchday staff have warned that stewards often lack sufficient protection when crowds move suddenly.

Safety advisory groups have urged clubs to consider earlier deployments of police, stronger barriers around players’ tunnels and improved communication with supporters before high-risk fixtures. Some clubs have also introduced stricter ticket checks and dedicated “rapid response” teams in an attempt to prevent people reaching the perimeter.

Polly Abbott, chief executive of the Sports Ground Safety Alliance, said fines alone were unlikely to change behaviour unless clubs and authorities worked together before matches. “A pitch invasion can turn from celebration to catastrophe in seconds,” she said. “Clubs need robust planning, but supporters also have to understand that one moment of excitement can lead to lifelong consequences for themselves and others.”

The FA has reminded all clubs that they can be held responsible for the conduct of spectators, regardless of whether disorder is spontaneous. It also urged fans to report anyone planning to encroach on the pitch.

The commission reduced the financial penalty after recognising the club’s early guilty plea, previous good safety record and cooperation with investigators. However, it warned that future cases could result in larger fines, partial stadium closures or matches being played behind closed doors.

For many supporters, the scenes revived memories of traditional end-of-season celebrations, when crowds once routinely gathered on pitches. Yet authorities insist the modern context is different, with larger attendances, faster movement through stands and repeated evidence of assaults, clashes between rival fans and near-misses involving children.

The club has been ordered to pay the fine within 28 days and submit an updated safety management plan before its first home fixture of next season. It said it would consult police, the local safety advisory group and supporter organisations in an effort to ensure the scenes are not repeated.

Grant Proposal: Millwood Public Library Community Oral History Project
Applicant: Millwood Public Library, Millwood, Ohio
Total Requested Funding: $14,850
Project Duration: 18 months

 Project Summary
The Millwood Public Library (MPL) proposes the Millwood Voices Oral History Project, a community-centered initiative designed to document, preserve, and amplify the underrecorded lived experiences of residents across the city’s diverse neighborhoods. While MPL holds 140 years of local newspapers, municipal records, and printed local history collections, these materials largely center the perspectives of civic leaders and business owners, excluding the voices of working-class residents, Black and Indigenous community members, refugee populations, disabled residents, and LGBTQ+ elders who have shaped Millwood’s identity but remain absent from official archival records. This project will fill that critical gap, creating a free, publicly accessible oral history archive hosted at MPL to intergenerational connection, historical accountability, and civic belonging.

 Project Description
Over 18 months, MPL will partner with the Millwood Historical Society, local public schools, and senior service organizations to record 75 high-quality, long-form oral history interviews with residents across four priority cohorts: residents who lived in Millwood prior to the 1968 urban renewal displacement, first- and second-generation refugee and immigrant residents who settled in the city after 1990, local labor organizers and frontline workers, and LGBTQ+ residents who built community networks before 2000. Each 60–90 minute interview will be conducted by trained community volunteers, with project staff providing free professional transcription, closed captioning, and descriptive metadata for every recording. All materials will be hosted on a free, ADA-compliant public portal linked to MPL’s existing digital archive, with no paywalls or access restrictions. The project will also include 12 free public events at MPL branches: interview listening sessions, intergenerational story slams for teens and elder residents, and curriculum workshops for K-12 local history teachers to integrate interview clips into classroom lessons. Twenty percent of project slots will be reserved for interviews conducted in residents’ first languages, including Spanish, Somali, and American Sign Language, with professional interpreters provided to eliminate language barriers to participation.

 Budget Justification
The requested $14,850 will cover three core cost categories. First, $7,200 will fund a part-time project coordinator (10 hours weekly for 18 months) recruited from the Millwood community, who will oversee volunteer training, partner coordination, and accessibility compliance. Second, $4,900 will cover one-time equipment and production costs, including four portable audio recorder kits for volunteer use, secure cloud storage for archival files, professional transcription and translation services for non-English interviews, and ASL interpreter fees for Deaf participants and events. Third, $2,750 will support public programming costs, including printing of free printed interview excerpt booklets for distribution at library branches, event supplies for listening sessions, and small $50 honoraria for interview participants to compensate them for their time contributing to the community record. MPL will contribute $6,200 in in-kind support, including staff time, dedicated archive space, and free access to library meeting rooms for all events and training sessions.

 Expected Outcomes and Evaluation
The project will deliver measurable, community-focused outcomes over its duration. First, it will produce a permanent, accessible archival collection of 75 oral history interviews, projected to reach over 3,000 unique users in its first year online, including local students, researchers, and family members seeking to connect to their community’s history. Second, it will train 30 local community volunteers in ethical oral history practice, archival standards, and accessible interviewing techniques, building long-term local capacity for community storytelling. Third, public programming will draw an estimated 1,200 in-person attendees, with post-event surveys targeting an 85% satisfaction rate and 70% of respondents reporting increased connection to neighbors from different generational or cultural backgrounds. Long-term, the archive will be integrated into MPL’s permanent local history collection, with annual updates to add new interviews, ensuring the project remains a living, evolving resource for Millwood residents for decades to come.

title: congressional research report|the history and current debate over agricultural subsidies
text:
Evolution and Contemporary Debate Over U.S. Agricultural Subsidies
Since the 1933 Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA), U.S. agricultural subsidies have evolved from emergency crisis relief into a $20–25 billion annual federal program, shaped by shifting economic crises, geopolitical priorities, and partisan disagreement over government intervention in food systems. The original AAA, enacted amid the Dust Bowl and Great Depression, established price supports, supply controls, and non-recourse loans to stabilize collapsing farm incomes, when 25% of the U.S. workforce lived in rural areas and farm household earnings averaged 40% of non-farm levels. Early programs were explicitly tied to conservation: the 1936 Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act replaced portions of the AAA struck down by the Supreme Court, linking payments to soil erosion mitigation on idled acreage. The post-WWII era saw the 1949 Agricultural Act codify permanent price support frameworks, while the 1973 Agriculture and Consumer Protection Act shifted toward target price deficiency payments to reduce government stockpiles and align domestic production with global export markets. The 1996 Federal Agriculture Improvement and Reform (FAIR) Act marked a neoliberal turn, phasing down supply controls and replacing fixed price supports with decoupled direct payments tied to historical acreage, intended to phase out subsidy reliance by 2002; the reform was effectively abandoned amid late-1990s commodity price crashes, which spiked emergency ad-hoc farm aid to $23 billion in 1999 alone. Subsequent farm bills (2002, 2008, 2014, 2018) layered revenue insurance subsidies, shallow-loss coverage, and conservation compliance requirements onto the existing framework, with crop insurance premium subsidies now accounting for roughly 40% of baseline farm support.

Contemporary debate divides sharply along lines of market efficiency, equity, environmental impact, and food security. Proponents of the current subsidy regime emphasize countercyclical stabilization: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Economic Research Service data shows commodity and crop insurance payments offset 32% of net farm income losses during the 2012 drought and 2020 COVID-19 demand collapse, preventing widespread farm failures and limiting disruptions to domestic food supply chains. Supporters also note that subsidized federal crop insurance, which covers 85% of planted U.S. corn, soybean, and wheat acreage, reduces systemic lending risk for rural community banks and preserves U.S. competitive advantage in global commodity markets, where the European Union and China provide higher per-acre producer support. National security advocates further frame subsidies as a tool to maintain domestic productive capacity amid export volatility and supply chain fragility exposed by the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Critics from both the left and right challenge the distributional and market distortions of existing programs. Environmental and progressive advocacy groups cite USDA data showing 70% of commodity payments flow to the largest 10% of farming operations, primarily concentrated in corn, soy, cotton, and rice monocultures, while less than 8% of support reaches fruit, vegetable, and specialty crop producers, and less than 2% is allocated to small and mid-sized socially disadvantaged farms. Public health researchers argue that subsidies for staple commodity crops artificially lower the cost of processed food ingredients by an estimated 10–15%, contributing to dietary disparities and elevated rates of diet-related disease. Fiscal conservatives, meanwhile, decry the $1.3 trillion ten-year baseline of the 2023 farm bill, arguing that decoupled insurance subsidies incentivize planting on environmentally fragile marginal land and disproportionately benefit large agribusiness firms rather than family farms, despite statutory payment limits weakened by regulatory loopholes. Environmental groups add that current conservation compliance requirements, which tie premium subsidies to wetland and soil protections, are underenforced, and that subsidies incentivize fertilizer-intensive production contributing to Gulf of Mexico hypoxia and greenhouse gas emissions.

Current legislative negotiations center on competing proposals: the Biden administration’s 2023 farm bill framework seeks to redirect $20 billion in existing subsidies to climate-smart conservation practices, specialty crop grants, and debt relief for historically underserved producers, while House Republican proposals push for tighter income eligibility caps, work requirements for nutrition assistance paired with farm support, and reduced funding for conservation easements. Bipartisan consensus exists only around preserving the core crop insurance program, leaving structural reform of subsidy allocation largely unresolved.

title: BBC-style news article|flooding forces hundreds of families from their homes in a Welsh valley
text:
Hundreds of families across a south Wales valley have been forced to evacuate their homes after torrential overnight rainfall triggered widespread flash flooding, with emergency services declaring a major incident as water levels rose to waist height in some residential streets. The Rhondda Valley, which saw more than 110mm of rain fall in a six-hour window between 21:00 BST on Wednesday and 03:00 on Thursday, has borne the brunt of the unseasonably heavy downpours, which the Met Office has linked to a slow-moving Atlantic weather front stalled over the south Wales coalfield.

Rescue teams from South Wales Fire and Rescue Service deployed 22 fire engines, four specialist water rescue units and more than 80 personnel to door-knock at-risk properties through the early hours, ferrying stranded residents, including 17 elderly people and three young children, to temporary rest centres set up at local leisure centres and village halls. A spokesperson for the service said crews had responded to more than 230 flood-related calls by mid-morning on Thursday, including reports of people trapped in cars, collapsed garden walls, and raw sewage spilling into ground-floor homes after drainage systems were overwhelmed by the sheer volume of water.

Siân Evans, 62, who has lived in her terraced home in the village of Treorchy for 38 years, said she woke at 01:30 to the sound of water rushing through her front door. “I’ve never seen anything like it, not even in the bad floods of 2007,” she told reporters, wrapped in a foil blanket at the temporary rest centre at Treorchy Leisure Centre. “It came up so fast. I grabbed my cat, my medication and a photo of my late husband, and that was all I had time for. The water was up to my knees by the time I got to the top of the street. Everything downstairs is gone – the carpets, the furniture, the kitchen units. I don’t know when I’ll be able to go back.”

Rhondda Cynon Taf Council said 317 households had registered for emergency accommodation as of Thursday afternoon, with council officers working alongside the British Red Cross to distribute food, dry clothing, bedding and hygiene products to displaced residents. Council leader Andrew Morgan said teams had been out clearing blocked culverts and drain grates through the night, but the intensity of the rainfall had outstripped even the most pessimistic flood defence projections for the area. “We’ve invested more than £12m in flood defences across the valley over the last decade, but no amount of permanent infrastructure can fully mitigate against that volume of rain falling in such a short space of time,” he said. “Our immediate priority is making sure every displaced family has somewhere safe to stay, and that we can get people back into their homes as soon as it is safe to do so.”

The Met Office has downgraded its earlier amber weather warning for south Wales to a yellow warning for heavy, scattered showers through the rest of Thursday, but has warned that further localised surface water flooding remains possible as river levels on the Rhondda Fawr and Rhondda Fach continue to peak. Natural Resources Wales said it was continuing to monitor river gauges across the catchment, and had deployed temporary flood barriers in the lower-lying areas of Pontypridd downstream as a precaution.

Local MP Chris Bryant, who visited affected communities on Thursday morning, said he would be pressing the Welsh Government for emergency funding to support affected households, many of whom do not have home insurance that covers flood damage. “People here have lost everything in the space of a few hours,” he said. “This isn’t just about mopping up water – it’s about replacing ruined furniture, fixing electrical systems, making homes safe again, and supporting people who have been left traumatised by what they’ve been through. We can’t leave families to pick up the pieces on their own.”

There have been no reports of serious injuries connected to the flooding, though two people were treated by paramedics for mild hypothermia after being stranded in their vehicles for more than an hour on the A4061, which remains closed between Treherbert and Treorchy while crews clear flood debris and standing water from the carriageway. Council officials said it would likely be at least three days before most evacuated residents are able to return to their properties, with structural safety assessments and water level checks required before homes can be declared habitable. GOVERNMENT AUDIT REPORT
 Oversight of Veterans' Disability Claim Processing Times

Report Number: VA-OIG-2024-017  
Date Issued: October 24, 2024  
Auditing Entity: Office of Inspector General, United States Department of Veterans Affairs  
Subject: Audit of Controls Over Veterans Disability Claim Processing Time Oversight  

 Executive Summary
This report presents the results of our audit of the Veterans Benefits Administration’s (VBA) oversight mechanisms for disability compensation claim processing times, conducted pursuant to the Inspector General Act of 1978. The audit evaluated fiscal year 2023 operations across 56 regional processing offices, focusing on compliance with statutory timeliness mandates, data integrity, and effectiveness of performance accountability frameworks. Our objective was to determine whether VBA maintained reliable controls to ensure claims were processed accurately, efficiently, and within publicly reported timelines, while safeguarding veterans’ entitlement to timely benefits.

We found that systemic weaknesses in oversight contributed to persistent processing delays, inconsistent performance reporting, and inadequate mitigation of backlog growth. While VBA reported an average 127-day processing time for fiscal year 2023, our independent testing identified a 19% understatement of actual elapsed days for 400 sampled claims, primarily due to improper exclusion of pending medical examination and evidence-gathering periods. Approximately 32% of sampled claims exceeded the statutory 180-day target, with 11% pending for over 365 days, disproportionately affecting veterans in rural regions and those filing complex post-traumatic stress disorder and toxic exposure claims. These deficiencies occurred because VBA’s oversight design prioritized volume-based metrics over end-to-end timeliness, failed to validate third-party data feeds, and lacked standardized escalation protocols for aged claims. We are making seven recommendations to strengthen data governance, realign performance incentives, and enhance independent monitoring of processing timelines.

 Background
VBA administers disability compensation benefits for over 5 million veterans, receiving approximately 1.8 million new disability claims annually. Under 38 U.S.C. § 5109, the agency is required to adjudicate claims within reasonable timeframes, with internal policy establishing a 180-day target for fully developed claims and a 125-day goal for standard claims. Processing timelines encompass intake, evidence collection, medical examination scheduling, rating decision issuance, and notification to claimants. VBA’s National Workforce Management Center and Office of Field Oversight share responsibility for monitoring office-level performance, allocating resources, and reporting monthly processing metrics to Congress and the public.

Since 2021, claim volume has increased 21% following implementation of the Honoring our PACT Act, while staffing levels rose only 8% over the same period. Prior Office of Inspector General reports in 2022 and 2023 identified recurring gaps in time-code documentation and backlog tracking, prompting VBA to launch a process modernization initiative in early 2023. This audit assessed whether corrective actions resolved prior weaknesses and whether current oversight activities provided reasonable assurance of timely, accurate claim adjudication.

 Audit Findings
First, performance measurement systems contained material data inaccuracies that impaired oversight visibility. VBA’s Veterans Benefits Management System automatically paused processing-time clocks when requests were sent for military service records or contract medical examinations, regardless of actual delay duration. Testing confirmed that 76 of 400 sampled claims excluded 30 or more days from calculated timelines without documented justification, and regional staff had unrestricted ability to manually adjust time codes without supervisory approval. Aggregate regional office rankings used for executive performance reviews relied exclusively on these unvalidated metrics, creating incentives to prioritize claims with shorter processing requirements and defer complex, high-evidence claims.

Second, oversight activities did not effectively target root causes of delay. Monthly regional office performance reviews focused primarily on completed claim volume rather than aging inventory, and only 3 of 56 offices maintained dedicated teams to monitor claims pending over 180 days. Follow-up on delayed contract medical examinations was inconsistent: 42% of examination-related delays in our sample lacked documented follow-up within 14 days, despite contractual requirements for vendor completion within 45 days. VBA national leadership did not aggregate vendor-specific delay data or impose contractual penalties for late examinations, eliminating a key oversight lever to reduce processing lags.

Third, internal audit and quality assurance functions provided limited independent assurance over timeliness. VBA’s Quality Review Service sampled less than 2% of claims annually for accuracy, and timeliness verification was not included in standard review protocols. The agency did not conduct periodic risk assessments to identify offices or claim categories at elevated risk of delay, and staffing allocation formulas did not incorporate regional backlog age or claim complexity data. As a result, offices serving high concentrations of veterans with Agent Orange and burn pit exposure claims carried 27% higher per-staff caseloads than the national average despite longer average processing requirements.

 Recommendations and Management Response
We recommend that the Under Secretary for Benefits implement system controls to restrict manual time-code adjustments, validate all pauses exceeding 10 days, and publicly report both active and cumulative processing times. VBA should establish mandatory aging claim review protocols, integrate vendor performance penalties into medical examination contracts, and revise staffing models to account for claim complexity and backlog age. Additionally, the Quality Review Service should include timeliness validation in annual claim sampling and conduct quarterly risk assessments of regional processing operations.

VBA management concurred with all seven recommendations and provided a corrective action plan targeting full implementation by September 30, 2025. The Office of Inspector General will monitor completion of corrective actions and conduct a follow-up audit in the second quarter of fiscal year 2026.

University of Washington Launches $42M Pacific Northwest Battery Innovation Hub to Cut Grid Storage Costs by 70% by 2030

SEATTLE, Oct. 16, 2024 — The University of Washington today formally opened the Washington State Battery Technology Research Center (WaBat), a cross-disciplinary facility anchored in the College of Engineering, backed by $27M in state economic development funding, $10M in corporate partnerships, and $5M in federal Department of Energy (DOE) grants, with an additional $5M in university matching funds for early-career researcher fellowships.

The center, housed in a renovated 28,000-square-foot former clean energy lab on UW’s Seattle campus, will be led by Dr. Priya Mehta, a 17-year veteran of lithium-sulfur battery research who previously led stationary storage development at Tesla Energy before joining UW’s materials science faculty in 2019. Unlike most university battery labs focused on incremental improvements to electric vehicle battery chemistry, WaBat’s core mandate is to solve the biggest bottleneck to 100% renewable power adoption: long-duration grid storage that can deliver power for 100+ hours at a cost of less than $20 per kilowatt-hour, down from current average costs of $75/kWh for lithium-ion grid storage.

“Right now, when the wind dies down for three straight winter days across the Columbia River Gorge, utilities are firing up natural gas peaker plants to fill the gap because existing batteries are too expensive to deploy at that scale,” Dr. Mehta told reporters at a launch event Wednesday, flanked by Washington Governor Jay Inslee and representatives from founding industry partners including Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL), Seattle-based battery startup Group14 Technologies, and utility firm Puget Sound Energy. “We’re not chasing 10% range gains for EVs here. We’re building chemistry that lets a small town in Eastern Washington run entirely on stored wind and solar through a week of cloudy, calm weather, without relying on fossil fuels.”

WaBat’s first three flagship research projects will launch Nov. 1: a sodium-ion battery prototype that uses no rare earth metals or lithium, sourced entirely from Pacific Northwest mineral deposits; a non-flammable solid-state electrolyte designed to eliminate fire risk for grid-scale storage installations; and a closed-loop battery recycling program that will recover 98% of cathode materials from spent EV and grid batteries, in partnership with the state’s Department of Ecology. The center will employ 22 full-time faculty, 34 graduate research assistants, and 12 industry-embedded postdoctoral fellows, with a dedicated tech transfer office to move lab breakthroughs to Washington-based manufacturing partners within 36 months of discovery, rather than the current 7-10 year average for battery tech commercialization.

Governor Inslee noted at the launch that the center is projected to create an estimated 1,200 local advanced manufacturing jobs by 2030, as partner firms scale production of WaBat-patented chemistries at facilities across the Puget Sound and Columbia Basin. “For decades, the Pacific Northwest led the world in hydroelectric innovation,” Inslee said. “This center cements our role as the global leader for the next era of clean power, right here where our region’s researchers, utilities, and clean energy firms can turn lab breakthroughs into jobs and lower electric bills for every Washington resident.”

The first public tour of WaBat’s lab facilities will be held for regional clean energy stakeholders on Nov. 14, with the first round of seed grants for student-led battery research opening for applications Dec. 1.

title: government audit report|delays and cost overruns in a federal broadband grant program
text:
This audit reviewed the federal Broadband Access and Equity Grant Program, administered by the Department of Commerce, to assess project timelines, award oversight, cost controls, and compliance with grant conditions. The review covered awards made between fiscal years 2021 and 2023 and examined 84 sampled grants totaling approximately $1.2 billion, along with program records, recipient reports, procurement files, and agency monitoring data.

The audit found that delays and cost overruns were widespread and materially reduced the program’s near-term impact. At the time of fieldwork, 61 percent of sampled projects were behind schedule, with an average delay of 14 months. Twenty-two projects had not begun construction despite receiving awards more than 18 months earlier. Program officials attributed delays primarily to incomplete environmental reviews, right-of-way negotiations, permitting backlogs, and inaccurate initial engineering estimates. While some causes were external, the department did not consistently verify project readiness before award approval and often accepted applicant schedules without independent validation.

Cost growth also exceeded expectations. Forty-three percent of active sampled projects reported estimated or actual cost increases, averaging 27 percent above the original approved budget. In aggregate, sampled projects anticipated approximately $148 million in additional costs, primarily from rising materials prices, labor shortages, redesign requirements, and underestimated make-ready work on utility poles. The department allowed recipients to revise budgets and timelines without consistently documenting whether alternatives had been evaluated, whether costs remained reasonable, or whether delays were attributable to recipient mismanagement.

Weak project planning contributed significantly to the problems found. Thirty-one of the 84 grant files lacked adequate pre-award engineering assessments, and 24 did not contain evidence that applicants had secured necessary local commitments, such as franchise agreements, access to rights-of-way, or pole attachment understandings. In several cases, recipients began work only after award and then encountered jurisdictional restrictions or unexpected infrastructure conflicts. The department’s pre-award review emphasized application completeness but did not sufficiently test technical feasibility or construction readiness.

Grantee monitoring was inconsistent and, in some regions, untimely. Quarterly progress reports were frequently submitted late, and agency staff did not always follow up on missed milestones or unexplained spending. The audit identified 19 projects in which recipients reported schedule slippage for two or more consecutive quarters before program officials initiated formal corrective action. Nine grant files lacked current budgets or revised project schedules, limiting the department’s ability to assess whether federal funds were being used efficiently.

Procurement and cost documentation deficiencies were also noted. In 15 sampled awards, recipients did not adequately demonstrate that contracts had been competitively procured or that costs were allowable under federal standards. Unsupported costs totaling approximately $3.7 million were questioned, including change orders without price analysis, equipment purchases not tied to approved project scopes, and subcontractor charges lacking sufficient invoice detail. An additional $12.4 million was classified as unsupported pending receipt of documentation.

The department also did not adequately track service outcomes. Although grants were intended to expand affordable broadband to unserved and underserved locations, reporting systems focused mainly on obligations and expenditures rather than verified premises passed, active subscribers, or service speeds. As a result, officials could not readily determine whether delayed projects continued to target the highest-need communities or whether rescoped projects preserved the intended public benefit.

The audit makes seven recommendations. The department should strengthen pre-award readiness reviews, require independent cost estimates for larger projects, establish clear milestone escalation procedures, conduct timely risk assessments of delayed grants, improve review of change orders and procurement records, recover or disallow unsupported costs where documentation is not provided, and implement outcome-based reporting with verification of locations served and adoption results. Until these controls are improved, the program remains at continued risk of avoidable cost growth, delayed benefits, and reduced accountability for federal broadband investments.
