text:
Market Research Report: Consumer Demand for Electric Bicycles in Europe
Report Date: October 2024
Research Scope: 8,200 respondents across 12 core European markets (Germany, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain, Poland, Sweden, Denmark, Belgium, Austria, Portugal, Czechia) covering age groups 18–75, with data triangulated from 2023–2024 retail sales figures and policy document reviews.

Overall Market Trajectory
The research records a 17.2% year-on-year rise in European e-bicycle unit sales in the first half of 2024, reaching 3.14 million units, with consumer demand projected to push total annual sales to 6.8 million by the end of the year. Unlike the 2020–2022 pandemic-driven sales spike, current demand is rooted in structural shifts in consumer mobility priorities, rather than temporary public health restrictions.

Core Demand Drivers
First, cost-of-living pressures are the top cited purchase motivator, with 62% of respondents noting that e-bicycles cut monthly transport costs by 60–80% compared to private car use, particularly amid sustained high fuel and urban parking fees across EU member states. Second, policy support amplifies demand: 58% of purchasers who bought e-bikes in the past 12 months accessed national or municipal subsidy schemes covering 20–40% of purchase costs, while 47% cited expanding dedicated cycling infrastructure as a key factor reducing perceived safety risks of two-wheeled travel. Third, demographic shifts are expanding the consumer base: while 18–34-year-old urban commuters remain the largest segment (41% of buyers), demand from consumers aged 55+ grew 23% year-on-year, as this group prioritizes low-impact personal mobility for leisure and local errands.

Segmented Demand Preferences
Cargo e-bikes represent the fastest growing subcategory, with 28% of prospective buyers listing them as a preferred option, driven by demand from families seeking car replacements for school runs and grocery shopping. Commuter-focused lightweight e-bikes with 40–60km battery range hold a 49% market share, with consumers prioritizing removable batteries, anti-theft tracking, and integrated lighting as non-negotiable features. Price sensitivity varies by market: consumers in Northern Europe (Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden) show a 32% higher willingness to pay for premium models with carbon frames and smart connectivity, while price points under 1,500 euros dominate demand in Southern and Central Eastern Europe.

Key Barriers to Uptake
The research identifies three core constraints on demand. First, 48% of non-buyers cite high upfront purchase costs as the primary barrier, even with available subsidies. Second, 39% express concern about battery theft and limited secure public parking facilities in dense urban areas. Third, 27% note uncertainty about long-term battery replacement costs, which can account for 30–40% of total e-bike value.

Strategic Implications
Brands and retailers are advised to prioritize mid-range product lines for mass market appeal, partner with municipal authorities to promote secure parking solutions, and offer transparent battery warranty and replacement schemes to reduce consumer risk perceptions. The long-term demand outlook remains strong, with 61% of respondents who do not currently own an e-bike indicating they plan to purchase one within the next three years. (Word count: 597)

title: op-ed column|why cities should ban cars from their historic centres
text:
Ban Cars from Our Historic Centres—Before There’s Nothing Left to Save
Last spring, I dodged a white delivery van idling on the cobblestones of Florence’s Via dei Calzaiuoli, its exhaust curling around the marble facade of Orsanmichele, while a group of Japanese schoolchildren pressed handkerchiefs to their mouths. The street, completed in its current form in 1842 to link the Duomo to Palazzo Vecchio, was never built for two-tonne metal boxes. It was built for footsteps. Yet 70% of vehicles entering Florence’s UNESCO-listed centre in 2023 were private passenger cars, according to the city’s mobility office—2.1 million car trips a year, grinding against 800-year-old stone, spewing nitrogen dioxide that blackens Renaissance frescoes, and squeezing the life out of streets designed for conversation, not combustion.

Cities across Europe are finally waking up. On October 16, 2024, Brussels fully enforced its historic centre car ban, barring private cars from 50 hectares of medieval lanes around the Grand-Place; early data shows pedestrian foot traffic up 32% and local shop revenue up 18% in six months. Pontevedra, a small Spanish city that banned cars from its 12th-century old town in 1999, cut traffic accidents by 97% and saw its city-centre population rise by 12% over two decades, reversing the post-war flight to suburbs. These are not utopian experiments. They are corrections to a 70-year mistake.

The arguments against are always the same: “What about deliveries? What about elderly residents? What about small businesses?” Florence already has answers. Its limited-traffic zone (ZTL), in place since 1990 but long weakened by exemptions, allows electric delivery vans only between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m., and residents hold permits for underground garages on the centre’s edge, with free electric shuttles running every five minutes. No one is arguing for zero access. We are arguing for priority: people first, not 1.5-tonne private cars that spend 95% of their time parked, occupying 12 square metres of public land each.

The stakes are not merely aesthetic. In 2019, a 47-year-old tourist was killed by a tour bus on Venice’s Riva degli Schiavoni; in 2022, a driver crashed into the barriers of Rome’s Trevi Fountain, damaging the 1762 landmark. Last summer, Paris measured nitrogen dioxide levels of 68 micrograms per cubic metre in the Marais—nearly triple the WHO’s annual guideline limit—right outside the 17th-century Hôtel de Sully. Stone does not regenerate. Lungs do not easily heal.

Critics call bans elitist, but it is car dependency that is elitist: it forces cities to surrender their most precious shared heritage to the minority who drive, while children, the disabled, the poor and the elderly navigate broken pavements and toxic air. When Oslo closed its historic city centre to cars in 2019, it installed 200 kilometres of protected cycle lanes and cut public transport fares by 30%; within three years, 70% of trips downtown were on foot, bike or transit.

A historic centre is not a drive-through museum. It is a living place, and living things sicken when choked by fumes and shaken by engines. The choice is no longer between cars and convenience. It is between streets our grandchildren can walk, and stone reduced to rubble by neglect.

title: NGO policy brief|improving childhood nutrition in rural Kenya
text:
Policy Brief: Reducing Rural Childhood Malnutrition in Kenya
 Section 2: Supply-Side Gaps in Community-Led Complementary Feeding Programming
Across Kenya’s arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs) and highland smallholder communities, 26% of children under five experience stunting, with prevalence rising to 40% in Turkana and West Pokot counties, per 2022 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey (KDHS) data. While national policy mandates universal provision of micronutrient powders (MNPs) and infant and young child feeding (IYCF) counselling through public health facilities, 62% of rural households report never receiving MNP supplies in the past 12 months, and only 18% of caregivers can name the three core components of age-appropriate complementary feeding for children 6–23 months old. This implementation gap stems not from insufficient national budget allocations—Kenya has met the African Union’s 1% of GDP target for nutrition spending since 2020—but from last-mile supply chain failures, under-resourced community health worker (CHW) networks, and misalignment between agricultural extension services and nutrition priorities.

Field research conducted by the Kenya Nutrition Advocacy Forum (KNAF) across 120 rural villages in Busia, Kitui, and Kakamega counties in 2023 found that 71% of CHWs tasked with delivering IYCF support serve catchment areas of more than 150 households, double the 75-household benchmark recommended by the World Health Organization. Most CHWs work on a volunteer stipend of less than KSh 500 (US$3.50) per month, with no dedicated transport allowance to reach remote households during rainy seasons, when road access cuts off 38% of rural villages for 3–4 months annually. MNPs, which have a 12-month shelf life, often sit in county health stores for 8 months or longer due to delayed disbursement of last-mile transport funds, leading to 29% of distributed batches expiring before reaching caregivers. Compounding these gaps, agricultural extension programs that support smallholder production of nutrient-dense crops (including orange-fleshed sweet potato, amaranth, and local legumes) rarely coordinate with CHW teams: only 11% of caregivers interviewed reported receiving both agricultural training on growing nutrient-dense foods and counselling on how to incorporate those foods into age-appropriate child meals.

The consequences of these gaps are both humanitarian and economic. The 2023 Kenya National Nutrition Action Plan estimates that childhood stunting reduces lifetime earnings by 16% on average, costing the national economy US$3.2 billion annually in lost productivity and avoidable healthcare costs. Yet evidence from KNAF’s 2021–2023 pilot program in 30 villages in Siaya county demonstrates that targeted, community-centered fixes can cut stunting prevalence by 9 percentage points within two years. The pilot provided CHWs with monthly performance stipends tied to home visit targets, allocated dedicated petty cash for MNP transport to village drop-off points, and embedded nutrition training into existing farmer field school curricula, leading to 89% MNP coverage and a 62% increase in household production of nutrient-dense crops among participating households. Scaling this model across 20 high-burden rural counties would require an annual investment of US$28 million, equivalent to 0.03% of Kenya’s 2024 national budget, and deliver an estimated US$420 million in long-term economic returns by reducing chronic malnutrition’s lifelong impacts. Without closing these last-mile implementation gaps, Kenya will miss its 2030 target of reducing stunting to 15% among under-fives, entrenching intergenerational poverty in the rural communities that are already most vulnerable to climate shocks and food insecurity.

Dear Shareholders,

It is with great pride and confidence that I write to you on behalf of the entire board and management team to present the annual report for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024. This past year marked a defining chapter in our company’s history, as we executed a deliberate and disciplined strategy to grow our footprint, strengthen our market position, and deliver long-term value to all our stakeholders. The theme of this year’s report is expansion in every meaningful sense of the word, from new store openings and distribution capabilities to enhanced customer experiences and community investment.

Our company, which began as a single neighborhood grocery store more than three decades ago, has always believed that growth should never come at the expense of the values that define us. During the year under review, we remained committed to offering fresh, high-quality products, fair pricing, and friendly, knowledgeable service, while extending these commitments to more communities than ever before. The result was a year of solid financial performance, measurable operational progress, and increasing recognition of our brand across the region.

Financially, fiscal 2024 demonstrated the strength and scalability of our business model. Total revenue reached 1.48 billion dollars, representing an increase of 14.2 percent compared with the prior year. Comparable store sales rose by 6.8 percent, reflecting improved customer traffic, stronger basket size, and continued loyalty among our shoppers. Net income for the year was 62.3 million dollars, or 2.49 dollars per diluted share, compared with 53.7 million dollars, or 2.15 dollars per diluted share, in the prior year. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization increased to 118.6 million dollars, underscoring both our top-line momentum and our ability to manage costs during a period of significant investment.

A central achievement of the year was the successful opening of 11 new supermarkets, bringing our total store network to 78 locations across six states. These new stores were carefully selected based on demographic research, community need, and long-term growth potential. Each location was designed to reflect the character of its neighborhood while offering an expanded selection of fresh produce, meat and seafood, bakery items, prepared foods, and everyday household essentials. Early performance from the new stores has been encouraging, with customer reception exceeding our expectations and average weekly sales tracking ahead of our initial projections.

Our expansion program also included major investments in infrastructure. In April, we completed the expansion of our regional distribution center, adding approximately 280,000 square feet of temperature-controlled and ambient storage capacity. This investment has improved delivery frequency, reduced transportation costs, and allowed us to support future store growth without compromising product freshness or operational efficiency. We also upgraded our inventory management and forecasting systems, enabling better coordination between suppliers, stores, and distribution teams. These enhancements are particularly important as we navigate ongoing volatility in food costs and supply chain conditions.

Equally important to our physical expansion was the continued evolution of the customer experience. We accelerated investments in digital convenience by enhancing our online shopping platform, expanding curbside pickup to all full-service stores, and introducing same-day delivery in 22 additional markets. Digital sales grew by 31 percent during the year and now represent 9.4 percent of total revenue. While our stores remain at the heart of our business, we recognize that customers increasingly choose when, where, and how they shop. Our objective is to make every interaction with our brand simple, reliable, and personal.

We also deepened our commitment to local sourcing and community partnership. During the year, we expanded our Local Producers Program, adding 47 new regional farmers, bakers, and food manufacturers. Purchases from local suppliers increased by 18 percent, allowing us to offer distinctive products while supporting small businesses and reducing transportation-related emissions. Our community giving initiatives provided more than 4.2 million dollars in food donations, sponsorships, and hunger-relief programs, and our team members volunteered thousands of hours with local schools and nonprofit organizations.

None of this progress would have been possible without our dedicated workforce. We now employ more than 11,800 team members, and we continued to invest in competitive wages, training, leadership development, and health and well-being benefits. We also strengthened our succession planning processes and expanded programs designed to help store-level associates build long-term careers with the company. Our people are the face of our brand, and their dedication is the foundation of our success.

Looking ahead, we enter fiscal 2025 with strong momentum and a clear strategic agenda. We plan to open eight to ten additional stores, continue remodeling existing locations, and make further investments in technology, freshness, and sustainability. We will also maintain a disciplined approach to capital allocation, balancing growth investments with balance sheet strength and appropriate returns to shareholders.

On behalf of the board of directors, I extend my sincere thanks to our team members, customers, suppliers, and communities for their trust and support. To you, our shareholders, I express our gratitude for your confidence in our long-term vision. This was a year of expansion, but more importantly, it was a year in which we proved that growth and values can go hand in hand. We remain excited about the opportunities ahead and committed to building a stronger, more resilient regional grocery leader.

Sincerely,

Thomas R. Whitfield
President and Chief Executive Officer
Harvest Valley Regional Grocers, Inc.

title: encyclopedia article|the life and career of a nineteenth-century railway engineer
text:
Sir John Fowler, 1st Baronet (1817–1898)  
A towering figure of Victorian civil engineering, John Fowler’s career shaped the physical and economic fabric of 19th-century Britain and its global imperial networks, earning him a reputation as both a technical innovator and a pragmatic steward of public safety. Born in Wadsley, near Sheffield, on 15 July 1817, Fowler cut his teeth in the smoky workshops of the Sheffield and Rotherham Railway at 16, before articling to John Towlerton Leather, a leading waterworks and railway engineer, in 1837. His first major independent commission came at 26, when he was appointed chief engineer of the Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire Railway (MS&LR) in 1843, overseeing the construction of the gruelling Woodhead Tunnel: at 3 miles 22 yards, the longest railway tunnel in Britain when it opened in 1845, driven through millstone grit by 1,500 navvies working round-the-clock shifts, with 32 fatalities from collapses and cholera—a toll that galvanized Fowler’s lifelong advocacy for better worksite welfare and structural redundancy.

Fowler’s breakthrough came in the 1850s, when he pioneered the “Fowler tie,” a wrought-iron structural bracket that eliminated the dangerous lateral sway in iron-girder bridges, adopted as standard across three-quarters of Britain’s railway network by 1860. He also championed the use of the 4-4-0 steam locomotive design for passenger routes, working closely with locomotive manufacturer Patrick Stirling to develop models that cut journey times between London and York by 45 minutes after the opening of the Great Northern Railway’s King’s Cross terminus in 1852, for which he served as consulting engineer. His most celebrated domestic work, however, was the Metropolitan Railway, the world’s first underground passenger line, which opened in January 1863. Rejecting the shallow brick-arched “cut and cover” proposals of rival engineers, Fowler devised a system of interlocking iron segment linings for the tunnels and implemented forced gas ventilation to reduce smoke buildup, even as critics warned the tunnel would collapse under the weight of London’s streets. The line carried 38,000 passengers on its first day of operation, recouping 40% of its £1.3 million construction cost in its first year.

Knighted in 1885 for his work on Egypt’s first railway line from Alexandria to Cairo, Fowler shared the 1890 contract to design Scotland’s Forth Bridge with Benjamin Baker, his long-time collaborator. Completed in 1890 at a cost of £3.2 million, the 8,296-foot cantilever bridge was the first major steel structure in Britain, designed to withstand 120-mph winds after the 1879 Tay Bridge disaster—a failure Fowler had publicly testified was caused by inadequate wind bracing, a critique that initially alienated peers but was vindicated by the Tay inquiry. He served as president of the Institution of Civil Engineers from 1866 to 1867, and retired in 1893 to his estate in Dorset, where he died on 20 November 1898, leaving an estate valued at £760,000. Unlike many of his contemporaries, Fowler rarely sought public acclaim; his obituary in *The Engineer* noted that “he built not for spectacle, but for the hundred years ahead”—a judgment borne out by the fact that the Forth Bridge and sections of his Metropolitan Railway tunnels remain in constant use 130 years later. title: travel guide|two days in Lisbon on a budget
text:
Two Days in Lisbon on a Budget
Lisbon rewards slow, curious travel: tiled facades, hilltop views, vintage trams and riverside walks need not come with a premium price tag. With a little planning, €50–€60 per day, excluding accommodation, can cover transit, a handful of classic sights, substantial meals, pastries and coffee. Start early, wear sturdy shoes, and use the city’s hills as a route planner rather than an obstacle.

 Day One: Alfama, Baixa and the River

Begin in Alfama, Lisbon’s oldest quarter, before the narrow lanes fill with tour groups. The district is best enjoyed simply: follow Rua de São João da Praça toward the cathedral, pause beneath washing strung between balconies, and listen for fado posters marking tiny restaurants that open after dark. A walk through Alfama costs nothing, and its miradouros, or viewpoints, are among the city’s finest.

The Sé de Lisboa, or Lisbon Cathedral, is a useful first landmark. Entry to the main church is inexpensive, while the cloister and treasury carry a separate charge; budget travellers pressed for time may prefer to admire the austere Romanesque façade and move on. From there, climb toward Miradouro de Santa Luzia, a leafy terrace wrapped in bougainvillea and azulejos, with views over terracotta rooftops toward the Tagus. Nearby Miradouro das Portas do Sol is broader and busier, but equally rewarding at sunrise.

For one paid sight, choose the Castelo de São Jorge only if medieval walls and archaeological remains appeal; tickets are not cheap by Lisbon standards. A more economical alternative is to wander the castle-adjacent streets and save the entrance fee for lunch. Near the Sé, Casa Portuguesa do Pastel de Bacalhau serves a crisp codfish cake with cheese for a few euros, but simpler bakeries across Alfama offer equally filling savoury snacks.

Descend toward Baixa, the orderly grid rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake. Walk through Praça do Comércio, the grand riverside square framed by yellow arcades, then head inland along Rua Augusta. The triumphal arch’s viewing platform is skippable on a tight budget; the surrounding streetscapes are more memorable from ground level. At the elevadores, or funiculars, check whether a ride is included in your transit pass; otherwise, the staircases beside the tracks offer much the same ascent for free.

Take the Elevador da Glória or walk up to Praça dos Restauradores if using a 24-hour transit pass, then continue to Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara for a panoramic view across to the castle. End the afternoon along the Ribeira das Naus waterfront, where benches and lawns face the Tagus. For dinner, look away from the river-facing terraces. In Alfama, Graça or Mouraria, petiscos such as grilled chouriço, bread, olives, cheese and a bowl of caldo verde can make a modest, satisfying meal. Avoid the couvert unless you intend to pay for it; in many restaurants, bread, olives and spreads brought to the table are not complimentary.

 Day Two: Belém and LX Factory

Reserve the second day for Belém, best reached by train from Cais do Sodré to Belém station, a short and reasonably priced journey along the river. Arrive early, because the district’s major monuments attract long queues. The exterior of the Jerónimos Monastery and the Church of Santa Maria de Belém can be admired without a full ticket; if you choose one interior, the monastery’s Manueline cloister is remarkable, but it is the most expensive stop in this itinerary. Budget travellers may prefer the free exterior, the adjoining gardens and the striking Padrão dos Descobrimentos from ground level.

Cross beneath the approach road to see the Belém Tower, a compact Manueline fortress set near the water. Photographs from the surrounding paths are free and often better than a rushed visit inside. Nearby, the Antiga Confeitaria de Belém has sold custard tarts since 1837. One pastel de nata, dusted with cinnamon and icing sugar, remains an affordable rite of passage; expect queues, but they move quickly.

For lunch, choose a neighbourhood tasca rather than a monument-facing café. Grilled fish, rice, salad and a drink can cost less than a mediocre tourist menu. Later, walk inland toward the 25 de Abril Bridge and visit LX Factory, a former textile and printing complex now occupied by bookshops, studios, design stores and cafés. Browsing costs nothing, and the site is useful for travellers seeking modern Lisbon without a museum ticket. The rooftop and street-art views are free; restraint in the shops is essential.

Return uphill at sunset to Miradouro da Senhora do Monte in Graça, one of the least commercial viewpoints in central Lisbon. For a final inexpensive dinner, choose prato do dia, the dish of the day, often served at lunch but sometimes available in simpler eateries in the evening. Pork, chicken, fish or vegetable plates with potatoes and rice generally offer better value than petiscos ordered without discipline.

 Practical Budget Notes

Buy a rechargeable Viva Viagem card and load it with transit credit or a daily pass; trams, funiculars and trains are cheaper this way than buying single tickets on board. Use the famous Tram 28 sparingly, as it is crowded and often less useful than walking plus one short leg by tram or bus. Drink espresso at the counter, seek bakeries away from major squares, and reserve paid sights for those you genuinely care about. In Lisbon, the best experiences are frequently the least expensive: a hillside terrace, a warm pastry, a river breeze and an unhurried walk through tiled streets.

title: legal memorandum|whether a non-compete clause is enforceable under state law
text:
This memorandum analyzes the enforceability of the non-compete clause contained in the employment agreement between our client, a regional residential home security services provider, and its former senior sales representative, under applicable state law, which for purposes of this analysis is the law of Illinois, the state where the employment relationship was centered, the client operates its primary place of business, and the former employee now works for a direct competitor. Under longstanding Illinois common law, as most recently codified in the Illinois Freedom to Work Act (820 ILCS 90/) effective January 1, 2022, non-compete clauses are only enforceable if they meet three core, conjunctive requirements: first, the restriction must be no greater than is necessary to protect a legitimate business interest of the employer; second, the restriction must not impose an undue hardship on the employee; and third, the restriction must not be injurious to the general public. Critically, the 2022 statutory updates impose additional threshold bars: non-competes are per se unenforceable against employees earning less than $80,000 per year (adjusted annually for inflation, at $88,500 for 2024), against employees terminated without cause, and against any employee who was not provided the clause at least 14 days prior to starting employment to allow for review and negotiation.
Applying these standards to the clause at issue, the agreement restricts the former employee from working for any residential or commercial security company, smart home services provider, or home monitoring platform within a 50-mile radius of the client’s 12-county service area for a period of 24 months following separation, regardless of the reason for separation. First, the threshold earning requirement is satisfied here: the former employee earned $112,000 in base salary plus commission in their final year of employment, placing them above the 2024 statutory earnings threshold, and records confirm the clause was provided 18 days prior to their start date, satisfying the notice requirement. However, the clause faces significant enforceability gaps. The client asserts a legitimate business interest in protecting its 18 months of proprietary customer lead lists, proprietary service pricing structures, and 12 years of cultivated customer goodwill tied to long-term service contracts, all interests explicitly recognized as protectable under Illinois state law. That said, the scope of the restriction is likely overbroad on three counts. First, the 50-mile radius extends 22 miles beyond the client’s actual service territory, where the former employee never worked, had no client contacts, and would not be leveraging any proprietary information to the client’s detriment. Second, the 24-month duration is twice the 12-month period repeatedly upheld as reasonable by Illinois state courts for sales employees with direct client contact, particularly given that residential security customer churn averages 11 months in the region, meaning any risk of client solicitation largely dissipates within that window. Third, the restriction applies even if the employee is terminated without cause, a scenario that the statute explicitly bars from non-compete enforcement, though in this case the employee resigned voluntarily to take the competing role, so that bar does not apply here. The clause also imposes limited undue hardship: the competing role offers a 15% pay increase but is based 17 miles outside the client’s core service territory, and the former employee could perform substantially similar work serving commercial clients outside the restricted zone without violating a narrowed restriction, meaning enforcement of a properly tailored clause would not bar him from working in his chosen field. Finally, the public interest is not disserved by a narrowed restriction, as Illinois courts have held that protecting legitimate business investments in customer relationships does not improperly restrict consumer choice or labor mobility when the clause is appropriately tailored.
On balance, the clause as written is likely unenforceable in its current form, but a court would almost certainly apply the state’s “blue pencil” doctrine to narrow the restriction to a 12-month duration limited to the client’s actual 12-county service area, and bar only work that involves solicitation of the client’s existing residential security customers, rather than a total bar on all work in the security industry. We advise the client that pursuing full enforcement of the overbroad clause carries significant risk of a judicial finding the clause unenforceable in its entirety, as well as potential liability for the employee’s attorney fees under the Act’s fee-shifting provision for frivolous non-compete enforcement actions. The client should instead first seek to negotiate a narrowed agreement consistent with state standards before initiating litigation.

title: legislative bill summary|a bill to expand tax credits for small businesses that hire apprentices
text:
Summary: H.R. 4721, the Small Business Apprenticeship Expansion Act of 2025
Introduced: March 12, 2025  
Sponsor: Rep. Elena Marquez (D-CA-37)  
Original Co-Sponsors: Rep. Thomas Hale (R-OH-08), Rep. Priya Mehta (D-NJ-06), Rep. Darrell Sloane (R-TX-25)  
Referred to: House Committee on Ways and Means; House Small Business Committee

H.R. 4721 amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to expand and restructure the existing Apprenticeship Tax Credit (ATC) for eligible small businesses, with the goal of cutting youth and mid-career worker unemployment in skilled trades while reducing the upfront cost of structured work-based learning for firms with fewer than 50 full-time equivalent employees. The bill responds to a 2024 Department of Labor (DOL) Office of Apprenticeship report documenting 612,000 unfilled registered apprenticeship slots nationwide, 68% of which are at small firms that cited administrative and wage costs as their primary barrier to launching programs.

Under current law, businesses claiming the ATC receive a credit equal to 10% of an apprentice’s first-year wages, capped at $1,000 per apprentice per year, with a maximum annual claim of 10 apprentices per firm. H.R. 4721 raises the credit rate to 40% of first-year wages for firms with 25 or fewer full-time equivalent (FTE) employees, and 30% for firms with 26 to 49 FTEs, with a per-apprentice cap of $6,000 for the first year of the apprenticeship and $3,000 for the second year. The annual per-firm cap rises to 25 apprentices. The credit is structured as a partially refundable credit: 60% of the credit amount is refundable for firms with gross receipts of $1 million or less in the prior taxable year, a provision designed to ensure startup and very small firms with limited tax liability can access the benefit.

The bill adds targeted bonus credits for underrepresented apprentice populations. Firms that hire apprentices between the ages of 18 and 24, veterans, formerly incarcerated individuals, or residents of federal Promise Zones qualify for an additional 10% credit on those workers’ wages, raising the total maximum first-year credit to $7,500 per eligible apprentice. It also creates a separate $1,500 one-time credit per new apprenticeship program to cover DOL registration fees, related instructional materials, and up to 8 hours of paid administrative training for a designated on-the-job mentor. This administrative credit responds to a 2024 National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB) survey finding that 72% of small construction, manufacturing, and healthcare firms had never registered an apprenticeship program due to unfamiliarity with federal reporting requirements.

To prevent misuse, H.R. 4721 restricts eligibility to apprentices enrolled in DOL-registered Apprenticeship Programs (RAPs) or federally recognized state apprenticeship agency programs, and requires participating businesses to submit quarterly wage and completion verification forms alongside their annual tax filing. The credit is reduced proportionally for any apprentice who is terminated without cause within the first six months of employment, and firms that claim credits for unregistered programs face a 200% penalty on improperly claimed amounts.

The nonpartisan Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT) estimates the bill will cost $2.18 billion over the 2026–2030 budget window, offset by a 0.2% increase in the federal unemployment tax base wage cap, adjusted annually for inflation. The DOL projects the provisions will create 148,000 new registered apprenticeship positions over five years, with 62% of those slots at firms with fewer than 25 employees. The House Ways and Means Committee marked up the bill on May 7, 2025, approving it by a 28–17 vote, with floor consideration scheduled for the week of June 16, 2025. A companion bill, S. 2294, was introduced in the Senate by Sen. Margaret Hale (R-OH) and Sen. Carlos Mendez (D-CA) on April 3, 2025, and has been referred to the Senate Finance Committee.

Federal Reserve Holds Benchmark Rate Steady as Inflation Cools, Signals Patience on Future Cuts
*WASHINGTON, Sept 18 (Reuters) —*

The Federal Reserve held its benchmark federal funds rate steady at a 22-year high of 5.25% to 5.5% on Wednesday, marking the second consecutive policy meeting with no rate adjustment as central bank officials weigh mounting evidence that inflation is slowing without tipping the U.S. economy into a widely forecast recession.

The unanimous decision by the Fed’s rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) leaves borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and business credit at their highest level since 2001, a deliberate choice policymakers said was designed to ensure inflation continues its downward trajectory toward the central bank’s 2% annual target while avoiding unnecessary harm to the labor market.

In a statement released at the conclusion of its two-day meeting, the FOMC upgraded its assessment of the economy, noting that “recent indicators suggest that economic activity expanded at a strong pace in the third quarter,” a shift from its September characterization of “solid” growth that underscored surprising resilience in consumer spending and business investment despite 18 months of aggressive rate hikes. The committee also acknowledged that job gains have “moderated since earlier in the year but remain strong,” and that “inflation remains elevated,” while adding a new line pointing to “tighter financial and credit conditions for households and businesses” that are “likely to weigh on economic activity, hiring, and inflation,” a nod to a recent surge in U.S. Treasury yields that has done some of the Fed’s work for it by driving up long-term borrowing costs independent of policy changes.

Since the Fed last raised rates in July, inflation data has shown a steady cooldown: the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the central bank’s preferred gauge, rose 3.4% in the 12 months through September, down from a peak of 7.1% in June 2022, while core PCE, which strips out volatile food and energy costs, fell to 3.7% year-over-year, its lowest level since May 2021. Wage growth has also eased, with the Labor Department’s employment cost index rising 4.3% in the third quarter, down from a 4.5% annual pace in the second quarter, reducing fears of a wage-price spiral that could force additional rate hikes.

Speaking at a press conference following the decision, Fed Chair Jerome Powell stressed that policymakers were “not confident yet” that monetary policy was sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation fully back to 2%, and left the door open to an additional rate hike at the committee’s December meeting if progress on inflation stalls. But he signaled that a run of softer data had reduced the urgency for further tightening, noting that “the risks of doing too much versus doing too little are becoming more balanced” after months in which the central bank had prioritized stamping out above-target price increases over all other concerns.

“Given how far we have come, along with the uncertainties and risks we face, the committee is proceeding carefully,” Powell told reporters. “We will make decisions about the extent of additional policy firming and how long policy will remain restrictive based on the totality of the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.”

The decision to hold rates steady comes amid growing optimism on Wall Street that the Fed may be able to pull off a so-called soft landing, in which inflation returns to target without a sharp rise in unemployment or a recession. The U.S. economy grew at a 4.9% annual rate in the third quarter, according to advance government data released last week, far faster than economists had expected at the start of the year, while the unemployment rate held at 3.8% in October, near a 50-year low.

But Powell pushed back against market expectations that the Fed could begin cutting rates as early as March, noting that policymakers had not yet discussed the timing of rate cuts and that it would take “some time” for inflation to fall sustainably to 2%. “The fact is the committee is not thinking about rate cuts right now at all,” he said. “We’re not talking about cutting rates. We’re very focused on the first question, which is: have we achieved a stance of monetary policy that is sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation down to 2% over time?”

Ian Shepherdson, chief economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said in a note to clients that the statement’s reference to tighter financial conditions “is a clear signal that the Fed thinks the run-up in yields has reduced the need for further rate hikes,” but added that Powell “wanted to make clear that rate cuts are a long way off, to stop financial conditions from loosening too much and undoing the work of the past two years.”

The FOMC will next meet on Dec. 12-13, when it will release updated economic projections including its latest forecasts for interest rates, inflation, growth and unemployment. As of September, the median projection among FOMC participants showed one additional rate hike in 2023 followed by two rate cuts in 2024, though several officials have said in recent weeks that the rise in Treasury yields may mean that final hike is no longer necessary. text:
Configuring a home network router for parental controls establishes device-specific access rules, content filtering, and usage monitoring without requiring software on every endpoint. Begin by confirming the router supports parental control features; most modern routers include basic tools, while advanced models offer category filtering, time scheduling, and activity reporting.

Connect a computer to the router using Ethernet or join the default Wi-Fi network. Open a browser and enter the router administration address, commonly 192.168.1.1, 192.168.0.1, or an address printed on the router label. Log in with the administrator credentials. If the defaults are unchanged, use the credentials supplied by the manufacturer, then immediately set a strong administrator password to prevent unauthorized changes.

Before creating restrictions, identify each device on the network. Open the connected devices or DHCP client list, which usually displays hostnames, MAC addresses, and assigned IP addresses. Locate phones, tablets, game consoles, and computers used by children and assign descriptive labels, such as "Child-Tablet" or "Bedroom-PC." For consistent enforcement, configure DHCP address reservation or static IP assignment for those devices. If devices receive changing IP addresses, parental rules may fail to apply after a lease renewal.

Navigate to the parental controls, access control, or family safety section. Enable the feature globally if a master switch is present. Create a child profile or user group, then add the reserved devices to that profile. Grouping devices simplifies management when multiple devices belong to the same child and allows shared schedules or filtering policies.

Set internet access schedules according to household rules. Typical policies block access during homework time, late-night hours, and school-night bedtime. Select the appropriate days and time ranges, choosing between an allow-list model, where internet access is permitted only during defined periods, or a block-list model, where access is always available except during blocked periods. Prefer the allow-list approach for younger children because it defaults to denial outside approved hours. Ensure the router’s time zone and daylight saving settings are correct, preferably using automatic NTP synchronization, because schedule enforcement depends on accurate system time.

Configure content filtering next. Basic routers may allow manual domain blocking, where you enter specific websites such as social media or adult-content domains. More capable routers provide category-based filters covering adult material, violence, gambling, proxies, anonymizers, malware, phishing, and online games. Select the categories to block, but avoid excessively broad categories that may block legitimate educational resources. Some routers support safe search enforcement for Google, Bing, and YouTube. Enable this option where available, as it directs supported search engines to restricted content modes.

For application-level control, inspect whether the router includes application identification or QoS-based service rules. Streaming, gaming, and social media services can sometimes be blocked or scheduled independently. If the router lacks application awareness, create outbound port or domain rules carefully, because incorrect rules can disrupt services for all users. Remember that router controls operate at the network layer and may not perfectly distinguish between individual apps on encrypted services.

Enable logging and reporting if available. Activity logs may show connection attempts, blocked domains, and access times. Review reports regularly with children rather than using monitoring secretly. Notifications can alert administrators when a new device joins the network or when filtering rules are bypassed. Disable remote administration unless it is necessary, and if remote management is used, restrict it to HTTPS and protect it with multi-factor authentication when supported.

Guests and older children may attempt to bypass controls by changing device MAC addresses, using cellular data, connecting to alternate DNS services, or using VPNs. Mitigate these by enabling DNS filtering through the router or a family-safe DNS provider, blocking common VPN protocols selectively, and securing the Wi-Fi with WPA2 or WPA3. Create a separate guest network for visitors and apply either no child restrictions or a distinct policy as appropriate.

After saving the configuration, test restrictions from a child device. Verify blocked sites are inaccessible during scheduled times, allowed sites work correctly, and safe search is enforced. Reboot the router if required, then reconnect all devices. Finally, document each profile, blocked category, schedule, and reserved address, and revisit the rules periodically as children mature and devices change.

Product Review: AudioCore AC720 Mid-Range Active Noise-Cancelling Headphones – Three-Month Long-Term Assessment
As an urban commuter and part-time remote content editor, I spent 12 weeks testing the AudioCore AC720, a mid-range active noise-cancelling (ANC) headphone priced at $179, a segment crowded with brands promising premium features at accessible price points. My testing covered 90-minute daily subway commutes, open-office work sessions, home entertainment, and occasional cross-country work trips, to evaluate performance beyond the controlled conditions of initial unboxing reviews.
Starting with core noise cancellation, the AC720 delivers performance that outperforms most peers in its price bracket for low-frequency ambient noise. During rush-hour subway rides, it reduces the low rumble of train tracks and engine vibration by an estimated 85%, enough to let me listen to spoken-word podcasts at 50% volume without cranking levels to compensate for background noise. It is less effective with sharp, high-frequency sounds: office chatter, the high-pitched beep of crosswalk signals, or a neighbor’s doorbell still cut through at lower volumes, though activating the maximum ANC setting softens these interruptions by roughly 40%. A notable pain point emerged after two months of use: the ANC developed a faint, high-pitched static hiss when activated in completely silent rooms, a flaw not present in the first month of testing that creates mild distraction during late-night work sessions.
Audio performance balances consumer-friendly tuning with enough clarity for regular use. The low end is warm and pronounced without the muddy over-bass that plagues many budget mid-range models, making pop, hip-hop, and electronic tracks feel immersive without drowning out vocal detail. Mids are clear enough for podcast and call use, though classical and jazz listeners may notice a subtle roll-off in upper treble that softens the crispness of string instruments and cymbals. Call quality is a standout for the price: three months of work calls across noisy sidewalks and café environments found that the dual built-in microphones filtered out wind and background conversation consistently, with only one reported instance of a caller struggling to hear me during a particularly gusty walk.
Comfort and build quality hold up reasonably well for daily use, with a few caveats. The memory foam ear cups have enough depth to avoid pressing on my ears even during four-hour work blocks, and the adjustable headband distributes weight evenly enough that I rarely feel the need to take the headphones off to relieve pressure. The plastic chassis feels sturdy enough for being tossed into a work bag, though the synthetic leather on the ear pads developed a small crease along the left edge after eight weeks, a sign of wear that suggests the pads may need replacement within 18 months of regular use. Battery life matches the advertised 30 hours with ANC activated across my testing, and the 10-minute quick charge feature reliably delivered five hours of use when I forgot to charge them overnight, a practical benefit for busy schedules. The physical control buttons on the right ear cup, however, feel stiffer than ideal, and I often fumbled to skip tracks or adjust volume while wearing gloves during winter commutes.
Overall, the AudioCore AC720 is a solid mid-range option for users who prioritize reliable low-frequency noise cancellation, all-day comfort, and strong call quality without paying premium flagship prices. The emerging static in ANC mode and minor wear on ear pads after three months are notable flaws, but they do not outweigh the value the headphones deliver for daily commuting and office use. I would recommend them to budget-focused buyers who do not require studio-grade audio or perfect high-frequency noise cancellation, and who are willing to accept minor long-term wear for a $100+ saving over top-tier ANC models. Flooding forces hundreds from Welsh valley homes  
Hundreds of families were forced to evacuate their homes in a south Wales valley after sustained heavy rainfall triggered severe flash flooding, submerging streets, damaging properties and cutting off key transport links.  

The local council declared a major incident late on Sunday, with emergency services working overnight to rescue residents from ground-floor flats and cottages in the steep-sided [valley name omitted], where water levels rose rapidly within hours.  

Wales has seen repeated flooding events in recent years, linked by scientists to increasingly intense rainfall driven by climate change. The latest downpour follows a week of saturated ground, leaving waterways with little capacity to absorb further rain.  

Emergency responders used boats to reach households trapped by fast-flowing water, while mountain rescue teams and fire crews carried out door-to-door checks in the worst-affected villages. At least two people were treated for minor injuries, officials said.  

A rest centre set up at a leisure centre in the nearby market town housed more than 200 people overnight, with many families describing how they fled with only essential medication, documents and pets. Council staff and charities were providing food, dry clothing and temporary bedding, while a number of hotels also offered rooms.  

“I looked out at about 7pm and the water was already over the wall,” said Carys Morgan, 41, a primary school teacher who left her rented cottage with her husband and two children. “Within 40 minutes it was coming through the front door. We grabbed the children, the dog and as much as we could carry. There was nothing else we could do.”  

Ms Morgan said the family had lived in the valley for six years and had never seen flooding of this severity. “You watch these things on the news and think it won’t happen here,” she said. “But the speed of it was terrifying. The road outside had become a river.”  

The River [name omitted] burst its banks after more than [amount omitted] of rain fell in parts of the area over a six-hour period, according to Natural Resources Wales. Several flood warnings remained in place across the region on Monday morning, urging communities not to attempt to return to properties until safety checks had been completed.  

Abergavenny’s Main Street was among the areas worst hit, with water reaching waist height in places. Shops, a pub, a garage and a medical practice were inundated, while parked cars were swept short distances or left submerged. A section of the A-road through the valley collapsed in one spot, and several smaller routes remained closed due to debris and standing water.  

Rail services through the valley were suspended after floodwater covered tracks and damaged signalling equipment. Network Rail said engineers were assessing the line, but disruption was expected to last throughout the day. Bus companies were running limited replacement services where roads were passable.  

Council leader [name omitted] said the priority was ensuring people were safe and preventing anyone from entering unstable buildings. “This has been an extraordinarily distressing event for our communities,” she said. “Properties have been flooded, possessions have been lost and people have had to leave their homes in frightening circumstances.”  

She added that council teams would begin structural and environmental health inspections as soon as water levels receded, but warned that some homes could be uninhabitable for weeks or longer. “We know people will be desperate to get back and assess the damage, but there are risks from contaminated water, electrics and weakened structures,” she said.  

Emergency services urged drivers not to ignore road closure signs after a small number of vehicles became stranded. South Wales Fire and Rescue Service said it had responded to more than 150 flood-related calls between Sunday afternoon and early Monday.  

Chief fire officer [name omitted] said: “The water on the roads may look calm in places, but it can be deep, fast-moving and hiding debris. People should not drive through it or return to evacuated areas until emergency services and local authorities confirm it is safe.”  

Natural Resources Wales said further showers were forecast, although they were not expected to be as intense. The agency warned river levels could remain high and that surface water could continue to pose a danger.  

Climate experts said the event highlighted the growing risk of flash flooding in hilly regions where steep slopes funnel rain quickly into narrow valleys and built-up areas. With soils already waterlogged after repeated storms, even moderate additional rainfall can produce rapid runoff.  

Communities Secretary [name omitted] said the UK and Welsh governments were in contact with local authorities and that support would be made available through emergency funding schemes. “Our thoughts are with all those who have had to leave their homes,” she said. “We will continue to work around the clock with partners to respond to this incident.”  

For residents gathering at the leisure centre on Monday, the immediate concern was when they might be allowed home and what would remain.  

“My late mother’s photographs, the children’s toys, our furniture—I don’t know what’s salvageable,” Ms Morgan said. “The house can eventually be repaired, but we need answers, support and somewhere stable while this is sorted out.”

title: encyclopedia article|the life and career of a nineteenth-century railway engineer
text:
George Turnbull was born in 1809 in the small Perthshire town of Auchterarder, Scotland, the 11th child of a local surveyor and land agent whose work introduced him to precision measurement and landscape assessment from childhood. After attending Perth Grammar School, he apprenticed at 16 to civil engineer James Jardine in Edinburgh, where he worked on early canal surveys and harbour improvements before moving to London in 1831 to join the office of George and John Rennie, the leading civil engineering firm of the era. His early projects with the Rennies included assisting with surveys for the London and Southampton Railway, and supervising construction of the 18-arch Surrey Quays viaduct, where he first developed a reputation for meticulous cost tracking and strict attention to worker safety, uncommon for a period when railway construction often saw casualty rates as high as one death per mile of track laid.

In 1840, Turnbull was appointed chief resident engineer for the Eastern Counties Railway, overseeing the 54-mile stretch from London to Colchester, where he resolved persistent drainage issues in the Thames marshes by designing a layered embankment of brushwood, gravel and compacted clay that eliminated the regular track subsidence that had plagued earlier attempts to lay rail across the soft floodplain. When the railway mania of the mid-1840s collapsed, leaving dozens of half-finished lines and bankrupt contractors across Britain, Turnbull was retained by the East Indian Railway Company in 1850 to lead construction of the first rail link connecting Calcutta to the upper Ganges plain, a project initially dismissed by many colonial officials as logistically impossible across the region’s monsoon-soaked lowlands and dense river systems.
Over the next 12 years, Turnbull supervised the laying of 541 miles of 5ft 6in broad gauge track, designing 113 major bridges including the 1.5-mile long Son River viaduct, then the longest rail bridge in the British Empire. He insisted on raising track beds three feet above recorded maximum flood levels, a choice that saved the line from total destruction during the catastrophic 1860 monsoon, when competing narrower-gauge lines built to lower specifications were washed away entirely. Unlike many colonial engineers of the period, he prioritized hiring and training local workforces rather than importing large teams of British navvies, establishing on-site technical schools to train Indian masons, surveyors and locomotive fitters, a move that cut construction costs by 40% and created a cohort of local railway workers who would go on to build much of the subcontinent’s later rail network.
Turnbull returned to Britain in 1862, where he served as a consulting engineer for a series of Welsh narrow-gauge mineral lines and sat on the 1867 parliamentary commission investigating railway safety, where he successfully advocated for mandatory block signalling and continuous brake systems on all passenger lines, reforms that reduced railway collision fatalities by 70% over the following decade. He retired to his home in Cornwall in 1877, where he spent his final years compiling detailed memoirs of his railway work and advocating for improved old-age pensions for retired railway navvies, a cause he championed until his death in 1889 at the age of 80. Though less widely celebrated than better-known contemporaries like Isambard Kingdom Brunel, Turnbull’s work formed the backbone of two of the 19th century’s most transformative rail networks, with more than 70% of the East Indian Railway main line he built still in active use for passenger and freight traffic as of the early 21st century. His emphasis on flood-resilient construction, local workforce development and evidence-based safety regulation set enduring standards for railway engineering across the British Empire and beyond. Government Audit Report: Oversight of Veterans' Disability Claim Processing Times

 Audit Objective and Scope

This audit was conducted by the Office of Inspector General to evaluate the Department of Veterans Affairs' (VA) oversight of disability claim processing times. The review covered claims processed between October 1, 2022, and September 30, 2024, focusing on whether the VA established effective controls to meet statutory timeliness requirements, accurately reported processing metrics, and addressed persistent delays affecting veterans awaiting benefit determinations. Audit procedures included data analysis of 1.2 million claim records, site visits to eight regional processing offices, interviews with 75 VA personnel, and surveys of 300 veterans with pending or recently adjudicated claims. The audit also assessed compliance with the Veterans Appeals Improvement and Modernization Act and internal policies governing quality assurance and workload management.

 Background

Veterans filing disability compensation claims rely on the VA to deliver timely decisions that determine access to health care, monthly financial benefits, and dependent support services. The VA's stated operational goal is to complete initial disability claims within an average of 125 days, with a 90-day target for fully developed claims submitted through streamlined documentation channels. During the audit period, the VA reported national average processing times of 184 days for initial claims and 241 days for appeals-related supplemental claims, figures that agency leadership attributed to staffing shortages, increased claim volume following expanded presumptive condition policies under the PACT Act, and complexities associated with military medical records retrieval. Prior audits issued between 2019 and 2022 identified recurring deficiencies in processing time tracking, regional office performance accountability, and veteran communication protocols, prompting this follow-up review to assess corrective action implementation.

 Audit Findings

 Finding 1: Inaccurate and Inconsistent Processing Time Reporting

The audit determined that the VA's national processing time metrics understated actual veteran wait times by an average of 32 days per claim. Agency calculation methodologies excluded periods when claims were pending external records requests from military service departments, private medical providers, and vocational examination vendors. Analysis of a stratified random sample of 400 closed claims found that 68 percent included excluded delay periods ranging from 14 to 127 days, with no standardized documentation justifying their removal from official timelines. Regional offices applied exclusion criteria inconsistently: offices in the southeastern region excluded records request waits in 89 percent of sampled claims, while northeastern offices applied such exclusions in only 31 percent of comparable cases. Additionally, 19 percent of claims listed as completed in the VA's Corporate Case Processing System contained data entry errors, including incorrect receipt dates, misassigned processing timestamps, and duplicate claim records that inflated reported completion rates. These deficiencies prevented leadership from obtaining reliable data to allocate resources and obscured the true magnitude of processing delays from veterans and congressional stakeholders.

 Finding 2: Inadequate Regional Office Oversight and Accountability

The VA's Performance and Accountability Office failed to implement consistent monitoring of regional processing center performance against timeliness standards. Seven of the eight visited regional offices did not maintain formal workload management plans aligned with national staffing models, and four offices reported vacancy rates for claims processors exceeding 28 percent, compared to the agency's authorized 12 percent maximum vacancy threshold. Supervisory reviews required for high-complexity claims involving post-traumatic stress disorder and traumatic brain injury were completed within mandated timeframes for only 42 percent of sampled cases. The audit also found that performance incentive programs for regional executives emphasized total claim output over processing accuracy and timeliness, creating incentives for staff to prioritize simpler claims while complex cases aged beyond 365 days. As of September 30, 2024, approximately 89,000 initial claims and 127,000 supplemental claims had been pending for longer than six months, with 21,000 claims exceeding two years in pending status.

 Finding 3: Deficient Veteran Communication During Extended Delays

Veterans experiencing processing delays did not receive timely, actionable status notifications as required by VA policy. Survey responses indicated that 61 percent of veterans with claims pending longer than six months had not received any written status update beyond the initial claim acknowledgment letter. Agency standards require notification every 30 days when claims exceed target processing times, but the automated notification system was not functional for 11 months during the audit period due to a failed information technology update. Call center data showed that veterans seeking status information waited an average of 47 minutes to reach a representative, and 34 percent of calls were abandoned before resolution. For veterans experiencing worsening medical conditions or financial hardship during prolonged waits, the VA's expedited claim process was not consistently applied: 57 percent of sampled expedite requests lacked documented eligibility determinations, and 41 percent of approved expedited claims still took longer than 90 days to complete.

 Recommendations

The audit makes seven recommendations to the Under Secretary for Benefits. First, revise processing time calculation methodologies to include all periods from claim receipt to final decision, with standardized, auditable criteria for any excluded periods, and implement quarterly independent validation of reported metrics. Second, deploy a centralized workload management system that tracks claim age, complexity, and staffing capacity across all regional offices, with mandatory monthly performance reviews for offices exceeding 150-day average processing times. Third, establish binding staffing targets for claims processing positions, including accelerated hiring schedules for offices with vacancy rates above 15 percent and retention incentives for employees in high-complexity claim units. Fourth, redesign executive performance metrics to assign equal weight to processing timeliness, decision accuracy, and veteran satisfaction rather than claim volume alone. Fifth, repair and test the automated veteran notification system to ensure 30-day status updates for all delayed claims, with mailed notices for veterans without electronic accounts. Sixth, standardize expedited claim procedures with clear eligibility documentation requirements and a 15-day maximum review period for expedite requests. Seventh, create a cross-agency task force with the Department of Defense to reduce military medical records retrieval times to a maximum of 30 days per request.

 Management Response and Conclusion

VA management concurred with all seven recommendations and provided a corrective action plan with target completion dates ranging from March 2025 for notification system repairs to September 2026 for full implementation of revised workload management systems. The Office of Inspector General will conduct follow-up audits at six-month intervals to verify implementation and assess whether processing time transparency and veteran outcomes improve. Reliable oversight of disability claim processing is essential to fulfilling the nation's obligation to veterans who incurred service-connected injuries and illnesses. Without consistent data, accountable regional operations, and proactive communication, systemic delays will continue to impose significant financial and health-related burdens on the veteran population entitled to timely and accurate benefits determinations.

Maple Creek Family Health Patient Information Leaflet | Updated October 2024
*Reviewed by Dr. Lena Marquez, MD, CDE; Lead Dietitian Priya Mehta, RD, CDCES*
*For patients with newly or previously diagnosed type 2 diabetes: non-insulin dependent, not on GLP-1 agonist therapy*

If you left your last appointment with a prescription for metformin and a vague note to “eat better and move more,” you’re not alone: 62% of Maple Creek’s type 2 diabetes patients tell us they get no clear, actionable guidance on lifestyle changes in their first 6 months post-diagnosis. This leaflet is designed to fix that, with targets tailored to our clinic’s patient population, drawn from 2024 American Diabetes Association (ADA) guidelines and 12 years of local patient outcome data.

 Diet: No Fad Diets, Just Measurable Swaps
Skip the zero-carb and “diabetes superfood” trends you see on social media. Our clinic data shows patients who stick to the below targets lower their A1c by an average of 1.2% in 3 months—equal to the effect of adding a second oral diabetes medication, without the side effects.
- Aim for 30–45g of total carbohydrates per main meal, 15g per snack, prioritizing low-glycemic options: rolled oats (not instant), roasted sweet potato, whole-grain sourdough, and black beans. A 2023 ADA study found 100g of cooked white rice (a staple in 41% of our local patient households) spikes blood glucose 28% higher than an equal serving of cooked quinoa; swapping just one weekly rice serving for quinoa lowers 3-month A1c by an average of 0.3%.
- Follow the *Maple Creek Plate Rule* for every main meal: ½ non-starchy vegetables (roasted broccoli, sautéed spinach, raw bell peppers), ¼ lean protein (baked salmon, skinless chicken thigh, lentils, firm tofu), ¼ low-glycemic carb as above. Skip pre-packaged “diabetic” snacks: 90% contain added sugar alcohols that cause blood glucose spikes and GI distress, per 2024 Consumer Reports testing.
- If you drink boba (a weekly habit for 27% of our patients under 45), a standard 500ml taro milk tea with 50% sugar packs 72g of carbs—equal to 4 slices of white bread. Swap for 0% sugar oolong boba with almond milk to cut that to 18g, and limit to one serving every 2 weeks.
- Limit alcohol to 1 standard drink (12oz beer, 5oz wine) per day max, and never drink on an empty stomach: it raises hypoglycemia risk for up to 24 hours after consumption.

 Exercise: No Gym Required
You do not need to run a 5k or pay for a gym membership to see results. Our 2022 patient cohort found these two simple targets lower A1c by 0.8% on average in 3 months, and cut cardiovascular disease risk by 17% over 2 years:
- 10 minutes of light walking within 90 minutes of finishing every main meal: a 2022 *Diabetes Care* study found this habit reduces post-meal blood glucose spikes by 22%—more effective than a single 30-minute daily walk taken at a random time. This can be pacing while on a work call, walking around the block with your dog, or looping the grocery store before you shop.
- 2 days per week of 12 minutes of bodyweight strength training: chair squats, wall push-ups, or glute bridges, done while watching TV. Muscle tissue absorbs 3x more blood glucose than fat tissue during activity, so building even small amounts of muscle lowers resting blood glucose long-term.
- Check your blood glucose before any activity lasting more than 20 minutes: if it is below 100mg/dL, eat a 15g carb snack (1 small apple, 4 saltine crackers) first to avoid hypoglycemia.

 Quick Reference Cheat Sheet
| Target | Goal |
|--------|------|
| Fasting blood glucose | 80–130mg/dL |
| 2-hour post-meal blood glucose | <180mg/dL |
| Weekly exercise total | 210 minutes light walking + 24 minutes strength training |
| 3-month A1c target | <7% (adjusted for your age and health history by your provider) |

If you hit these targets for 3 months, you may be eligible to reduce or discontinue metformin, per Dr. Marquez’s clinic protocol. Book a free 15-minute check-in with Priya Mehta via the clinic patient portal if you need personalized meal plans, glucose log reviews, or free pedometer pick-up (available at the front desk while supplies last, funded by the Maple Creek Community Health Grant, September 2024).

title: encyclopedia article|the history of a small coastal town in Maine
text:
The history of the small coastal town of Brineport, Maine, is woven into the tides of Frenchman Bay, where granite headlands shelter a narrow, ice-carved harbor. Archaeological evidence suggests Wabanaki people, particularly the Passamaquoddy and Penobscot, navigated these waters for thousands of years, harvesting clams, salmon, and seals while maintaining seasonal camps along the shore. Long before European surveyors arrived, the point now called Barter's Head was a meeting place for trade, ceremony, and shared knowledge of the sea.

European settlement began in the 1760s, when Massachusetts, which then governed Maine, granted coastal townships to soldiers and land speculators. The first permanent household is traditionally dated to 1768, when Ephraim Trundy built a log cottage near a freshwater stream and established a tidal weir. Other families followed, mostly fishermen and farmers from southern New Hampshire and coastal Massachusetts. They cleared the lower slopes for hay and potatoes, but the ocean remained the center of economic life. The settlement was incorporated as Brineport in 1798, reportedly after a village vote chose a name suggesting both salt water and safe anchorage.

The early nineteenth century brought growth tied to fishing, shipbuilding, and coastal commerce. Brineport's first wharf was completed in 1804, and a fleet of small schooners soon carried dried cod, lumber, barrel staves, and firewood to Boston, Saint John, and the West Indies. Local shipyards launched more than ninety vessels between 1815 and 1890, ranging from fishing sloops to three-masted coastal schooners. The yards also shaped the town's social geography: ship carpenters, caulkers, blacksmiths, sailmakers, and riggers lived along Harbor Street, while mariners' widows and families maintained homes during voyages that could last months or years.

Brineport residents participated in the broader conflicts of the young republic. During the War of 1812, British patrols threatened Maine's eastern coast, and local militia kept watch from Trundy Ridge. The town's most famous wartime episode occurred in 1814, when villagers hid supplies in the woods and extinguished shore beacons to prevent a British brig from entering the harbor at night. Although no battle took place, the episode became a central story in local memory, commemorated by a stone marker erected in 1912.

By the mid-1800s, Brineport supported a Methodist church, a one-room schoolhouse, several stores, a gristmill, and a customs office. The population peaked in 1880 at roughly 1,400 people. Grand banks fishing, herring pickling, lobster canning, and ice cutting supplemented older trades. Salt cod was spread on wooden flakes near the shore, while lobster canneries offered seasonal wages to women and younger workers. Yet prosperity was uneven. Storm losses, fluctuating fish stocks, and competition from larger rail-connected ports left many families vulnerable.

The arrival of the summer tourist trade transformed Brineport after the Civil War. Artists, teachers, clergymen, and wealthy families from Boston, Philadelphia, and New York discovered the town's rugged views and cool air. Old farmsteads became boardinghouses, and rustic cottages appeared on the bluffs. The Brineport House, opened in 1874, advertised sea bathing, sailing excursions, and "entire freedom from metropolitan excitement." Visitors also commissioned local guides for fishing and hunting, creating a seasonal economy that softened the decline of shipbuilding.

The twentieth century brought both decline and reinvention. The last major sailing vessel was launched in 1919, and several fisheries contracted during the Great Depression. The hurricane of 1938 damaged wharves and cottages, while wartime service drew young people into the military and industrial cities. After World War II, paved roads, automobiles, and expanded electricity connected Brineport more closely to Bar Harbor and Ellsworth. Lobstering emerged as the dominant commercial fishery, while tourism shifted from long summer stays to day trips, weekend rentals, and second homes.

Modern Brineport has about 650 year-round residents. Its working harbor remains central, with lobster boats moored beside excursion craft and pleasure yachts. The historical society occupies the 1892 customs house, and the annual Trundy Tide Festival celebrates boatbuilding, Wabanaki heritage, and seafood. Like many Maine coastal towns, Brineport continues to negotiate change: rising housing costs, climate-driven shoreline erosion, and shifting fisheries test its continuity. Still, the rhythms of fog, lobster traps, wooden boats, and family networks connect present-day villagers to more than two and a half centuries of coastal life.
