McCord's Box Turtle (*Cuora mccordi*)
McCord's box turtle (*Cuora mccordi*) is a small, semiaquatic geoemydid turtle endemic to Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region in southern China. Described in 1988 by herpetologist William Patrick McCord from specimens obtained through the Chinese animal trade, the species remained without a confirmed wild locality for nearly two decades; its native range was only documented by field biologists in 2007, when populations were recorded in the karst evergreen broadleaf forests of central Guangxi's Bama Yao Autonomous County and surrounding Donglan County.

Adults reach a straight carapace length of 14–18 cm, with males distinguished by slightly indented plastrons and longer, thicker tails. The domed carapace bears a warm chestnut-brown hue with a faint pale yellow vertebral keel, while the hinged plastron—capable of closing completely to shield the head and limbs—is marked by bold black radiating streaks on a cream-yellow base. The species occupies cool, shaded headwater streams and moist forest floor habitats at elevations between 400 and 900 m, foraging primarily on earthworms, fallen fruit, and freshwater snails, and laying clutches of 1–3 eggs annually between June and August.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature first assessed *C. mccordi* as Critically Endangered in 2000, a ranking it retains on the 2024 Red List. Surveys conducted across 12 stream catchments between 2010 and 2016 recorded only 17 wild individuals, yielding a mean encounter rate of 0.08 turtles per kilometer of stream transect. Population models published by the Turtle Conservation Coalition in 2018 estimated a total mature wild population of fewer than 250 individuals, with a continuing decline of 10–15% annually, driven overwhelmingly by unregulated collection for the international wildlife trade.

For decades after its description, *C. mccordi* commanded exceptionally high prices in East Asian exotic food and traditional medicine markets, with adult specimens selling for $1,200–$2,000 USD in Guangzhou and Hong Kong markets in the early 2000s. Even after China listed the species as a Class I protected animal under the 2018 revised Wildlife Protection Law, illegal poaching persists: Guangxi forestry authorities seized 21 wild-caught individuals from smuggling networks in 2021 and 2023. A 2022 genetic study of 680 captive turtles across Chinese turtle farms found that fewer than 8% were pure *C. mccordi*, with most stock representing hybrids with the golden coin turtle (*Cuora trifasciata*), severely limiting options for captive assurance colonies.

The species was added to Appendix I of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) in 2000, banning all cross-border commercial trade. Since 2009, the Kunming Institute of Zoology has run a targeted breeding program that released 42 head-started juveniles into a 1,200-hectare protected community reserve in Bama County between 2019 and 2024, with 68% of tracked individuals surviving their first 12 months post-release.

History of Brineport, Maine: Settlement and Maritime Foundations (1762–1890)
Brineport (population 387, 2020 census) is a coastal town in Knox County, Maine, situated on a narrow, sheltered inlet between Penobscot Bay and the western edge of Acadia National Park’s Schoodic District. Its 19th-century history is defined by the tension between its geographic isolation and the global reach of its maritime industries, a dynamic that shaped its demographic, economic, and architectural legacy into the 21st century.

The town’s first permanent European settlement was established in 1762 by three families from York, Maine—led by ship’s carpenter Ephraim Hale—who displaced the Wabanaki Confederacy communities that had harvested clams, herring, and seals from the inlet for millennia. Wabanaki oral histories collected by the Maine Indian Tribal-State Commission in 1999 document that the inlet, known as *Pesamkek* (“place of the smooth clam beds”), was a seasonal encampment site as early as 1200 CE; no formal land cession was ever negotiated with the Wabanaki, a fact acknowledged in a 2022 town proclamation apologizing for the displacement. The settlement was incorporated as Brineport in 1798, named for the natural brine springs along its northern shore that were used to preserve fish for transatlantic voyages.

By 1830, Brineport had emerged as a minor but specialized hub of the Gulf of Maine mackerel fishery, with a fleet of 22 schooners operating out of its 12-foot-deep harbor. Unlike larger nearby ports such as Rockland or Camden, which focused on bulk cargo and shipbuilding, Brineport specialized in “high-grade” salted mackerel packed in locally milled white pine barrels, bound for markets in Boston, Liverpool, and Bridgetown, Barbados. The industry’s wealth funded the town’s surviving historic core: the 1832 Greek Revival Hale House (now the Brineport Historical Society Museum), the 1841 Brineport Congregational Church with its locally quarried granite steeple, and the 1857 one-room schoolhouse that served the town until 1951. Census records from 1850 show that 62% of the town’s working-age men were employed in maritime trades, with a small supporting community of Irish immigrant laborers who arrived in the 1840s to work in the town’s brine processing sheds and barrel cooperages.

The town’s golden age of fishing was cut short by two interconnected crises: the collapse of the Gulf of Maine mackerel stock in the early 1870s, driven by overfishing from New England and Canadian fleets, and the catastrophic Gale of 1879, which destroyed 18 of Brineport’s 21 schooners and killed 47 men—roughly one-third of the town’s adult male population. The disaster left a permanent demographic scar: by 1890, the town’s population had fallen by 42% from its 1870 peak of 912, as families relocated to mill towns in central Maine or joined the westward migration to Oregon’s fishing communities. The remaining residents pivoted to small-scale lobstering and seasonal “rusticator” tourism, welcoming the first wave of wealthy East Coast summer visitors who built cottages on the town’s rocky bluffs starting in 1887.

Unlike many coastal Maine towns that redeveloped their waterfronts for large-scale tourism in the 20th century, Brineport retained its 19th-century harbor layout, with 27 wooden fishing wharves listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978. The town’s 19th-century legacy remains visible in its working waterfront, where multi-generational lobstering families still operate out of the same wharves built by mackerel fishermen, and in the annual Mackerel Memorial Service, held every August since 1880 to honor the men lost in the 1879 gale.

text:
Why Cities Should Ban Cars from Their Historic Centres

Across the world, historic city centres stand as living records of collective memory: medieval alleyways, neoclassical squares, timber-framed markets, and civic buildings that predate the automobile by centuries. Yet today, many of these places are treated primarily as traffic corridors. Private cars funnel through narrow streets, fill ancient squares with noise, and force pedestrians into competition with vehicles that were never part of the urban landscape’s design. Cities should therefore phase out private cars from historic centres, not as a punitive gesture, but as a practical way to protect heritage, improve public life, and make central neighbourhoods more sustainable.

The most immediate reason is safety and street design. Historic centres were built for walking, cycling, horses, and small-scale transport, not for streams of one-tonne machines moving at speed. Narrow pavements, blind corners, and irregular intersections create predictable risks for residents, tourists, children, and elderly people. Cars also dominate space inefficiently. A private vehicle may spend most of the day parked while consuming road and curb capacity that could be used for seating, trees, markets, cycling lanes, or simply safer movement. Removing through traffic does not erase access; it reassigns priority to people.

The environmental case is equally strong. Petrol and diesel vehicles contribute to local air pollution, exposing residents and visitors to nitrogen oxides and particulate matter. In dense historic districts, where streets are often enclosed by buildings, pollution can become trapped at street level. Noise and vibration add further harm, disrupting sleep, stressing communities, and potentially damaging sensitive structures over time. Lower-emission zones help, but they do not fully solve congestion, roadside danger, or the physical occupation of public space. A managed car ban, paired with clean transit and better logistics, can address these problems together.

Historic preservation itself requires bolder transport policy. Cities often protect individual monuments while allowing their surrounding atmosphere to deteriorate. Heritage is not only stone and plaster; it is also the experience of approaching, viewing, and using a place. A square framed by fountains and centuries-old facades loses much of its civic value when used as a shortcut or car park. Restricting vehicles helps cities preserve the scale, tranquility, and walkability that make historic centres meaningful.

Opponents rightly raise concerns about residents, businesses, disabled visitors, deliveries, and emergency services. These concerns must be taken seriously, but they are arguments for intelligent implementation rather than permanent inaction. Permits can preserve access for people who live in the zone or have limited mobility. Emergency vehicles should retain unobstructed routes. Goods deliveries can be scheduled outside peak hours or consolidated through electric cargo hubs. Taxis and ride-hailing services should be regulated under the same rules, rather than allowed to replace private car traffic with circulating vehicles. Businesses often discover that cleaner, calmer streets attract more visitors and encourage longer stays.

Public transport must also improve in tandem. Park-and-ride facilities, frequent buses, light rail connections, accessible shuttles, and secure bicycle parking can make car-free centres convenient rather than exclusionary. Cities should not simply ban cars and hope the system adapts; they must provide reliable alternatives before restrictions take full effect.

A historic centre is not a museum frozen in time. It must remain a functioning place where people live, work, trade, worship, and gather. But preserving that vitality requires choosing the forms of movement that best serve the common good. Removing unnecessary private cars would reduce pollution, protect irreplaceable heritage, prevent injuries, and return streets to the public. The question is not whether cities can afford to make these changes. It is whether they can afford another decade of treating their most historic streets as ordinary roads.

MEMORANDUM
TO: Marisol Hale, Client
FROM: Elias Voss, Lead Employment Counsel, Voss & Nakamura LLP
DATE: October 12, 2024
RE: Enforceability of Non-Compete Clause in Your 2022 Veridian Tech Solutions Employment Agreement Under Minnesota Law

This memo addresses whether the 12-month, 50-mile non-compete clause (NCC) in your August 15, 2022, employment agreement with Veridian Tech Solutions (“Veridian”) is enforceable under Minnesota law, as you prepare to launch your own residential HVAC smart-thermostat installation firm in Brooklyn Park.

First, controlling Minnesota precedent requires non-competes to be supported by adequate consideration at signing, narrowly tailored to protect a legitimate business interest, and reasonable in geographic and temporal scope. You signed the agreement three days after your formal start date as a Senior Sales Associate, when you were already receiving your $72,000 annual base salary and 8% commission structure. In *Freeman v. Duluth Clinic*, 760 N.W.2d 20 (Minn. 2009), the state Supreme Court held that continued employment alone, offered after a worker has already begun their role, does not qualify as sufficient consideration to bind an employee to a post-termination restriction. Veridian offered no signing bonus, promotion, raise, or additional paid time off in exchange for your signature on the NCC; payroll records confirm your compensation did not change in the 90 days before or after you signed. This alone renders the clause void on its face, but two additional flaws reinforce that conclusion.

Second, the clause’s scope is unenforceably overbroad. It purports to bar you from working for “any firm offering commercial or residential HVAC, building automation, or temperature control services” within 50 miles of Veridian’s Brooklyn Park headquarters—territory that covers the entire Twin Cities metro, stretching as far south as Lakeville and east to Hudson, Wisconsin. Veridian’s 2023 year-end revenue breakdown shows it derives 92% of its $14.2 million in annual revenue from commercial HVAC retrofits for office buildings, hospitals, and school districts; residential smart thermostat installations made up just 3.1% of its 2023 billings, entirely limited to high-end custom home projects in the western suburbs. The Minnesota Court of Appeals held in *Overboe v. Farmland Foods*, 697 N.W.2d 632 (Minn. Ct. App. 2005), that a non-compete cannot bar an employee from working in a segment of the industry where the employer does not maintain a meaningful market presence. You never accessed Veridian’s residential client list, per sales manager Tara Mendez’s September 2024 email confirming your entire portfolio was limited to commercial clients in the education sector, so Veridian cannot claim a legitimate protectable interest in preventing you from serving residential customers.

Finally, the clause’s 12-month duration is unreasonable given the fast-evolving smart thermostat market: Veridian’s current lead time for residential installation quotes is 14 days, and its pricing models are updated quarterly, meaning any client information or proprietary sales tactics you were exposed to will be commercially obsolete within four months of your departure, set for October 31, 2024.

For these reasons, we assess there is a 90% likelihood a Hennepin County district court would refuse to enforce the NCC in full. We recommend you proceed with your planned November 1 launch of Northside Home Climate, and notify us immediately if Veridian sends a cease-and-desist letter. We do not anticipate injunctive relief being granted against you should Veridian file suit.

text:
Agricultural Subsidies: Historical Evolution and Contemporary Policy Debates
Agricultural subsidies represent one of the federal government’s longest-standing and most contentious economic interventions, designed originally to stabilize volatile farm incomes but now entangled in disputes over market distortion, environmental impact, and equity. Since their modern inception in the 1930s, these programs have expanded from emergency Depression-era relief into a complex system of price supports, crop insurance premium subsidies, conservation payments, and disaster assistance, with outlays that routinely fluctuate between $10 billion and $30 billion annually, and spiked to more than $45 billion in 2020 amid trade retaliation and pandemic-related disruptions. Understanding the current reauthorization debate requires grounding policy arguments in the structural shifts that have reshaped both American agriculture and the rationale for federal support over nine decades.

The foundational framework of U.S. farm subsidies emerged through the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933, enacted in response to collapsing commodity prices, widespread farm foreclosures, and rural poverty during the Great Depression. The original program paid farmers to reduce planted acreage of seven “program crops”—corn, wheat, cotton, rice, peanuts, tobacco, and dairy—in an explicit effort to align supply with demand and raise market prices to parity levels relative to non-farm goods. Early implementation faced legal setbacks, including a 1936 Supreme Court ruling that struck down the original processing tax funding mechanism, but subsequent legislation cemented supply management, nonrecourse commodity loans, and federal price guarantees as core features of farm policy through the 1960s. The post-World War II era brought gradual policy liberalization: as agricultural productivity surged and global export markets expanded, Congress shifted away from strict supply controls toward more flexible income support, culminating in the 1973 Agricultural and Consumer Protection Act, which introduced target prices and deficiency payments that filled gaps when market rates fell below statutory thresholds.

A defining turn came with the 1996 Federal Agriculture Improvement and Reform Act, commonly called the “Freedom to Farm” law, which sought to phase out most direct commodity payments and eliminate planting restrictions in favor of market-oriented production decisions. The reform proved short-lived: a collapse in global commodity prices in the late 1990s prompted Congress to approve tens of billions in emergency ad hoc assistance between 1998 and 2001, effectively reversing the phaseout. The 2002 Farm Bill formalized a new system of fixed direct payments tied to historical acreage bases, while the 2014 Farm Bill eliminated those fixed payments in favor of expanded subsidized crop insurance and shallow-loss revenue programs triggered by modest declines in farm revenue. Today, the federal crop insurance program—through which the government covers roughly 60 percent of farmer premium costs and subsidizes private insurer delivery and underwriting—accounts for the largest recurring mandatory expenditure in the farm safety net.

Contemporary debate over subsidy policy turns on three core fault lines: distributional equity, trade and market effects, and environmental conditionality. Critics across the ideological spectrum note that more than 90 percent of commodity program and crop insurance support flows to producers of just five major field crops, with roughly 70 percent of total payments accruing to the largest 10 percent of farming operations; many fruit, vegetable, and livestock producers, as well as beginning and socially disadvantaged farmers, have historically received limited support. Fiscal conservatives argue that subsidized insurance encourages planting on environmentally fragile marginal land and insulates large operations from market risk that would otherwise drive efficiency, while progressive advocates emphasize that payment limits written into current law are easily circumvented through complex entity structures. Supporters counter that the safety net remains critical to offsetting inherent sector risks—weather shocks, global price volatility, and uneven negotiating power relative to concentrated input suppliers and grain buyers—and note that countercyclical payments automatically decline in high-price years, as they did during the 2022 commodity boom following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Environmental policy has emerged as the most contentious flashpoint in current farm bill negotiations, particularly around working-lands conservation programs funded through the commodity title. Advocacy groups and many congressional Democrats argue that existing subsidy flows should be tied to adoption of cover cropping, nutrient management, and wetland protection practices to reduce agricultural runoff, cut greenhouse gas emissions, and improve soil health, pointing to data showing that less than 8 percent of cropland is currently enrolled in the largest working-lands stewardship program. Many Republican lawmakers and major commodity groups oppose new cross-compliance requirements, framing them as regulatory overreach that would restrict producer autonomy and raise food costs, while noting that voluntary conservation enrollment has steadily increased since 2018. Parallel disputes persist over the scope of ad hoc disaster assistance, the size of crop insurance premium subsidies for high-revenue operations, and whether support should be recalibrated to reflect the dramatic consolidation of U.S. agriculture since the original New Deal programs were designed for a sector dominated by mid-sized family farms.

This environmental impact statement evaluates the proposed 800-megawatt offshore wind farm located 18 miles off the coast of Atlantic City, New Jersey, covering 122 square miles of federal outer continental shelf, with up to 82 turbines, two offshore substations, and undersea export cables connecting to the onshore grid at the former B.L. England Generating Station site in Upper Township. Construction is projected to begin in 2027, with a 30-year operational lifespan followed by full decommissioning.

For the marine environment, the primary construction-phase impact is temporary noise from pile driving, which could disrupt behavior of North Atlantic right whales, humpback whales, and harbor seals present in the area during seasonal migrations. Mitigation requires 30-minute pre-construction acoustic monitoring by federally permitted marine mammal observers, shutdown of pile driving if protected species are detected within 500 meters, and use of bubble curtain systems to reduce underwater noise levels by up to 90%. Turbine foundations will act as artificial reefs, supporting long-term increases in mussel, crustacean, and local fish populations, though they pose a low risk of entanglement for commercial fishing gear. Undersea cable installation will use jet plowing to bury cables 6 feet below the seabed, causing temporary, localized turbidity that will disperse within 72 hours of work completion, with no long-term impact on seagrass beds or benthic habitats, as sensitive hard-bottom reef areas were excluded from the final cable route.

For coastal and avian environments, post-construction monitoring data from operational East Coast wind farms indicates less than 0.01% annual collision risk for migrating songbirds, shorebirds, and raptors, as most migration occurs at altitudes well above turbine height. Long-tailed ducks and common loons wintering in nearshore New Jersey waters will experience minimal habitat displacement, as the turbine array is sited outside the highest-density foraging zones identified in three years of pre-construction aerial surveys. Onshore cable routing will follow existing utility corridors to avoid coastal wetland disturbance, with horizontal directional drilling used at all beach crossing points to prevent disruption to dune systems, nesting piping plover habitat, and public beach access. There will be no permanent disruption to recreational beach use, with construction at the onshore interconnection point limited to non-summer months to avoid conflict with tourism seasons.

For human communities, the project will generate enough electricity to power 320,000 New Jersey homes annually, reducing regional greenhouse gas emissions by 1.2 million tons per year, equivalent to taking 260,000 gas-powered cars off the road, supporting the state’s 100% clean energy target by 2035. Viewshed analysis shows turbines will appear as small, faint structures on the horizon from most coastal vantage points, with no measurable impact on coastal property values per peer-reviewed studies of existing Northeast offshore wind facilities. Commercial fishing impacts are minimized via a $24 million mitigation fund to compensate for lost access during construction, ongoing cooperative research with local fishing cooperatives to track gear conflict risks, and real-time turbine location data provided to all vessel operators. Low-level construction impacts include temporary increases in construction-related truck traffic near the onshore interconnection, restricted to non-rush hour periods, and minimal electromagnetic field exposure from buried cables, which falls well below federal safety thresholds for human and marine life. Long-term benefits include 300 full-time construction jobs, 50 permanent operations roles, and $18 million annually in local tax revenue supporting coastal community infrastructure and flood resilience projects. No significant disproportionate impacts to low-income or environmental justice communities were identified in the review area.

Flood-hit Welsh valley: Hundreds evacuated as clean-up begins

Hundreds of families spent another night away from their homes after severe flooding swept through a south Wales valley, leaving streets submerged, properties damaged and emergency crews warning that the risk had not fully passed.

Rhondda Cynon Taf council said about 230 households in the lower Cynon valley had been evacuated after the River Cynon and several smaller watercourses rose rapidly during heavy rain on Tuesday evening. Most were placed in emergency accommodation in Aberdare, Mountain Ash and Pontypridd, while others stayed with relatives.

At its height, water reached waist height in parts of Mountain Ash, inundating ground-floor flats, a doctors' surgery and the town's library. Firefighters used boats to reach residents in Duffryn Street and at a residential care home, where 18 people were moved to safety. Residents described a sudden surge rather than a gradual rise, with water pouring off hillsides and overwhelming drains within little more than an hour.

"I looked out at 6.30pm and the road was there," said Sian Rees, 54, who has lived in her terraced house in Oxford Street for 27 years. "By 7.15pm it was coming through the front door. We grabbed my mother's medication, the dog and a bag, and that was it. Downstairs is destroyed."

South Wales Fire and Rescue Service said it had received more than 260 flood-related calls between 17:00 GMT on Tuesday and 03:00 on Wednesday, and carried out 67 rescues. No serious injuries were reported, though a number of people were treated for shock and mild hypothermia. Natural Resources Wales (NRW) had five flood warnings in place for the Cynon, Taff and Rhondda catchments early on Wednesday, later downgrading them as river levels began to fall.

Council leader Andrew Morgan said the scale of damage had surprised even officers used to winter floods. "People think of these events as becoming part of life, but that does not make it any less devastating when water is in your living room," he said. "The speed with which this came through Mountain Ash and Abercynon was exceptional."

Engineers spent Wednesday pumping water from cellars and inspecting three road bridges after debris struck their structures. The A4059 remained closed between Abercynon and Mountain Ash, while bus services were diverted through Aberaman. Network Rail said services between Aberdare and Cardiff Central were unlikely to resume before Thursday lunchtime after floodwater covered the track near Penrhiwceiber.

The Welsh government said it had activated its flood response arrangements and emergency funding would be made available to the worst-affected councils. Climate Change minister Julie James, who visited Mountain Ash, said she had asked officials to examine whether recent dredging and tree-clearance work on tributaries had been sufficient.

For families facing a second night away, however, the immediate concern was the condition of their homes.

Gareth Phillips, 41, his partner and two children, aged seven and 10, were among residents taken to the Aberaman Pavilion leisure centre before being found temporary bed-and-breakfast accommodation. "The children were carried out through the water," he said. "We're safe, but I don't know when we'll get back in. Everything in the kitchen and front room is ruined."

NRW warned that further showers were forecast, though they were not expected to be as intense. It urged residents near rivers to keep checking flood warnings and avoid driving through standing water.

Insurance representatives were due in the valley on Thursday, but council officers warned that some properties may need drying and safety checks before residents can return.

Section 3.7: Marine Mammal and Sea Turtle Impacts, Proposed New Jersey Offshore Wind Energy Project (NJOWE)
*Bureau of Ocean Energy Management | October 2024 Draft Environmental Impact Statement*

The proposed 1.1-gigawatt NJOWE project, sited 13.2 nautical miles east of Atlantic City across 78,420 acres of federal Outer Continental Shelf (OCS), overlaps with designated critical habitat for four federally protected marine mammal species and three threatened or endangered sea turtle species, per 2023 National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) stock assessments. This section analyzes direct and indirect impacts to these taxa across all project phases: pre-construction geotechnical survey, turbine and subsea cable installation, 25-year operational life, and decommissioning.

Survey and pile-driving activities present the most acute near-term risk, primarily via exposure to underwater anthropogenic noise. Pre-construction high-resolution geophysical (HRG) surveys, scheduled to run from April 2026 to June 2027, will produce mid-frequency sonar pings (2–20 kHz) with source levels up to 210 dB re 1 μPa rms at 1 m, which overlaps with the hearing range of North Atlantic right whales (*Eubalaena glacialis*)—a critically endangered species with a remaining population of approximately 360 individuals, whose migratory corridor passes directly through the NJOWE lease area between November and April each year. Installation of 82 14-megawatt monopile turbines will require impact pile driving with peak source levels up to 220 dB re 1 μPa peak at 1 m, sufficient to cause temporary threshold shift (TTS) in hearing for baleen whales at ranges up to 12 km, and permanent threshold shift (PTS) within 1.2 km, per NMFS’s 2023 acoustic exposure criteria. Baseline monitoring conducted across the lease area between 2021 and 2024 recorded 127 right whale vocalization events, 43% of which occurred during periods previously assumed to be low-use for the species.

Mitigation measures proposed by the developer, and refined via agency consultation, include a mandatory seasonal moratorium on all pile driving and HRG survey activity between November 1 and April 30 to align with peak right whale presence; exclusion zones extending 1.5 km from active construction, monitored by NMFS-certified protected species observers (PSOs) with authority to halt operations if a whale or turtle is detected within the zone; and the use of bubble curtain attenuation systems during pile driving, which reduce broadband noise levels by 15–20 dB, shrinking the TTS impact range by an estimated 40%. Even with these measures, quantitative risk modeling estimates that 1.3% of the western North Atlantic right whale population could experience TTS over the 14-month construction period, with PTS risk reduced to <0.001%—below the 0.1% annual threshold set by NMFS for jeopardy determinations.

Indirect impacts from operational turbine noise, electromagnetic fields (EMF) from subsea transmission cables, and long-term habitat displacement present lower-magnitude but persistent risks. Operational turbine noise (140–160 dB re 1 μPa rms at 1 m) is below injury thresholds for all protected taxa, but modeling indicates it will mask baleen whale communication calls within 3 km of turbines, potentially altering foraging or migratory movement patterns for humpback and fin whales. EMF emitted by buried cables (1–2 m below the seabed) will be within the detection range of loggerhead and leatherback sea turtles at ranges up to 20 m from cable routes, though existing studies of operating East Coast wind farms have found no evidence of sustained barrier effects to turtle movement. Long-term displacement of harbor porpoise from up to 7% of the lease area during construction is projected to reverse within 5 years of operations, per monitoring data from the nearby Block Island Wind Farm.

Residual unavoidable impacts include short-term behavioral disruption to marine mammals during non-migratory season construction, and temporary displacement of foraging sea turtles during cable installation, which are not expected to contribute to population-level declines for any listed species, provided required monitoring and adaptive management protocols are enforced for the full project lifecycle. title: op-ed column|why cities should ban cars from their historic centres
text:
Walk through any city’s oldest quarter and the past usually arrives first as noise: the growl of engines, the shriek of reversing lorries, the impatient tap of a horn. Then comes the smell, a cocktail of exhaust and hot brakes, settling over medieval stone, Victorian arcades, or sun-bleached plazas that were built for conversation, not combustion. Historic centres are not merely streets with old buildings; they are shared living rooms, and for decades we have allowed two tons of speeding metal to dominate spaces designed for feet. Cities serious about preserving both their heritage and their quality of life should ban private cars from their historic centres.

The case begins with preservation. Pollution does not merely obscure the view; it eats the architecture. Nitrogen oxides and fine particulate matter blacken facades, erode carvings, and accelerate decay in stone and mortar. Traffic vibration cracks foundations, while the constant pressure of vehicles demands endless road works that alter original surfaces and underground fabric. Venice understands this intuitively, having largely excluded cars, but too many other cities treat exhaust-stained monuments as an unavoidable cost of modern life. A car ban is, in effect, a conservation policy delivered by traffic management.

Then there is safety and simple civility. Narrow lanes, blind corners, and crowded pavements were never engineered for drivers looking for parking. Tourists, children, elderly residents, and delivery vans compete for inches, and the result is too often injury, fear, or death. Removing through-traffic returns the street to the pace at which humans notice one another. Children can walk to school without guardians acting as bodyguards; café chairs can spill outside without forming a crash barrier; cyclists can travel without feeling like contestants in a violent game.

Opponents warn of economic collapse, yet evidence from the dozens of European cities that have pedestrianised central areas points the other way. Freed from cars, streets become destinations rather than corridors. People linger, browse, eat, drink, and return. Retailers often discover that shoppers arriving on foot, bicycle, or public transport spend more over the course of a month than drivers who circle for twenty minutes, dash into one shop, and flee congestion. The businesses most at risk are not necessarily shops but the lazy assumption that every customer must be able to park at the door.

A fair ban, however, cannot be a gesture aimed only at tourists. Residents, disabled people, emergency services, and essential suppliers need reliable access. The sensible model is not a total absence of vehicles but the elimination of private through-traffic, with limited loading hours, accessible permits, zero-emission ambulances and taxis, and excellent park-and-ride connections. Trams, buses, cycling routes, and walking corridors must be improved before the bollards go up, not after. A ban imposed on an underserved neighbourhood becomes punishment; one accompanied by better alternatives becomes liberation.

This is also an issue of climate and public health. Historic districts are often dense, poorly ventilated canyons where pollution accumulates at exactly the height of a child’s lungs. Keeping cars out is one of the fastest ways to reduce asthma, cardiovascular disease, and carbon emissions in the places where people gather most densely. It also sends a message: the city belongs to its inhabitants, not to the storage of private automobiles.

Nostalgia alone is a poor reason to make policy. The point is not to recreate an imagined pre-industrial past, but to repair a mistaken present in which ancient streets are forced to behave like motorways. Historic centres survived plagues, wars, and industrial revolutions; they should not be slowly destroyed by the daily commute. Banning cars is not an act of hostility toward modernity. It is an act of confidence in cities: confidence that their most valuable spaces are meant for people, and that the best way to honour history is to let it be lived in, safely and breathingly, again.

Cambridge, UK – October 16, 2024 – The University of Cambridge today officially announced the launch of the Cambridge Global Centre for Advanced Battery Technology (C-GCABT), a £75 million cross-disciplinary research hub dedicated to delivering breakthroughs in sustainable energy storage, addressing critical gaps in global battery performance, circularity, and supply chain resilience. The centre, which brings together 42 leading researchers from engineering, materials science, chemistry, economics, and public policy, will open its purpose-built laboratory on the university’s West Cambridge Site in January 2025, with initial funding from the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, industry partners including Jaguar Land Rover and Britishvolt, and private philanthropic gifts.
University Vice-Chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice presided over the launch event, joined by UK Energy Security Secretary Claire Coutinho, industry leaders, and early-career researchers who will lead core centre projects. “Energy storage is the linchpin of the global net-zero transition, yet current battery technology remains constrained by limited range for electric vehicles, short grid storage lifespans, reliance on critical rare earth minerals, and end-of-life waste streams that undermine sustainability goals,” Professor Prentice said in her opening address. “C-GCABT will break down traditional academic silos to turn lab-scale discoveries into deployable, equitable solutions that benefit communities in the UK and worldwide, while training the next generation of battery innovation leaders.”
The centre’s research agenda is structured around three core pillars. First, next-generation solid-state battery development: researchers will target 90% higher energy density than current lithium-ion models, 15-minute fast-charging capabilities, and non-flammable electrolyte materials to eliminate safety risks for consumer electronics, electric vehicles, and aviation applications. Second, circular battery systems: teams will design 100% recyclable battery architectures, develop low-cost hydrometallurgical recycling processes that recover 98% of critical minerals including lithium, cobalt, and nickel, and create a digital battery passport framework to track material flows across the full product lifecycle, cutting embedded carbon from battery production by 60% by 2035. Third, equitable global supply chains: policy and economics researchers will partner with institutions in the Global South to develop ethical, localised mineral sourcing and battery manufacturing models, reducing geopolitical supply risks and ensuring low-income countries can access affordable energy storage for off-grid renewable power.

The centre will also launch a dedicated Battery Skills Programme in 2025, offering 60 fully funded PhD positions and 120 industry placement opportunities annually for students from underrepresented groups, as well as free public outreach programmes to build public understanding of energy storage technology.
“Battery technology is not just an engineering challenge – it is a social, economic, and environmental imperative,” said C-GCABT inaugural director Professor Serena Corr, a world-leading expert in sustainable energy materials. “This centre will deliver tangible progress: from batteries that allow remote rural communities to store solar power for 72 hours without grid connection, to EV batteries that last 50% longer than current models, to a fully circular battery economy that eliminates mining-related environmental harm. text:
Configuring Parental Controls on Your Home Network Router
Parental controls on a home network router enable centralized, device-level management of internet access, content exposure, and usage schedules—eliminating gaps that occur when controls are configured only on individual endpoints. This section covers pre-configuration preparation, core rule setup, and validation for most consumer and small-business routers running current firmware. Before making changes, back up your existing router configuration via the web administration panel (typically under System > Backup/Restore) to enable fast rollback if rule conflicts disrupt network access.

 Pre-Configuration: Device Inventory and Access Prerequisites
First, compile a complete inventory of devices that require restrictions, and map each to a fixed network identity. Dynamic DHCP address assignment will break access rules over time, as devices receive new IP addresses on lease renewal. For each child’s device (laptop, tablet, game console, smart TV, IoT device), locate its unique MAC address in the device’s network settings, then create a static DHCP reservation in your router’s LAN > DHCP Server menu. Tie the MAC address to a persistent local IP and add a clear descriptive label (e.g., “Child-Tablet-iPad”) to avoid misapplying rules to adult or work devices.

Next, confirm your router administrator account uses a unique, non-default password not shared with children; otherwise, users on the local network can modify or disable controls directly. If your router supports separate administrator and user access tiers, restrict configuration access to the admin account only. Firmware should be updated to the latest vendor release before configuration, as older firmware often lacks modern content filtering categories and contains known bypass vulnerabilities.

 Core Rule Configuration
Access the parental controls menu (labeled Parental Controls, Access Restrictions, or Content Filtering depending on vendor) and create a distinct policy profile for each child or user group, rather than applying a single global rule set. Assign the reserved IP addresses of relevant devices to the appropriate profile.

 1. Access Scheduling
Define time-based access rules aligned with household routines. Most routers support both daily recurring schedules and one-time exceptions. For school nights, for example, you may block general internet access from 22:00 to 06:30, while allowing continuous access to approved educational domains if the router supports whitelist exceptions during blocked windows. Avoid blocking all traffic during scheduled homework periods; instead, combine scheduling with content category restrictions. Ensure time settings in System > General Setup match your local time zone and enable NTP synchronization, as incorrect clock settings are the most common cause of misfired schedule rules.

 2. Content and Domain Filtering
Use the router’s category-based filtering to block access to adult content, violence, gambling, anonymizer/proxy services, and peer-to-peer file sharing. Enabling proxy and VPN blocking is critical, as these services allow users to bypass DNS-based content filters. For granular control, add domain-level blacklists for specific services (e.g., social media platforms during school hours) and whitelists for approved learning resources.
If your router supports custom DNS, configure it to use a family-safe recursive DNS service in WAN > DNS Settings, and disable DNS override by LAN clients to prevent devices from using public unfiltered DNS (such as 8.8.8.8) to bypass rules. For routers with built-in SafeSearch enforcement, enable the feature to force filtered results across search engines and video platforms.

 3. Usage Limits and Application Controls
Where supported, configure per-device daily or weekly data/time quotas for entertainment traffic. Some routers include deep packet inspection (DPI) to identify and throttle or block specific applications (games, streaming, messaging) independent of domain filters. Apply these restrictions only to assigned child profiles to avoid impacting work devices.

 Post-Configuration Validation and Maintenance
After saving policies, validate behavior on each restricted device: test access during both allowed and blocked time windows, attempt to reach blocked categories and known proxy sites, and confirm whitelisted resources remain reachable. Verify that adult devices are assigned to an unrestricted profile and retain full connectivity.
Review router logs weekly to review blocked connection attempts and identify attempted bypass methods. Update static reservations when new devices join the network, and adjust category and schedule rules as usage needs change. Keep firmware updated, and periodically test whether DNS over HTTPS (DoH) or alternate DNS settings on endpoints circumvent filtering; if your router does not natively block DoH, add firewall rules to drop traffic to known public DoH endpoints.

title: travel guide|two days in Lisbon on a budget
text:
Wake up your first morning in Lisbon’s Alfama district, where you can grab a €1.20 pastel de nata and a €1 espresso from a street corner bakery instead of sitting at a tourist-facing cafe, saving you at least €3 per person. Skip the paid viewpoints like the Santa Justa Lift’s upper platform, which charges €5 for entry; instead, climb the winding cobblestone lanes a 10-minute walk up to Miradouro da Senhora do Monte, the city’s highest free viewpoint, where you can spread out a small grocery store picnic of €2 local cheese, €1 crusty bread, and a €1.50 bottle of crisp vinho verde from the nearby mini-mercado while you watch terracotta rooftops stretch to the Tagus River. You won’t pay a cent to wander the narrow lanes of Alfama, where stray cats curl on sun-warmed stone steps and street musicians play fado for loose change; if you duck into the small, neighborhood fado bars in the late afternoon, many host free impromptu sets from local singers without the €20+ cover charge of the tourist-focused dinner shows. For lunch, pop into a family-run tasca off the main lanes, where a daily prato do dia (plate of the day) of bacalhau à brás or grilled sardines with salad and potatoes costs €7-9, half the price of restaurants on the main squares.
In the afternoon, walk 20 minutes downhill to the Baixa district, and skip the €3 hop-on hop-off bus by taking the iconic yellow 28 tram for the standard €1.50 public transit fare (remember to tap a reusable Viva Viagem card you buy for €0.50 at any metro station, to avoid the €3 on-board surcharge). Ride the tram all the way up to the Graça district, where you can wander the free community gardens at Miradouro da Graça, another unobstructed viewpoint that rarely draws the big crowds of the more famous paid lookouts. For dinner that night, head to the Time Out Market, but skip the high-end chef stalls and head for the back counters where local vendors sell €6 bifana pork sandwiches and €2 glasses of cold Super Bock beer, letting you eat for under €10 while you soak up the lively atmosphere. Grab a bed in a well-rated central hostel dorm for €18-22 a night, or split a basic Airbnb in Alfama or Graça for €30 total if you’re traveling with a friend, keeping accommodation costs low.
On your second day, catch the €3.30 round-trip commuter ferry from Cais do Sodré across the Tagus to Cacilhas, a quiet riverside neighborhood where you’ll get the best postcard views of Lisbon’s skyline for the price of a transit ticket, no paid river cruise required. Wander the waterfront promenade, where old fishermen repair nets by the docks, and grab lunch at a waterfront tasca serving €8 grilled octopus salad, far cheaper than the seafood spots in central Lisbon. If you’re craving beach time, walk 10 minutes from the ferry terminal to Praia de Cacilhas, a small pebbled public beach with free entry, where you can relax for an hour or two without paying for the train out to Cascais. In the late afternoon, take the ferry back and walk to LX Factory, a repurposed industrial complex where you can wander free street art murals, browse independent bookstores, and pop into small art galleries with no entry fee; skip the pricey rooftop bars and grab a €1.80 cold beer from a corner convenience store to sip as you watch the sunset over the bridge. For your final meal, seek out a neighborhood churrascaria in the residential Bairro Alto edges, where a half portion of peri-peri chicken with fries costs €6, enough to fill two people if you split a small side salad. Skip the overpriced souvenir shops selling mass-produced sardine tins; pick up small jars of local jam or tinned sardines from regular grocery stores for €2-3 each as cheap, authentic takeaways. Over the two days, you can easily stick to a budget of under €80 per person, including accommodation, meals, transit, and small treats, without skipping the best parts of the city.

UNIVERSITY OF PENNINGTON ANNOUNCES ESTABLISHMENT OF GLOBAL CENTRE FOR ADVANCED BATTERY TECHNOLOGY

New Interdisciplinary Research Hub Will Accelerate Sustainable Energy Storage Innovation, Workforce Development, and Industry Collaboration

PENNINGTON, United Kingdom – 12 October 2024 – The University of Pennington today announced the launch of the Global Centre for Advanced Battery Technology (GCABT), a state-of-the-art interdisciplinary research facility dedicated to accelerating breakthroughs in next-generation energy storage, sustainable battery manufacturing, and circular lifecycle solutions. The centre will address pressing global demand for reliable, low-cost, and low-carbon power storage supporting the transition to renewable energy and electric mobility.

Located within the University’s newly expanded Science and Engineering Quarter, the GCABT brings together more than 40 leading researchers from materials science, chemical engineering, electrochemistry, data science, environmental policy, and industrial sustainability. The University is investing £28 million in the facility, supported by a £12 million award from the National Clean Technology Fund and contributions from industry partners. The centre will feature dedicated dry-room laboratories, high-resolution materials characterisation equipment, pilot-scale cell fabrication capabilities, and advanced safety testing systems.

Professor Elena Marsh, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Pennington, said the new centre reflects the institution’s commitment to research with measurable societal and environmental impact.

“Battery technology is fundamental to the world’s ability to decarbonise transport, integrate renewable energy, and build more resilient energy systems,” Professor Marsh said. “The Global Centre for Advanced Battery Technology will position the University of Pennington at the centre of that transformation, connecting excellent fundamental research with practical industrial application and responsible environmental innovation.”

The GCABT will focus its work on four strategic research areas: solid-state and lithium-ion alternatives, fast-charging and high-density energy storage, battery safety and predictive diagnostics, and recycling and material recovery. Researchers will also explore sodium-ion, lithium-sulfur, and other emerging chemistries designed to reduce dependence on critical minerals and improve the sustainability of future battery supply chains.

A key priority for the centre will be bridging the gap between laboratory discovery and commercial production. Through its Battery Innovation Partnership Programme, the GCABT will collaborate with automotive manufacturers, energy companies, materials suppliers, and recycling specialists to test prototypes, scale production processes, and develop standards for performance, safety, and sustainability. The University said eight founding industry partners have already signed agreements supporting joint research, student placements, and shared access to pilot facilities.

Dr Raj Patel, appointed as the centre’s inaugural Director, said the facility’s integrated approach would help overcome barriers that often slow the deployment of new battery technologies.

“The challenge is not simply to invent a better cell,” Dr Patel said. “We must develop batteries that are safer, more durable, ethically sourced, efficiently manufactured, and recoverable at end of life. By combining materials research, engineering scale-up, data analytics, and lifecycle analysis under one roof, the GCABT will move ideas from discovery to demonstration with greater speed and confidence.”

The centre will also play a major role in training the next generation of clean energy specialists. Starting in September 2025, the University will launch new doctoral training programmes, industrial fellowships, and continuing professional development courses focused on battery science and sustainable manufacturing. The GCABT is expected to support more than 60 PhD students and 25 postdoctoral researchers within its first three years.

Local and regional leaders welcomed the announcement, noting that the facility is expected to strengthen the area’s growing advanced manufacturing and clean technology ecosystem. The University estimates that the centre will create approximately 85 direct positions, including academic, technical, and operational roles, while generating additional opportunities through industry partnerships and research commercialisation.

The GCABT will begin operations in January 2025, with full research and pilot-scale facilities expected to be operational by autumn 2025. An official opening event is planned for September 2025, bringing together academic leaders, government representatives, industry partners, and investors.

About the University of Pennington

The University of Pennington is a research-intensive institution recognised for excellence in engineering, environmental science, advanced materials, and sustainable technology. Through interdisciplinary collaboration and strong partnerships with industry and the public sector, the University delivers innovative solutions to global challenges in clean energy, climate resilience, and advanced manufacturing.

text:
*Rafetus swinhoei* (Swinhoe's Softshell Turtle)
*Rafetus swinhoei*, commonly known as Swinhoe’s softshell turtle, the Yangtze giant softshell, or locally as the *yuanbie*, is a critically endangered freshwater trionychid endemic to East Asia, with a historic range spanning the lower Yangtze and Red River drainages of southern China and northern Vietnam, and isolated fossil records from Taiwan dating to the late Pleistocene. First formally described by John Edward Gray in 1873 from a specimen collected in Shanghai by British naturalist Robert Swinhoe, the species ranks among the largest freshwater turtles on Earth: adult males reach a carapace length of 100 cm and mass of up to 210 kg, with flattened, leathery olive-grey shells marked by faint yellow periorbital streaks that fade with age, and elongated, snorkel-like snouts adapted for benthic foraging on fish, crustaceans, and riparian vegetation.
The species’ catastrophic decline tracks decades of unregulated exploitation, habitat fragmentation, and pollution across its range. Hunted for centuries for its meat, considered a luxury food in southern Chinese markets, and its carapace, used in traditional Chinese medicine preparations marketed as a cure for fevers and circulatory ailments, *R. swinhoei* populations collapsed by 99% between 1950 and 2000, according to 2018 IUCN Red List assessments. The construction of the Three Gorges Dam (completed 2006) and smaller cascade dams on the Red River eliminated 80% of the species’ known spawning sandbars, while untreated agricultural runoff and industrial discharge reduced prey biomass in remaining habitats by 60% between 1990 and 2010, per surveys by the Kunming Institute of Zoology.
As of 2024, only three confirmed wild individuals are known to exist: a 130 kg male first documented in Dong Mo Lake, Hanoi, Vietnam, in 2007, and two individuals (sex unconfirmed) detected in separate 2020 and 2023 environmental DNA (eDNA) surveys in separate 15-kilometer stretches of the Yunnan section of the Red River. The last known captive female, held at Suzhou Zoo in Jiangsu, China, died in April 2019 following a failed artificial insemination attempt, ending a 13-year coordinated breeding program that sought to match her with a 110-year-old male transferred from Changsha Zoo in 2008. That male remains at Suzhou Zoo, the only confirmed captive individual of the species.
Conservation efforts are now coordinated across the IUCN Tortoise and Freshwater Turtle Specialist Group (TFTSG), the Asian Turtle Program (ATP), and Chinese and Vietnamese wildlife authorities, with ongoing eDNA surveys of under-monitored Red River tributaries in Yunnan and Laos to locate additional individuals, and 24-hour patrols of Dong Mo Lake to prevent poaching and disturbance during nesting season (May–July). Local community outreach programs in Vietnamese riverside villages, launched in 2018, have trained 120 resident monitors to report sightings and enforce no-fishing zones around confirmed *R. swinhoei* habitats, though the species’ extreme rarity, low reproductive rate (females lay an average of 20 eggs per clutch per year, with a 30% hatching rate in wild conditions), and persistent demand for turtle products in regional black markets mean its long-term survival remains precarious. title: market research report|consumer demand for electric bicycles in Europe
text:
Europe has become one of the world’s largest and fastest-growing markets for electric bicycles, supported by environmental awareness, urban congestion, high fuel prices, improved cycle infrastructure and government incentives. Consumer demand is no longer limited to cycling enthusiasts; e-bikes are increasingly purchased by commuters, older riders, families and delivery workers as practical substitutes for cars and public transport.

Germany, the Netherlands, France, Italy, Spain and the Nordic countries represent the major national markets. Germany remains the largest by value, with strong demand for mid-range and premium city and trekking e-bikes. The Netherlands already has high bicycle ownership, but electrification continues as riders replace conventional bikes. France and Italy have grown rapidly through purchase subsidies, commuting schemes and expanding bike lanes. Spain’s market is smaller but expanding quickly, especially in tourist cities and hilly urban areas. Northern Europe shows high willingness to pay for quality, sustainability and integrated digital features.

Consumer motivations vary by segment. Daily commuters value reliability, low operating cost, parking convenience and reduced travel time. They typically seek comfortable upright designs, integrated lighting, mudguards, racks and batteries with enough range for weekly travel. Older consumers are a key demand group because e-bikes reduce physical strain, make hills and headwinds manageable and support independent mobility. Recreational riders use e-bikes for touring and weekend exercise, while families show increasing interest in cargo e-bikes for school runs and shopping. Food and parcel delivery firms also create substantial demand for durable, long-range models, though this is partly a business-to-business segment.

Product preferences are shifting from basic conversion-style bicycles toward purpose-built e-bikes. Mid-drive motors remain popular in premium city and trekking models because of their balanced ride and efficiency, while hub-drive motors remain common in affordable urban bicycles. Removable batteries are expected by most consumers because many European homes lack outdoor charging. Riders increasingly ask for ranges of 50 to 120 kilometres, depending on use. Display quality, motor responsiveness, braking performance, weight, security features and after-sales service are becoming more important than motor power alone.

Price is still the main barrier. Mass-market consumers often consider e-bikes expensive compared with conventional bicycles, even when fuel and parking savings are clear. Demand is strongest between roughly 1,800 and 3,500 euros for city and trekking models, while premium and cargo models often exceed 4,000 euros. Subsidies, employer benefit schemes, tax reductions and trade-in programmes have a strong effect on purchase timing, but consumers are also sensitive to changing policy conditions. Financing, leasing and subscription models are becoming more common, particularly in Germany, France and the Netherlands.

Safety and theft concerns strongly influence buying behaviour. European consumers prefer established brands, certified components, hydraulic disc brakes, robust locks, GPS tracking and integrated lighting. Cargo e-bike buyers pay special attention to braking, stability, child restraints and weather protection. Because e-bikes are heavier and often used in traffic, rider education and maintenance services also matter.

The retail landscape is hybrid. Traditional independent bicycle dealers remain essential for test rides, fitting, servicing and warranty support, especially for premium models. Online sales are growing, but consumers remain cautious about assembly, software updates, returns and long-term servicing. Brands that combine online information and ordering with local service networks have a competitive advantage.

Looking ahead, demand is expected to keep growing, though at a more rational pace after recent pandemic-era expansion. Market maturity will bring greater price competition, stricter regulation and consolidation among brands. The strongest opportunities lie in dependable commuter models, accessible senior-oriented bikes, family cargo bikes, connected anti-theft systems and flexible leasing. Long-term growth will depend less on novelty and more on affordability, infrastructure, safety, battery confidence and accessible maintenance. Overall, European consumers increasingly view e-bicles as credible everyday transport rather than recreational luxuries, making the market structurally attractive for brands that can balance quality, service and cost.

title: legal memorandum|whether a non-compete clause is enforceable under state law
text:
LEGAL MEMORANDUM
TO: Supervising Attorney, Employment Law Practice
FROM: Associate, Employment Litigation Team
DATE: October 12, 2024
RE: Enforceability of Non-Compete Clause in Ms. Elena Marquez’s Employment Contract Under Illinois State Law
QUESTION PRESENTED
Under Illinois’ Freedom to Work Act (820 ILCS 90/) and binding state appellate precedent, is the 18-month, 50-mile non-compete clause in Ms. Marquez’s 2022 employment contract with Veridian Tech Solutions enforceable, given her $83,000 annual base salary, her role as a mid-level client success associate, and the clause’s broad restriction barring work with any firm offering competing SaaS products for small business payroll management?
BRIEF ANSWER
The clause is almost certainly unenforceable. First, the clause fails the statutory threshold: Illinois’ 2024 amended Freedom to Work Act only permits non-competes for employees earning at least $105,000 in annualized salary, a threshold Ms. Marquez does not meet. Second, even if the salary threshold were satisfied, the clause’s overbroad geographic scope, lengthy duration, and lack of narrow tailoring to protect a legitimate business interest would render it unenforceable under longstanding state common law standards.
FACTS
Ms. Marquez was hired as a mid-level client success associate at Veridian in July 2022, with an annual base salary of $83,000 and no performance-based equity or bonus structure that would lift her total annual compensation above $90,000 in any year of employment. Her role involved routine check-ins with 120 assigned small business clients, troubleshooting platform access issues, and relaying client feedback to the product team; she did not have access to Veridian’s proprietary source code, secret product development roadmaps, or trade secret client pricing algorithms. The contract she signed on her first day includes a non-compete clause barring her from working for any firm offering payroll-focused SaaS products to small businesses within a 50-mile radius of Veridian’s Chicago headquarters for 18 months after her departure. Ms. Marquez resigned in September 2024 to take a client success role at PaySimple Inc., a competing SaaS firm located 32 miles from Veridian’s office, and received a cease-and-desist letter from Veridian last week demanding she abandon the new role or face litigation.
DISCUSSION
Illinois courts apply a two-part framework to evaluate non-compete enforceability: first, compliance with statutory requirements under the Freedom to Work Act, and second, satisfaction of the common law “rule of reason” test. Statutorily, Public Act 103-0218, which took effect January 1, 2024, sets a minimum annual compensation threshold for enforceable non-competes, adjusted annually for inflation; for 2024, that threshold is $105,000 for non-exempt and mid-level employees. 820 ILCS 90/5. Veridian incorrectly cites the 2021 threshold of $75,000, but the 2024 amendment applies retroactively to contracts enforced after its effective date per *McElroy v. RPM Construction*, 2023 IL App (1st) 230114. As Ms. Marquez’s total annual compensation never exceeded $89,400, the clause is statutorily void on its face.
Even if the salary threshold were met, the clause fails the common law test, which requires non-competes to be (1) ancillary to a valid employment relationship, (2) supported by adequate consideration, (3) narrowly tailored to protect a legitimate business interest (such as trade secrets or near-permanent client relationships), (4) reasonable in geographic and temporal scope, and (5) not unduly harsh to the employee or harmful to the general public. *Reliable Fire Equipment Co. v. Arredondo*, 2011 IL 111871. Veridian claims it needs the clause to protect its client relationships, but Ms. Marquez did not have exclusive, long-term control over client accounts; clients were reassigned to different associates every six months per company policy, and she had no access to confidential pricing data. The 50-mile radius covers the entire Chicago metropolitan area, where 78% of regional SaaS payroll firms operate, and the 18-month duration is twice the 9-month period Illinois courts have found reasonable for client-facing roles without trade secret access, per *Instant Technology v. DeFazio*, 2014 IL App (1st) 133309. The clause would bar Ms. Marquez from working in her chosen field across the region, imposing an undue hardship that outweighs Veridian’s minimal protectable interest.
CONCLUSION
Veridian’s non-compete clause against Ms. Marquez is unenforceable under Illinois statutory and common law. We recommend sending a response letter to Veridian citing the statutory compensation threshold and relevant precedent, and advising Ms. Marquez she may proceed with her new role without liability. Managing Type 2 Diabetes with Diet and Exercise  
Patient Information Leaflet — Published March 2024 by Dr. Eleanor Voss, Consultant Diabetologist, St. Jude’s Community Health Trust  

A diagnosis of type 2 diabetes does not mean giving up the foods you love or spending hours in a gym. Small, steady changes to what you eat and how you move can lower blood glucose, reduce medication needs, and cut the risk of complications such as nerve damage, kidney disease, and heart attack. This leaflet explains what to do, why it matters, and how to begin safely.  

 Understanding the numbers

Type 2 diabetes develops when the body cannot use insulin effectively, causing glucose to build up in the blood. For most adults, the agreed target is:

- HbA1c: 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or below at diagnosis, with an individualised target usually between 48 and 53 mmol/mol  
- Fasting plasma glucose: 5–7 mmol/L  
- Glucose 2 hours after meals: below 9 mmol/L  
- Blood pressure: below 140/90 mmHg, or below 130/80 mmHg if you have kidney or eye complications  

Your GP or practice nurse will check your HbA1c every 3–6 months until it is stable, then annually.

 Eating well: practical changes

Diet helps by slowing the absorption of carbohydrate and reducing the amount of glucose entering the bloodstream after meals.

1. Choose lower-glycaemic-index carbohydrates. Replace white bread, instant noodles, and mashed potato with granary bread, porridge oats, bulgur wheat, sweet potato, and basmati rice. Aim for roughly one fist-sized portion of carbohydrate per meal.  
2. Fill half your plate with non-starchy vegetables. Try spinach, broccoli, courgettes, peppers, cabbage, and green beans. One quarter should be lean protein — chicken, turkey, fish, eggs, tofu, beans, or lentils — and one quarter a starchy food.  
3. Reduce added sugar. Avoid sugary drinks, sweetened cereals, and large quantities of cake or biscuits. Fresh fruit is fine; aim for 2–3 portions a day and choose whole fruit rather than juice, which can rapidly raise glucose.  
4. Use healthier fats. Olive or rapeseed oil, avocado, nuts, and oily fish such as salmon or mackerel support heart health. Limit processed meats, butter, palm oil, and deep-fried foods.  
5. Keep alcohol within limits. Current UK guidance advises no more than 14 units a week, spread across several days, with several alcohol-free days. A pint of standard lager is about 2 units; a medium glass of wine is around 2.3 units.  

Reading labels helps. Look for “green” or “medium” values for sugars, saturated fat, and salt using the front-of-pack traffic-light scheme.

 Becoming more active

Exercise improves insulin sensitivity for up to 48 hours after a session. Current guidelines, updated by the Association of British Clinical Diabetologists in 2023, recommend:

- At least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity each week, such as brisk walking, cycling, swimming, or dancing — roughly 30 minutes, five days a week.  
- Resistance exercise twice a week, for example squats, wall press-ups, lifting light weights, or using resistance bands. Stronger muscles use glucose more efficiently.  
- Breaking up sitting every 30 minutes with a short walk or simple stretching.  

If you have not exercised recently, begin gently: ten minutes of comfortable walking after lunch, building by five minutes each week. Wear well-fitting shoes and inspect your feet daily for blisters or redness.

 Getting started safely

Ask for a referral to an NHS dietitian or the free Healthier You Diabetes Prevention Programme. Keep a food and activity diary for two weeks; many people find this reveals habits they can adjust without feeling deprived. Contact your GP before starting vigorous exercise if you have chest pain, severe neuropathy, or proliferative retinopathy.

For further information, contact the St. Jude’s diabetes nursing team on 01632 960 442, Monday to Friday, 9am–5pm.

title: encyclopedia article|the life and career of a nineteenth-century railway engineer
text:
Isambard Kingdom Brunel (1806–1859)
 Career: The Broad Gauge and Railway Infrastructure, 1833–1845
In 1833, at the age of 27, Isambard Kingdom Brunel was appointed chief engineer of the newly incorporated Great Western Railway (GWR), a scheme conceived to link London to the major Atlantic port of Bristol and, as Brunel would later argue, to form the first leg of a seamless integrated transport network connecting Britain to transatlantic shipping routes and imperial trade networks. His appointment followed a well-received survey of the proposed route, which avoided the steep gradients and sharp curves that limited speeds on earlier intercity lines such as the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, prioritising gentle alignments that would permit reliable, high-speed long-distance travel.

Brunel’s most controversial decision for the GWR was his rejection of the 4 foot 8½ inch (1,435mm) track gauge that had become the de facto standard on northern English railways, derived from the wheel spacing of pre-industrial colliery wagons. After conducting trials on track sections laid across his father’s Thames Tunnel worksite, he settled on a 7 foot ¼ inch (2,140mm) broad gauge, arguing that the wider spacing would allow for larger, more stable rolling stock, lower centre of gravity, and sustained running speeds of up to 60 miles per hour—double the average speed of standard gauge services at the time. The decision drew fierce criticism from railway promoters and rival engineers, most notably George Stephenson, who decried the unnecessary capital expenditure of constructing a non-interoperable network, but Brunel defended the choice in testimony to the 1845 Gauge Commission as a forward-looking investment that would avoid the permanent constraints of a gauge “born of the mine, not of scientific calculation.”

The GWR’s main line, opened in stages between 1838 and 1841, showcased Brunel’s gift for elegant, structurally efficient civil engineering. The Box Tunnel, at 1.83 miles the longest railway tunnel in the world when completed, was driven through oolitic limestone outside Bath at a cost of more than 100 worker lives, its alignment deliberately set so that the rising sun on Brunel’s birthday, 9 April, shines through its full length. The route also included the Wharncliffe Viaduct at Hanwell, the first major railway structure to use hollow, cellular brick piers to reduce weight and material cost, and the Maidenhead Railway Bridge, whose two semi-elliptical brick arches remained the flattest, widest-span brick arches in the world for more than a century, defying contemporary critics who predicted the structure would collapse under the weight of passing trains. When the first through service ran from London Paddington to Bristol Temple Meads in June 1841, *The Times* praised the line as “the most perfect work of its kind in existence,” noting that its gentle gradients allowed passengers to travel the 118-mile route in under four hours, a journey that had taken 12 hours by stagecoach a decade earlier.

Brunel’s tenure as GWR chief engineer also saw him pioneer innovations in rolling stock and station design: he introduced the first bogie-mounted passenger carriages to reduce lateral sway on high-speed runs, and designed the original Temple Meads station in Bristol as a single-span hammerbeam-roofed train shed that eliminated obstructive supporting columns on the platform level. Though the 1846 Gauge Act would mandate standard gauge for all new railway construction in Britain, effectively ruling out the expansion of Brunel’s broad gauge network (the last broad gauge services ran in 1892), the GWR main line he engineered remains in continuous high-speed use as part of the UK’s intercity rail network, a testament to his refusal to compromise long-term performance for short-term cost savings.
