Project Title: Millvale Echoes: Capturing the Unheard Voices of Millvale Borough’s Working-Class River Heritage
Submitted To: Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission Local History Grant Program
Submitted By: Millvale Public Library, 213 Grant Ave, Millvale, PA 15209
Requested Funding: $14,875 | Project Period: January 15–December 15, 2025

Millvale Public Library serves 3,722 residents in the river borough tucked along the Allegheny River’s north bank, across from Pittsburgh’s Lawrenceville neighborhood. For 112 years, our stacks have held census records, newspaper clippings, and company archives documenting Millvale’s life as a 20th-century industrial hub—but 70% of those materials center mill owners, elected officials, and civic leaders, with almost no record of the people who made the borough run: the 1,200 union steelworkers who staffed the Jones & Laughlin Mill until its 1982 closure, the Eastern European and Black domestic workers who commuted to Pittsburgh’s East End through the 1960s, the flood survivors who rebuilt after the 1936 St. Patrick’s Day flood and 2004 Hurricane Ivan inundation, and the queer residents who ran underground social spaces in the borough before Pennsylvania’s 1980 anti-discrimination ordinance passed.

Millvale Echoes will fill that gap. Over 12 months, part-time project coordinator Elena Marquez—a Millvale native and public historian whose 2022 documentary *Beneath the Mill Smokestacks* won the Pittsburgh City Paper’s Best Local History Award—will train 12 local high school volunteers from Millvale Junior/Senior High School in oral history ethics, audio recording, and archival processing, per Oral History Association guidelines. The team will conduct 45 90-minute interviews with residents aged 65 and older, recruited via the Millvale Senior Center, local church congregations, and the borough’s three remaining labor union locals (USW Local 1211, IBEW Local 5, and AFSCME Local 251). We have already secured written pre-commitments from 27 interviewees, including 89-year-old retired J&L crane operator Joe Zaluska, who helped organize the mill’s 1959 strike; 78-year-old Ruthie Carter, who ran the borough’s first integrated soul food diner on Sheridan Avenue from 1972 to 1996; and 82-year-old former flood warden Bill Novak, who coordinated boat rescues during Hurricane Ivan.

Grant funds will cover: $9,200 for Marquez’s 10 hours/week stipend; $1,800 for high-quality Tascam audio recorders, lapel mics, and archival cloud storage; $1,200 for printed interview transcripts and accessibility accommodations (ASL interpretation, large-print transcripts for hard-of-hearing interviewees); $1,675 for a free public launch event at the Millvale Community Center on October 11, 2025, where interviewees will share short clips and receive free copies of their recordings; and $1,000 for a dedicated public portal on the library’s website, where all interviews will be streamable for free, with keyword search and lesson plans aligned to Pennsylvania 4th-grade state history standards for use in local schools.

Millvale’s senior population is declining at a rate of 4.2% annually, per 2023 Allegheny County health data; 19 long-term residents over 70 died between 2021 and 2024, taking with them unrecorded stories of the borough’s labor, civil rights, and disaster resilience history. This project will not only preserve those stories for future generations, but will build intergenerational connection: the student volunteers will earn service learning credit, and interviewees will have the chance to see their lives centered in the borough’s official historical record, rather than sidelined. We have already secured $5,200 in in-kind matching funds from the Millvale Historical Society (archival processing support) and local coffee shop 412 Brew (catering for volunteer trainings and the launch event), meeting the commission’s 25% match requirement. At the project’s close, all recordings and transcripts will be deposited both in the library’s local history room and the Pennsylvania State Archives, ensuring permanent public access.

title: travel guide|two days in Lisbon on a budget
text:
Two Days in Lisbon on a Budget  
Lisbon rewards slow, curious travel on modest means: its richest pleasures—sunlit miradouros, cobblestoned old quarters, Atlantic light, and simple, ingredient-led food—rarely require lavish spending. This two-day itinerary centres on walkable historic neighbourhoods, low-cost public transit, and freely accessible public space, with an estimated core cost (excluding accommodation and international travel) of €55–€70 per person. It prioritises value without cutting corners on the city’s defining culture, architecture, and food. Practical assumptions are based on 2024 local pricing; small surcharges may apply in peak summer or at major festival periods. A reusable water bottle is essential, as tap water is safe and public fountains are widespread across central districts.  

 Planning and transit basics  
Lisbon’s hills make unbroken walking tiring, but its centre remains highly navigable with a Viva Viagem/ Navegante card (€0.50 one-time fee). Add a 24-hour public transport pass for €6.80, covering buses, trams, metro, and funiculars, or use single fares at €1.85–€3.10 depending on mode. For two days, one 24-hour pass used across the busiest transit day plus a handful of singles is usually cheaper than two full passes. Budget stays concentrate in Martim Moniz, Anjos, Intendente, and Alfama’s outer edges; hostels commonly offer dorm beds from €18–€30, while basic guesthouses and budget rooms begin around €45–€70 double outside peak season. Avoid taxis for routine journeys; metro from Aeroporto Humberto Delgado reaches central Lisbon in about 20 minutes for under €2, depending on ticket type and zone rules.  

 Day one: Alfama, Sé, and the Tagus riverside  
Begin early in Alfama, Lisbon’s oldest district, before narrow lanes fill with tour groups and midday heat. The neighbourhood itself is free to explore: alleys, tiled facades, laundry strung between windows, and sudden views toward the Tagus define the walk. Follow Rua de São João da Praça toward the Sé de Lisboa, the city’s austere Romanesque cathedral. Admission to the main church is free; cloisters and the treasury carry separate fees, but travellers on a tight budget may skip them without missing the essential visit.  

From the Sé, climb or take short uphill sections toward Miradouro de Santa Luzia and Miradouro das Portas do Sol, two of Lisbon’s finest free viewpoints. Santa Luzia’s bougainvillea, tile panels, and terracotta rooftops make it especially rewarding in morning light; Portas do Sol offers a broader panorama over Alfama and the river. Continue to the Castelo de São Jorge perimeter if time allows, but note that castle entry costs around €15–€20. Budget travellers should instead trace the castle-facing lanes and enjoy views from adjacent streets, reserving paid entry only when medieval battlements are a personal priority.  

For lunch, seek neighbourhood tasca staples rather than riverside terraces with marked-up menus. A lunch-prato do dia, or daily set dish, often costs €8–€12 and may include soup or a drink. Reliable choices include grilled fish, caldo verde, carne de porco à alentejana, or a simple omelette with salad. Near Alfama’s edges, busy bakeries sell savoury pastries such as bifana pork sandwiches or empadas for €2–€4, useful for a lighter meal.  

In the afternoon, descend toward Praça do Comércio, Lisbon’s grand riverfront square, framed by yellow arcades and an equestrian statue of José I. Walking the square and riverside is free. Continue along the refurbished Tagus promenade toward Cais do Sodré; the Ribeira das Naus area is ideal for resting and watching ferries move across the water. If transit legs are sore, use the 24-hour pass for the E15 tram along the river rather than paying for a sightseeing tram. The famous E28 can be crowded and is not automatically better than walking or using less famous routes.  

For dinner, choose a simple tasca away from the most photographed Alfama lanes. Petiscos—Portugal’s answer to sharing plates—can make an economical meal: chouriço assado, grilled peppers, olives, cheese, bread, and clams or octopus salad shared between two may cost €12–€18 per person with a drink. Do not assume every placed starter is complimentary; in Portugal, couvert items brought to the table are often charged if eaten. Politely decline anything not ordered. End the evening near Miradouro de Santa Catarina in Bica/Chiado, where sunset, buskers, and river views cost nothing. A café bica, as espresso is commonly called, usually costs €0.80–€1.50.

text:
The English Football League has imposed a £125,000 fine on second-tier side Millerfield United, with a further £75,000 suspended for two seasons, after hundreds of supporters invaded the pitch following the club’s final-day promotion win last month, marking one of the harshest pitch invasion penalties handed to an EFL club in the past decade.
An independent regulatory panel concluded the club failed to implement adequate pre-match safety planning, did not deploy sufficient trained stewards to block pitch access points, and failed to issue repeated, clear warnings to fans in the minutes after full-time, when a 2-1 win over local rivals Harthill Town clinched Millerfield’s first promotion to the Premier League in 22 years.
Footage shared widely on social media in the aftermath of the 18 May fixture showed more than 400 fans climbing over advertising hoardings within 10 seconds of the final whistle, with dozens swarming players, coaching staff and match officials. The EFL confirmed three match stewards sustained minor injuries in the crush, two Harthill players reported being verbally abused and having items of kit stolen, and a section of the away end segregation barrier was damaged when a small group of home fans attempted to reach travelling supporters. The fixture was also halted for 23 minutes while officials cleared the pitch, delaying the post-match trophy presentation and leading to 12 arrests by West Mercia Police for public order offences.
In a written ruling published on Wednesday, the panel rejected Millerfield United’s initial claim that the invasion was an “unforeseeable, spontaneous outpouring of joy”, noting club leadership had been repeatedly warned by safety advisory groups in the lead-up to the high-stakes fixture that fan messaging around post-match celebrations had been overly permissive. The club had advertised a planned post-match pitch parade for players on social media in the week before the game, which the panel found “created a reasonable expectation among supporters that pitch access would be permitted at full time”, despite no formal safety certificate for such an event being approved.
Millerfield United chief executive Diane Hale said in a statement the club accepted the ruling unreservedly, and would not appeal the penalty. “We know the scenes at full time, while born of decades of waiting for this moment, put people at risk, undermined the hard work of our players and staff, and failed to live up to the standards our community expects of us,” Hale said. “The full £125,000 fine will be ringfenced from our club community budget, and we will be rolling out enhanced fan education, new pitch access barriers, and a dedicated steward training programme ahead of our first top-flight season, alongside a lifetime ban for the 12 fans charged with public order offences related to the invasion.”
The EFL’s chief operating officer, Mark Sutcliffe, said the penalty sent a clear message that pitch invasions would not be treated as harmless celebration, amid a 35% rise in reported pitch encroachment incidents across the top four English divisions in the 2023-24 season. “We understand the passion that drives fans at decisive moments in the season, but pitch invasions carry very real risks of serious harm to players, staff, stewards and fellow supporters,” Sutcliffe said. “Clubs bear a clear responsibility to plan for high-stakes fixtures, and to send unambiguous messaging that entering the playing surface without permission will lead to serious consequences, both for individual fans and for the clubs they support.”
Harthill Town said in a short statement it welcomed the ruling, and had been in contact with the two players targeted by fans to offer additional welfare support. West Mercia Police said investigations into a further seven individuals identified from social media footage as having taken part in aggressive behaviour during the invasion were ongoing. SoundPeats Space Pro: Three Months With the $79.99 Headphones That Refuse to Embarrass Me
Purchased March 3, 2024, Amazon | Tested through June 2, 2024 | Commute: 45 minutes each way on Chicago’s Red Line

I bought the SoundPeats Space Pro on a rainy Sunday after my 2022 Sony WH-CH710N split its headband at the Roosevelt Road station, 10 minutes before I was due to lead a client onboarding call. My budget cap was $100, and I picked these over the highly rated Anker Soundcore Life Q30 for one specific reason: SoundPeats listed a 40-hour ANC battery life on the box, compared to the Q30’s 30. Three months, 12 Red Line round-trips a week, and 27 hours of work calls later, that spec wasn’t marketing fluff—and neither were most of the claims that made me click “buy.”

Let’s start with the noise cancellation, because that’s the whole reason anyone shops this category. I ran an unscientific but consistent test every weekday for the first month: I played my usual commute playlist at 55% volume, the level I used with my old Sony, and noted when I could make out announcements or track rattle. The Space Pro’s hybrid ANC cuts 80% of the low-end train rumble between Lake and Grand stops, right in line with SoundPeats’ stated 35dB max noise reduction. The high-pitched screech of the Red Line’s older 2600-series cars still cuts through, as do bus turn signals and baristas calling names at my regular Wicker Park coffee shop, but that’s true of every pair under $150 I tested at Best Buy on February 28. Transparency mode is genuinely useful too: I can order a oat milk latte without yanking the ear cup off, and I never miss my building’s front door intercom when I’m on a work call from my apartment.

Battery life has been the biggest surprise. I charge them for 10 minutes every Sunday night on my Anker 511 Nano charger, and I only hit 12% battery once: on May 17, after a week of forgetting to charge, 12 total hours of use, and ANC left on accidentally overnight. The advertised 40-hour figure tracks: I get 38 hours with ANC on and volume at 60%, 47 hours with ANC off, per the battery readout in the SoundPeats app. Multipoint pairing works without the stutters that plagued my old Sony: they switch from my iPhone 14 to my 2020 M1 MacBook Pro in about two seconds, which saved me on a April 22 client call when my phone rang mid-presentation.

They’re not perfect. The plastic headband picks up scuffs if you toss them in a backpack unprotected (I have three faint white marks from my water bottle by week two). The default bass is muddy on 90s hip-hop: I had to set the app equalizer to -2dB sub-bass, +1dB midrange to make *Illmatic* sound like it should. At 258 grams, they’re 12 grams lighter than the Q30, but I still get a faint pressure on the crown of my head after three straight hours of calls, fixed by adjusting the headband one notch looser.

For $79.99, these don’t compete with $300 Sony XM5s—but they don’t have to. They survived three months of Chicago commutes, rain spills, and back-to-back work calls without a single glitch, and they’ve already outlasted the pair that cost me twice as much two years ago. If you don’t need studio-grade ANC and hate wasting money on overhyped flagship markup, they’re the easiest pick in the mid-range.

Policy Brief: Closing the Nutritional Gap for Rural Kenyan Children
 Section 2: Systemic Barriers to Equitable Child Nutrition in Arid and Semi-Arid (ASAL) and High-Potential Agricultural Zones
The 2022 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey (KDHS) confirms that 26% of children under five in rural areas suffer from chronic stunting, 11% from acute wasting, and 34% from vitamin A deficiency—rates 2.3 times higher than those recorded in urban Nairobi and its peri-urban settlements. While the Government of Kenya’s 2019 National Food and Nutrition Security Policy (NFNSP) set a target to reduce stunting to 15% by 2030, implementation gaps across rural counties have left 1.8 million children at elevated risk of irreversible cognitive impairment, reduced educational attainment, and intergenerational poverty. This section outlines three interconnected structural barriers that undermine progress toward these targets, drawing on 18 months of primary data collected by the Rural Livelihoods and Nutrition Alliance (RLNA) across 12 counties in the ASAL and Western Kenya highlands.
First, fragmented delivery of community-based nutrition interventions erodes coverage of life-saving services for the most vulnerable households. The NFNSP mandates that Community Health Volunteers (CHVs) deliver quarterly growth monitoring, micronutrient supplementation, and infant and young child feeding (IYCF) counseling to all caregivers of children under two, the critical 1,000-day window for long-term development. But RLNA surveys found that 41% of rural CHVs serve catchment areas of more than 100 households, exceeding the Ministry of Health’s recommended ratio of 1:50, and 68% report going three months or more without receiving stipends for transport or airtime to conduct home visits. In Turkana and Marsabit counties, recurrent drought-related population displacement means that 53% of acutely malnourished children are not registered in the national Community Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) program, as CHVs lack the mobility to track mobile pastoralist households.
Second, low agricultural diversity and post-harvest loss cut off household access to nutrient-dense foods even in food-secure regions. In Western Kenya’s high-potential maize-growing zones, 72% of smallholder households rely on maize as their primary staple, with less than 15% cultivating leafy green vegetables, legumes, or orange-fleshed sweet potato on their plots, per RLNA 2023 agricultural surveys. Post-harvest losses for perishable nutrient-dense crops reach 48% in Busia and Kakamega counties, due to lack of access to low-cost solar cooling storage and limited local market linkages for small-scale producers. While the government’s fertilizer subsidy program has boosted maize yields by 18% since 2022, it does not include provisions for subsidized seeds for micronutrient-rich crops, entrenching a production system that prioritizes caloric sufficiency over nutritional quality.
Third, weak regulatory enforcement of food safety and labeling standards exposes rural children to elevated risk of contaminated and nutritionally poor complementary foods. A 2024 RLNA market survey of 240 rural retail outlets across eight counties found that 62% of commercially sold complementary porridge flours failed to meet Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) requirements for minimum iron and zinc content, while 38% contained aflatoxin levels exceeding WHO safe limits, a known contributor to stunting and immune suppression. Unlike urban areas, where county public health officers conduct quarterly food safety inspections, 71% of rural retail outlets reported not having received an inspection in more than two years, due to understaffing and limited transport budgets for county health departments.
These barriers are not insurmountable, but they require a shift away from siloed, donor-funded short-term projects toward coordinated, county-led investment that links health system strengthening, agricultural livelihood support, and regulatory enforcement. Without targeted action to close these gaps, rural Kenya will remain off track to meet both NFNSP targets and the Sustainable Development Goal 2 targets for zero hunger by 2030.

text:
Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America, in Congress assembled,

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Data Breach Disclosure Act of 2025."

SEC. 2. FINDINGS AND PURPOSE.
(a) The Congress finds the following:
(1) Personal data is a cornerstone of modern commerce, civic life, and national security.
(2) Unauthorized access to or acquisition of sensitive personal information can cause identity theft, financial fraud, reputational harm, and loss of public trust.
(3) Timely notification enables individuals, regulators, and law enforcement to mitigate harm, preserve evidence, and prevent further misuse.
(4) Existing state notification laws create inconsistent obligations and compliance burdens for covered entities.
(b) The purpose of this Act is to establish a uniform national requirement that covered entities provide clear, prompt, and accurate notice following the discovery of a data breach affecting personal information.

SEC. 3. DEFINITIONS.
For purposes of this Act:
(1) COVERED ENTITY. — The term "covered entity" means any person, corporation, partnership, association, governmental body, or other organization that collects, maintains, stores, processes, or sells electronic personal information of residents of the United States.
(2) PERSONAL INFORMATION. — The term "personal information" means an individual's first name or first initial and last name, in combination with one or more of the following unencrypted or unredacted data elements:
(A) Social Security number, taxpayer identification number, passport number, or other government-issued identification number;
(B) financial account number, credit card number, or debit card number, together with any required security code, access code, or password that would permit access to an account;
(C) unique biometric data;
(D) username or email address in combination with a password or security question and answer that would permit access to an online account; or
(E) health information as defined under applicable federal health privacy law.
(3) BREACH OF SECURITY. — The term "breach of security" means an unauthorized acquisition or access to computerized data that compromises the security, confidentiality, or integrity of personal information. Good-faith acquisition by an employee or agent for legitimate business purposes does not constitute a breach if the information is not used or further disclosed in an unauthorized manner.
(4) DETERMINATION. — A covered entity shall be deemed to have discovered a breach when it knows or reasonably should know that a breach has occurred.

SEC. 4. NOTIFICATION REQUIREMENT.
(a) IN GENERAL. — A covered entity that experiences a breach of security shall notify the Federal Trade Commission and each affected individual whose personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired or accessed without authorization not later than 72 hours after discovery.
(b) LAW ENFORCEMENT DELAY. — Notification may be delayed only if a federal, state, local, or tribal law enforcement agency determines in writing that notification would impede a criminal investigation or jeopardize national or cybersecurity security. The delay shall extend only for the period reasonably necessary to address the stated concern. The covered entity shall provide required notification promptly after that basis no longer exists.
(c) CONTENT. — Notification shall include, to the extent known: a description of the breach; categories and approximate number of individuals and records involved; types of personal information involved; steps taken to contain and remediate the incident; steps individuals may take to protect themselves; contact information for the covered entity; and information regarding credit monitoring or identity protection services when financial or Social Security numbers are involved.
(d) METHOD. — Individual notice shall be provided by email, first-class mail, or, where permitted, conspicuous electronic communication. Substitute notice may be used if direct contact information is unavailable, the cost of direct notice exceeds $250,000, or more than 500,000 individuals are affected.

SEC. 5. ENFORCEMENT AND PENALTIES.
The Federal Trade Commission shall prescribe regulations and enforce this Act. A covered entity that fails to provide timely notice without a reasonable basis or permitted law enforcement delay shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $100 per affected individual per day, capped at $5,000,000 per breach. Knowing or reckless violations shall be subject to penalties of not more than $1,500 per affected individual per day, capped at $15,000,000 per breach. Penalty amounts shall be adjusted periodically for inflation.

SEC. 6. RELATIONSHIP TO OTHER LAWS.
This Act supersedes inconsistent state data breach notification statutes and regulations, except that state attorneys general may bring actions on behalf of state residents to enforce this Act. Nothing in this Act shall limit obligations under sector-specific federal laws that provide equal or greater protection.

SEC. 7. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment and shall apply to breaches discovered on or after that date.

ONE HUNDRED EIGHTEENTH CONGRESS OF THE UNITED STATES
AT THE FIRST SESSION
H. R. 1287
To require entities that collect, process, or store personal identifying information of United States residents to notify affected individuals and relevant regulatory bodies of qualifying data breaches within 72 hours of breach confirmation, and for other purposes.

Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled,

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the “72-Hour Data Breach Disclosure Act of 2025”.

SEC. 2. FINDINGS AND PURPOSE.
(a) Findings. Congress finds that: (1) Unauthorized access to personal identifying information poses growing, measurable harm to U.S. residents, including identity theft, financial fraud, reputational damage, and emotional distress; (2) Existing state-level breach notification rules create a fragmented compliance framework, with reporting windows ranging from 30 days to no mandatory timeline, delaying critical protective action for consumers; (3) Delayed breach disclosure allows malicious actors to exploit stolen data for extended periods, increasing average consumer loss per incident by an estimated 37 percent per Federal Trade Commission (FTC) 2024 data; (4) A uniform, 72-hour notification standard aligns U.S. data protection norms with global best practices while reducing compliance burdens for covered entities operating across state lines.
(b) Purpose. The purpose of this Act is to establish a clear, uniform national requirement for timely data breach notification, enable affected individuals to take immediate steps to secure their personal information, and reduce systemic harm from preventable data security failures.

SEC. 3. DEFINITIONS.
For purposes of this Act: (1) “Covered entity” means any individual, partnership, corporation, nonprofit organization, or government agency that collects, processes, or stores personal identifying information of 1,000 or more U.S. residents annually, excluding national security agencies operating under classified authority. (2) “Personal identifying information” means any combination of data that can be used to identify a specific individual, including full name paired with a Social Security number, financial account number, health record, government-issued identification number, biometric identifier, or unique account login credential that grants access to financial or personal services. (3) “Qualifying data breach” means any confirmed incident of unauthorized access, acquisition, or disclosure of unencrypted personal identifying information that compromises the security, confidentiality, or integrity of such data, excluding incidents where the covered entity can demonstrate that access was accidental, by an authorized party, and no misuse of data has occurred or is reasonably likely to occur.

SEC. 4. MANDATORY NOTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS.
(a) Timing. Upon confirming a qualifying data breach, a covered entity shall provide required notifications no later than 72 hours following such confirmation. For purposes of this subsection, confirmation occurs when the covered entity has a reasonable basis to conclude that a qualifying breach has occurred, regardless of whether the full scope of the breach or total number of affected individuals has been determined.
(b) Notification Recipients. Covered entities shall notify: (1) All affected U.S. residents whose personal identifying information was reasonably determined to be subject to the breach, using clear, plain-language communication delivered via first-class mail, email (where the individual has consented to electronic communication), or prominent public notice if more than 500,000 individuals are affected to ensure timely receipt; (2) The Federal Trade Commission, which shall maintain a centralized public database of reported breaches and coordinate with state attorney general offices to avoid redundant reporting requirements; (3) National credit reporting agencies, if a breach affects more than 5,000 residents, to enable proactive fraud alert placement at no cost to affected individuals.
(c) Required Notification Content. All individual notifications shall include a plain-language description of the nature of the breach, the categories of data accessed, steps the entity has taken to contain the breach, recommended actions for individuals to protect themselves from harm, and a dedicated point of contact for questions related to the incident.

SEC. 5. ENFORCEMENT AND PENALTIES.
(a) The Federal Trade Commission shall enforce compliance with this Act pursuant to its authority under the Federal Trade Commission Act. Violations shall be treated as unfair or deceptive acts or practices under section 5 of such Act.
(b) Civil penalties for failure to comply with notification requirements shall not exceed $100 per affected individual per day of delayed notification, up to a maximum of $150 million per qualifying breach, adjusted annually for inflation. Penalties shall be waived only if a covered entity can demonstrate that delay was necessary to support active federal law enforcement investigations or prevent further compromise of system security, with written documentation provided to the FTC within the initial 72-hour window to qualify for such exception.

SEC. 6. PREEMPTION.
This Act supersedes any provision of state or local law relating to data breach notification timelines, but shall not preempt state laws that provide additional consumer protections related to data security standards or private rights of action for harms resulting from data breaches.

SEC. 7. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

Configuring Parental Controls on Home Network Routers
Technical Documentation Section | Network Security & Family Safety Suite  
*Version 2.1 – Last Updated: October 2024*

---

 7. Router-Level Parental Control Configuration

Router-level parental controls provide network-wide content filtering, access scheduling, and activity monitoring for all connected devices, eliminating the need for per-device configuration and preventing circumvention via unmanaged client settings. This section outlines standardized configuration procedures for compliant home routers (802.11ac/ax, firmware v3.1.0 or later), including prerequisite validation, policy definition, rule enforcement, and verification workflows.

 7.1 Prerequisite Preparation
Before modifying control configurations, complete the following pre-flight checks to avoid service disruption:
1.  Confirm administrative access to the router web management interface (default gateway address typically printed on the device label; standard private ranges: `192.168.0.1`, `192.168.1.1`, `192.168.8.1`). Authenticate using the unique administrative credential (default credentials must be changed prior to policy deployment to prevent unauthorized modification).
2.  Inventory all connected client devices via the router’s Attached Devices / DHCP Client List. Record each device’s hostname, MAC address, assigned IP address, and primary user (e.g., "Child-Tablet", "School-Chromebook", "Gaming-Console"). Assign static IP reservations or fixed DHCP leases for all child-assigned devices to prevent IP changes from breaking access rules.
3.  Update router firmware to the latest stable release to patch known control bypass vulnerabilities and ensure support for modern category filtering.
4.  Back up the current running configuration to a local encrypted storage volume, enabling rollback in the event of misconfiguration.

 7.2 Policy Definition & Device Grouping
Granular controls rely on logical device grouping to apply age-appropriate rules rather than blanket network restrictions.
1.  Nav to the Parental Controls / Access Restriction module in the management interface.
2.  Create distinct user/device profiles aligned with household requirements (e.g., *Young Child*, *Teen*, *Unrestricted Adult*). Assign the inventoried child devices to corresponding groups using their reserved IP or MAC hardware address. Note that devices using randomized MAC addresses (common on iOS 14+/Android 10+) must have private address disabled for the home SSID to maintain consistent group mapping.
3.  Define content filtering rules by category:
    - Mandatory high-risk blocks: Malware, phishing, anonymizer/VPN/proxy sites, and explicit adult content.
    - Age-based optional blocks: Social media, streaming video, online gaming, gambling, and user-generated content platforms.
    - Enable safe-search enforcement at the DNS layer to force filtered results for Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, and supported YouTube restricted mode.
    Administrators may add custom allow/block lists for specific domains; wildcard entries (e.g., `*.example.com`) apply rules to all subdomains.

 7.3 Time-Based Access Scheduling
Network access schedules enforce bedtime, school hours, and homework-time restrictions independent of content filters:
1.  For each restricted profile, define weekly time schedules using 24-hour format, specifying both *allowed access windows* or *blocked access windows*.
2.  Configure differentiated rules for weekdays and weekends; recommend hard blackout periods overnight (e.g., 22:00–06:30) and school hours on instructional days.
3.  Optional: Configure daily total usage quotas (in 15-minute increments) and temporary bypass codes for supervised extended use. Avoid applying full internet blocks to critical infrastructure devices (security cameras, smart thermostats, medical devices), which should be placed in an unrestricted device group.

 7.4 Enforcement, Logging, and Verification
Most consumer routers enforce filtering via DNS sinkholing and layer-3/4 access control lists; advanced models support deep packet inspection (DPI) for application-level blocking.
1.  Enable HTTPS/DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) blocking on the router to prevent client devices from bypassing filters via encrypted third-party DNS. For enhanced reliability, configure upstream filtered public DNS (e.g., family-focused DNS resolvers) in WAN settings.
2.  Enable connection and filtering event logging, with logs retained locally or forwarded to a designated monitoring email. Logs record blocked domain attempts, schedule trigger events, and device online/offline status.
3.  Validate deployment from a restricted test device:
    - Attempt to access a known blocked category domain to confirm the block page renders.
    - Verify safe search is forced on search engines.
    - Test schedule enforcement by temporarily setting a 1-minute blocked window to confirm connectivity drops and restores as configured.
    - Confirm that connecting via a public VPN does not bypass category rules.

 7.5 Limitations and Complementary Controls
Router parental controls cannot filter content within encrypted traffic end-to-end, distinguish between multiple users on a shared device, or block content on cellular networks that bypass the home Wi-Fi. For complete coverage, supplement router rules with device-native screen time tools, platform-level parental controls, and periodic household policy review. Save and activate the configuration after all testing, and retain an offline copy of the final rule set for disaster recovery.

title: court opinion summary|a dispute over a contractor's failure to complete a home renovation
text:
This matter comes before the court on plaintiff Elara Mendez’s breach of contract claim against defendant Horizon Home Renovations LLC, arising from the contractor’s alleged failure to complete a residential kitchen and primary bathroom renovation at Mendez’s suburban Cook County home, for which Mendez paid $78,250 of the $82,000 fixed contract price in advance of final completion. The court has reviewed the executed contract, project correspondence, photographic evidence, independent construction inspection reports, and testimony from both parties and a third-party licensed contractor retained by Mendez to remediate outstanding defects, and issues the following findings and ruling.
First, the court finds the executed April 2023 contract between the parties is valid and enforceable, with explicit terms requiring Horizon to complete all specified scope of work—including custom cabinet installation, waterproof bathroom tiling, electrical outlet relocation, and appliance hookups—within 12 weeks of project commencement, with final payment of $3,750 due only after Mendez completed a walkthrough and signed a certificate of substantial completion. Testimony confirms Horizon commenced work on April 17, 2023, but by the contracted July 10, 2023, completion date, crews had abandoned the site after Mendez refused repeated requests for advance payment of the remaining final balance to cover what Horizon claimed were unanticipated supply cost overruns. The independent inspection report entered into evidence confirms 42 percent of the contracted scope remained incomplete as of mid-August 2023, including unleveled tile that posed a slip hazard, unconnected dishwasher and gas range lines, missing cabinet hardware, improperly vented bathroom exhaust fans that created a mold risk, and exposed wiring that violated local residential building codes.
Horizon argued at trial that Mendez had constructively breached the contract first by making repeated out-of-scope change requests that delayed work, and that supply chain disruptions for custom cabinetry constituted a force majeure event excusing delayed performance. The court rejects both arguments: evidence shows all change requests Mendez submitted were documented in signed change orders with adjusted timelines that Horizon itself approved, and the contract explicitly excluded ordinary material supply delays from force majeure protections, requiring Horizon to source alternative materials at its own cost if preferred supplies were unavailable. The court further finds Horizon’s demand for early final payment before completing contracted work violated explicit payment terms, and its unilateral decision to demobilize from the site without providing required 10-day written notice of work stoppage constituted a material breach of contract.
For remedies, the court awards Mendez $47,900 in direct damages, covering the full cost to remediate code violations and complete remaining work with the third-party contractor, plus $2,100 in temporary housing costs Mendez incurred when unconnected plumbing left her home uninhabitable for 10 days during the remediation period. The court declines to award Mendez’s requested $15,000 in emotional distress damages, as Illinois law does not allow non-economic damages for straightforward commercial contract disputes absent evidence of willful or wanton conduct, which the record does not support here. The court further awards Mendez $1,200 in court filing fees, but denies her request for attorney fees, as the contract does not contain a prevailing party fee-shifting provision. All claims and counterclaims between the parties are dismissed with prejudice upon entry of this judgment.

title: op-ed column|why cities should ban cars from their historic centres
text:
Why Cities Should Ban Cars from Their Historic Centres

The daily ritual of cars clogging historic city centers has become an intolerable contradiction to the very purpose these districts serve. In Rome, the Colosseum stands amid traffic fumes; in Prague, medieval lanes echo with engine noise; in Mexico City, colonial architecture suffers constant vibration damage. The time has come for municipalities worldwide to implement comprehensive car bans in historic centers—not as temporary experiments, but as permanent commitments to preserving humanity’s shared urban heritage.

Historic districts represent irreplaceable cultural assets that suffer irreversible damage from motor vehicle traffic. Air pollution accelerates stone erosion, discolors facades, and weakens structural foundations. The Parthenon’s marble degradation, caused partly by vehicle emissions, exemplifies this threat. Constant traffic vibrations undermine ancient foundations, while street-level parking obscures architectural vistas that took centuries to create. These centers were designed for human interaction, not mechanical transport, and allowing cars to dominate them amounts to cultural vandalism sanctioned by bureaucratic inertia.

Beyond preservation, pedestrianization delivers profound economic benefits. Evidence from over fifty European cities demonstrates that banning cars increases local commerce by fifteen to thirty percent. Copenhagen’s Stroget, transformed into a car-free zone in 1962, now ranks among Scandinavia’s most successful retail streets. Visitors linger longer, residents reclaim public spaces, and cafes expand into sidewalks that once hosted parked vehicles. Property values rise, tourism quality improves, and healthcare costs decline as air quality improves—creating a virtuous cycle of sustainable urban prosperity.

Public health considerations strengthen this case decisively. The World Health Organization estimates that traffic-related air pollution kills seven million people annually, with historic center residents facing disproportionate exposure due to narrow streets that trap pollutants. Nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter cause asthma in children, cardiovascular disease in adults, and cognitive impairment across populations. Eliminating cars removes these hazards while encouraging walking and cycling—simple activities that combat sedentary lifestyles and associated conditions like obesity and diabetes.

Critics raise legitimate concerns about accessibility, particularly for elderly residents and emergency services. Yet these challenges possess proven solutions. Electric shuttle systems, restricted permits for residents, and strategically placed underground garages preserve mobility without sacrificing environmental goals. Venice, despite its unique aquatic geography, demonstrates how essential services can function through coordinated delivery windows and specialized vehicles. Meanwhile, improved public transit connections ensure that visitors and workers reach historic centers efficiently, reducing rather than increasing overall travel times.

The psychological and social dimensions deserve equal attention. Historic squares currently dominated by parked cars become sites of human connection when pedestrianized. Children play safely, neighbors converse spontaneously, and strangers share experiences in spaces designed for community. This restoration of public life counters the social isolation characterizing modern cities while maintaining the authentic atmosphere that draws people to historic districts in the first place.

Implementing car-free zones requires political courage, not technological innovation. Cities must coordinate transit improvements, support affected businesses through transition periods, and engage communities in planning processes. Freiburg, Germany, and Pontevedra, Spain, offer blueprints where pedestrianization transformed declining centers into vibrant neighborhoods. Their success reflects consistent policy, adequate investment in alternatives, and willingness to prioritize people over vehicles.

The climate crisis adds urgency to this agenda. Transportation accounts for twenty-four percent of global carbon emissions, and urban journeys through historic districts typically involve short trips ideal for walking, cycling, or electric public transport. Banning cars in these zones reduces emissions directly while signaling broader commitment to sustainable mobility. It aligns cultural preservation with climate action, demonstrating that addressing environmental challenges can enhance rather than diminish urban living standards.

Historic city centers belong not merely to current residents but to generations past who built them and generations future who deserve to experience them. Allowing private automobiles to dominate these spaces privileges temporary convenience over millennial heritage, individual comfort over collective wellbeing, and destructive habits over enlightened policy. Cities that have already pedestrianized their historic centers report no regret—only wonder at why change took so long. The question is no longer whether car bans make sense, but why so many cities still delay the inevitable. Our urban ancestors designed these spaces for people. The twenty-first century must return them to their original purpose.

title: legislative bill summary|a bill to expand tax credits for small businesses that hire apprentices
text:
U.S. House of Representatives Bill Summary: H.R. 4271, the Skilled Trades Apprenticeship Expansion Act of 2024  
Introduced March 14, 2024, by Rep. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI-7), co-sponsored by Rep. David Valadao (R-CA-22) and 28 bipartisan Members  
Date of Markup: House Ways & Means Committee, April 18, 2024

This bill revises and expands the long-underutilized Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC) for small businesses hiring registered apprentices, addressing a 2023 Department of Labor (DOL) finding that 61% of small construction, manufacturing, and home health firms cannot afford to take on apprentices despite facing 870,000 unfilled skilled trades positions nationwide. The existing WOTC for apprentices, established in 2008, offers a maximum $1,200 credit per hire, with 72% of eligible small firms surveyed by the National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB) in 2023 reporting they had never claimed it due to overly strict eligibility rules and low credit value.

First, H.R. 4271 triples the base credit for firms with 50 or fewer full-time equivalent employees to $3,500 per qualifying apprentice hired after September 1, 2024, provided the apprentice remains employed in a DOL-registered apprenticeship program for at least 12 months and completes a minimum of 2,000 hours of on-the-job training plus 144 hours of required classroom instruction. The credit climbs to $5,000 per hire for businesses that hire apprentices from underrepresented groups in skilled trades: women, veterans, people with disabilities, Opportunity Zone residents, and individuals who aged out of the foster care system. Firms with 51 to 250 employees qualify for a scaled credit of $2,000 per apprentice, up from the current $1,200, with the same $1,500 bonus for hires from the targeted groups.

Unlike the existing credit, which only applies to the first year of employment, H.R. 4271 adds a second-year retention credit of $1,500 for all qualifying small firms, if the apprentice completes their second year of the program and remains on the job at a wage at least 20% above the local entry-level rate for their trade. The bill also eliminates two widely criticized barriers to access: it waives the requirement that businesses prove they would not have hired the apprentice “but for” the credit, and sets aside $22 million annually through 2030 for state workforce agencies to help small business owners file for the credit, including free tax prep clinics run by local Small Business Development Centers.

A Congressional Budget Office (CBO) score released April 11, 2024, estimates the bill will cost $1.28 billion over 10 years, offset by projected reductions in federal unemployment and public assistance spending as apprentices move into full-time trades roles paying a median $55,000 annual wage after program completion. CBO projects the credit will support 124,000 new apprenticeship hires over the next decade, 42% of them in rural counties where DOL data shows apprenticeship access is currently 38% lower than in metro areas. The bill includes carve-outs preventing large firms with more than 250 employees from claiming the credit, and requires annual GAO audits to ensure no firms claim credits for apprentices enrolled in unregistered or sham training programs.
